questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby assessed 5 minutes after birth is found to be pink, with blue extremities, and irregular respiration. Heart rate is 80 beats per minute. There is grimace and some flexion. What is the Apgar score for this baby?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 5

The Apgar score for this baby will be 5.

• Color; body pink, extremities blue: score-1
• Heart rate; 80 beats per minute: score 1
• Grimace: Score-1
• Some flexion: Score-1
• Irregular respiration: Score-1

The Apgar score is a systematic way of assessing the infant after birth at 1 and 5 minutes of life. It gives a maximum score of 10 which indicates the newborn is in the best possible condition. Scores between 0-3 require immediate resuscitation.

Changes in the Apgar scores denote the response of the infant to resuscitation. If the score at 5 minutes remains less than 7, the infant should be assessed again every 5 minutes for the next 20 minutes.

Causes for false positive Apgar score are:

• Prematurity
• Drugs like analgesics, narcotics, sedatives, magnesium sulfate
• Acute cerebral trauma
• Precipitous delivery
• Airway obstruction (choanal atresia)
• Congenital pneumonia or sepsis
• Hemorrhage- hypovolemia

False-negative Apgar score is seen in maternal acidosis and high fetal catecholamine levels.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child suffering from steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome is brought to the OPD for vaccination. Which of the following is true about vaccination in this child?
options: All live vaccines under NIS can be given as per schedule
All killed vaccines under NIS can be given
Only pneumococcal vaccine should be given to the child in acute phase
Live vaccines are contraindicated in the child’s sibling
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. All killed vaccines under NIS can be given

In a child with steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome, all killed vaccines can be given.

Option A: Live virus vaccines are administered with caution in children receiving corticosteroid therapy. They can be given to patients in whom the prednisone dose is below 1mg/kg daily or 2mg/kg on alternate days. If the patient is receiving corticosteroid-sparing agents (cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine), live virus vaccines are contraindicated.

Option C: Only live vaccines are contraindicated in this child. Full pneumococcal vaccination (with the 13-valent conjugate vaccine and 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine) and influenza vaccination can be given annually to the child and their household contacts.

Option D: Immunization of siblings/healthy household contacts with live vaccines is necessary to reduce the risk of infection transmission to the immunosuppressed child. Direct exposure to the gastrointestinal/respiratory secretions of the household contacts is avoided for about 3-6 weeks after vaccination.

Minimal change nephrotic syndrome is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome. It is characterized by heavy proteinuria, edema, hypoalbuminemia, and hyperlipidemia. The diagnosis is confirmed by performing a urinalysis and urine protein: creatinine ratio. Nephrotic range proteinuria is proteinuria greater than 3.5 g per 24 hours (3+ or 4+) or a urine protein : creatinine ratio exceeding 2.

The recommended initial treatment for nephrotic syndrome is a daily dose of 2mg/kg (max 60mg) of prednisolone for 6 weeks followed by an alternate dose of 1.5mg/kg (max 40mg) for the next 6-8 weeks.

Definitions regarding the course of nephrotic syndrome:

• Frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome: ≥2 relapses in 6 months or 3 or more relapses in 12 months.
• Steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome: Relapse during steroid tapering or within 2 weeks of discontinuation.
• Steroid resistance: Failure to achieve remission despite therapy with daily prednisolone for 6 weeks

Alternative drugs used in steroid-dependent patients, frequent relapsers, steroid-resistant patients, and those with severe corticosteroid toxicity are cyclophosphamide, calcineurin inhibitors: cyclosporine and Tacrolimus, mycophenolate, levamisole, and rituximab (a chimeric monoclonal antibody against CD20).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child transfers an object from one hand to another. What does it signify?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ability to compare objects

The milestone of transfer of objects from one hand to another in a child signifies the ability of the child to compare objects. The transfer of objects is a motor milestone occurring at 6 months of age.

Other options:

Option A: When the child reaches for objects it implies the onset of visuomotor coordination. It is attained at 4 months

Option C: Thumb finger grasp implies the ability to handle small objects. It is attained at 8 months.

Option D: The voluntary release/ Release phenomenon is used to denote the disappearance of the palmar grasp, which is seen at 4 months.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A young girl presents with the complaints of continuous dribbling of urine. However, she also voids normally. Her parents tell you that she had never been totally dry since her birth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ectopic ureter

The clinical presentation of a young girl with continuous dribbling of urine, despite normal voiding, strongly suggests the diagnosis of an ectopic ureter.

An ectopic ureter refers to a condition where the ureter drains outside the bladder. It is more common in females and opens either into the urethra below the sphincter or into the vagina. Hence, they present with constant urinary dripping all day, even though the child voids regularly (paradoxical incontinence).

The terminal part of the ureter is frequently narrowed, leading to hydroureteronephrosis. Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are common due to urinary stasis.

In males, ectopic ureters usually enter the posterior urethra above the external sphincter, hence they are usually continent and most patients present with UTI or epididymitis.

Investigations include renal ultrasound (USG), voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG), and renal scan to assess function. USG shows a hydronephrotic kidney or dilated upper pole and ureter. If there is a satisfactory function, the recommended treatment options are ureteral reimplantation into the bladder or ureteroureterostomy. The poor function may require partial or total nephrectomy.

Other options:

Option B: A ureterocele is a cystic dilation of the terminal ureter, typically obstructive due to a small ureteral opening. In childhood, they commonly present with infections. Larger ureteroceles can cause obstruction at the bladder neck.

Option C: Congenital megaureter (dilated ureter) presents UTI, urinary stones, hematuria, and flank pain because of urinary stasis.

Option D: Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) is characterized by the retrograde flow of urine from the bladder to the ureter and kidney. They usually present with recurrent attacks of UTI.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All the following PFT findings in a child are suggestive of asthma except?
options: Increase in FEV1> 12% after salbutamol inhalation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Day- night variation of FEV1 > 15%

Day-night variation of FEV1 > 15% is not suggestive of asthma, variation ≥20% is suggestive of asthma.

Lung Function Abnormalities in Childhood Asthma

• Spirometry showing airflow limitation: Low FEV1 (relative to the percentage of predicted norms) and FEV1:FVC ratio <0.80 (option B)
• Bronchodilator response (to inhaled β-agonist): Improvement in FEV1 ≥12% and ≥200 mL after inhalation of a short-acting beta agonist (option A).
• Exercise challenge: Worsening in FEV1 ≥15% (option D)
• Daily peak expiratory flow (PEF) or FEV1 monitoring: day to day and/or A.M.-to-P.M. variation ≥20%
• Exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO): A value of >20ppb (parts per billion) supports the clinical diagnosis of asthma in children.

FEV1: Forced expiratory volume in 1 sec; FVC: Forced vital capacity.

Childhood asthma can be classified into two types: recurrent wheezing in early childhood, often triggered by respiratory viral infections and resolves during preschool/lower school years, and chronic asthma associated with allergies that persist into later childhood and adulthood.

Based on the severity, acute asthma is classified as mild, moderate, and severe.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Identify the vitamin which when deficient can lead to neonatal seizures.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pyridoxine

Pyridoxine deficiency can cause refractory seizures in the neonatal period and infancy.

Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (P5P) is the active form of pyridoxine and functions as a cofactor for enzymes involved in neurotransmitter synthesis, amino acid metabolism, and glycogen metabolism. Intracellular P5P deficiency in the brain can lead to a seizure disorder that does not respond to typical anticonvulsant medications but shows a response to pyridoxine.

Antiquitin deficiency is the most common cause of pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (due to mutations in the ALDH7A1 alleles)

They primarily present with generalized seizures in the early days of life. The seizures can be of various types, recurrent focal motor seizures, generalized tonic seizures, and myoclonus. Additional manifestations may include dystonia, respiratory distress, abdominal distention with vomiting, hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, and hypothermia.

Increased α-aminoadipic semialdehyde and pipecolic acid levels are observed in the CSF, plasma, and urine. Treatment with vitamin B6 (50-100 mg/day) shows significant improvement in seizures. Life-long therapy is needed.

Other options:

Option B: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency causes beriberi.

Option C: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency causes glossitis, cheilosis, keratitis, and corneal vascularization.

Option D: Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) deficiency causes burning feet syndrome.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Phototherapy converts bilirubin to _________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lumirubin

Phototherapy converts bilirubin to lumirubin. It is used to manage clinical jaundice and indirect hyperbilirubinemia.

It involves exposing the patient to high-intensity light in the visible spectrum. Bilirubin absorbs light most effectively in the blue range (420 to 470nm).

Phototherapy converts toxic bilirubin into two forms: lumirubin, formed by irreversible structural isomerization that can be excreted by the kidneys, and a reversible isomer (4Z,15E-bilirubin), formed by photoisomerization that can be excreted in bile without conjugation.

The effectiveness of phototherapy depends on factors such as the appropriate wavelength range, distance to the infant, skin surface area exposure, and the infant's bilirubin metabolism. The infant's eyes should be covered to prevent corneal damage. Continuous conventional phototherapy is typically used, with frequent repositioning of the infant.

Phototherapy can be discontinued once two TSB (total serum bilirubin) values 12 hours apart fall below current age-specific cut-offs.

Complications of phototherapy may include loose stools, erythematous macular rash, purpuric rash (linked to transient porphyrinemia), overheating, dehydration (due to increased insensible water loss and diarrhea), and hypothermia from exposure.

Bronze baby syndrome is a dark grayish-brown skin discoloration seen in infants undergoing phototherapy in the presence of direct hyperbilirubinemia. Porphyria is a contraindication for phototherapy because photosensitivity and blistering can be severe in these infants.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Surgical correction of VSD is performed in an infant. This will help in relieving which of the following features?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Failure to thrive

Surgery for ventricular septal defect (VSD) mainly helps to relieve congestive cardiac failure which manifests as a failure to thrive in an infant. The main aim of performing surgery in VSD is to get the symptoms of heart failure in control and to prevent the development of pulmonary vascular disease.

Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most common congenital heart disease. The most common subtype is the membranous type.

Small VSDs with trivial left-to-right shunts and normal pulmonary artery pressure (PAP) are the most common. These patients are asymptomatic. A loud, harsh, or blowing holosystolic murmur is present and heard best over the lower left sternal border, and it is accompanied by a thrill.

Small VSDs close spontaneously, especially within the first two years of life. Muscular VSDs have a higher closure rate (up to 80%) compared to membranous VSDs.

Large VSDs with excessive pulmonary blood flow and pulmonary hypertension can lead to signs of congestive heart failure in early infancy. These signs may include dyspnea, feeding difficulties, poor weight gain, profuse perspiration, irritability, weak crying, and recurrent pulmonary infections. The holosystolic murmur associated with a large VSD is less harsh and more blowing compared to that of a small VSD. This is due to the absence of a significant pressure gradient across the defect.

The indications of surgery in VSD are:

• Large defects in patients of any age with uncontrolled symptoms or failure to thrive.
• Moderate to large defects associated with pulmonary hypertension in infants between 6 and 12 months, even if symptoms are controlled by medication.
• Patients older than 24 months with a Qp: Qs ratio greater than 2:1 (ratio of total pulmonary blood flow-Qp to total systemic blood flow-Qs).
• Supracristal VSDs of any size, due to the higher risk of developing aortic valve regurgitation.

Severe pulmonary vascular disease nonresponsive to pulmonary vasodilators is a contraindication to VSD closure.

Other options:

Options A and C: Respiratory alkalosis and arrhythmia are other rare complications of VSD.

Options D: Heart block may occur perioperatively in VSD.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is least likely regarding Rh incompatibility in a newborn?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased urine bilirubin

Amongst the given options, increased urine bilirubin is least likely with Rh incompatibility in newborns.

Rh incompatibility leads to hemolysis in the newborn, causing the release of large amounts of hemoglobin. This hemoglobin is converted to biliverdin and then to unconjugated bilirubin.

The newborn liver has a limited capacity to convert this large amount of unconjugated bilirubin to its soluble form through glucuronide conjugation. As a result, levels of unconjugated bilirubin increase (option A). Unconjugated bilirubin, being water-insoluble and bound to albumin, is not excreted in urine.

Intestinal bacteria convert unconjugated bilirubin to urobilinogen and stercobilinogen, which are excreted in urine and stool (options B and D).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not a criteria for severe acute malnutrition?
options: Weight for height less than -3 SD
Weight for age less than -3 SD
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Weight for age less than -3 SD

Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) according to the WHO criteria is the weight for height (not age) less than minus -3 SD.

Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in children of ages 6 to 59 months is defined by the WHO as any of the following:

• Weight-for-length (or height) below −3 SD of the WHO child growth standards
• Presence of bipedal edema
• Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) <11.5 cm.

Management of SAM is given below:

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not a symptom of severe dehydration?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thirsty child

A thirsty child signifies some dehydration, not severe dehydration.

Clinical features of severe dehydration in a child include:

• Drowsy, lethargic, or unconscious, with deeply sunken eyes and absent tears
• Sunken fontanelle
• Drinks poorly or not able to drink
• Deep breathing
• Skin pinch goes back very slowly (recoil in >2 seconds)
• Tachycardia, with bradycardia in most severe cases
• Weak, thready, or impalpable pulse
• Prolonged capillary refill
• Cold, mottled, and cyanotic extremities
• Minimal urine output

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: "Blueberry muffin” rash in an infant most likely represents:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dermal erythropoiesis

A “blueberry muffin” rash in a newborn represents dermal extramedullary hematopoiesis (dermal erythropoiesis) caused by congenital infections—most commonly TORCH infections (especially congenital rubella and CMV)—leading to blue-purple papules due to hematopoietic cell infiltration of the skin.

Why not other options:

• B. Palpable purpura – Due to vasculitis (e.g., IgA vasculitis); lesions are purpuric from vessel inflammation, not dermal hematopoiesis.
• C. Hepatic metastasis – Can occur in neuroblastoma, but classic blueberry muffin rash is from extramedullary hematopoiesis.
• D. Viral lesion – Viruses cause vesicles/macules, not the nodular bluish lesions of dermal erythropoiesis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: 18-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, and clay-colored stools over 3 years, separated by asymptomatic periods. USG and MRCP are normal. Investigations • Total bilirubin = 20 mg/dL • Direct bilirubin = 16 mg/dL • ALP = 350 U/L • GGT = 10 U/L (normal) What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis

| Investigation | Dubin-Johnson | BRIC

| ------------- | ------------- | ----

| Serum bilirubin | ↑ Conjugated | ↑ Conjugated (during episode)

| Liver enzymes | Normal | Normal/mildly raised

| GGT | Normal | LOW (Type 1)

| Urine coproporphyrin | ↑ Type I (80%) | Normal pattern

| BSP test | Secondary rise at 90 min | Normal clearance

| Liver biopsy | Black pigment in hepatocytes | Normal histology

| Bile salts | Normal | ↑↑ during episodes

| ALP | Normal | Low/Normal

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: 28-year-old postpartum woman complains of sore nipple. A lactation specialist evaluates and tells the patient that the baby's attachment is poor. All of the following are signs of good attachment during breastfeeding except:
options: Baby's chin is touching the breasts
Lower areola more visible than upper
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lower areola more visible than upper

Proper latch (good attachment) during breastfeeding is essential to ensure effective milk transfer and prevent nipple pain or trauma.

Signs of good attachment include:

• Baby’s mouth wide open
• Chin touching the breast
• Lower lip everted (turned outward)
• More areola visible above the baby’s mouth than below

If the lower areola is more visible than the upper areola, it indicates poor latch, meaning the baby is not taking enough of the lower breast tissue into the mouth.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: 3-day-old neonate presented to the OPD with yellowish discoloration of the skin and sclera. His DBS TSH is high. What is the next best step in management?
options: Send venous TSH and free T4
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Send venous TSH and free T4

A dried blood spot (DBS) high TSH on neonatal screening is abnormal but not diagnostic of congenital hypothyroidism. The next step is to confirm the result with a venous TSH and free T4 sample, preferably after 72 hours of life, as the physiological neonatal TSH surge during the first 48–72 hours can produce false-positive screening results. L-thyroxine should be started immediately only if confirmatory testing shows overt congenital hypothyroidism. Thyroid ultrasonography and scintigraphy help determine the etiology but must never delay treatment.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 1-month-old infant, born at 35 weeks gestation, presents with blood-streaked, mucous-filled diarrhea after taking a standard cow's milk-based formula. Symptoms resolved upon switching the formula. If a biopsy was performed during the symptomatic period, which of the following histological findings would most likely be observed?
options: Neutrophilic crypt abscesses in the colon
Eosinophilic infiltration in the distal colon
Hemorrhagic necrosis of the intestinal wall
Presence of heterotopic gastric mucosa in the distal ileum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Eosinophilic infiltration in the distal colon

A young infant with blood-streaked, mucous-filled stools after ingestion of cow’s milk formula that improves after eliminating cow’s milk is characteristic of food protein–induced allergic proctocolitis (cow’s milk protein allergy).

• It is a non–IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to cow’s milk protein.
• The immune response leads to inflammation of the distal colon and rectum.

Histological finding:

• Eosinophilic infiltration of the colonic mucosa, particularly in the distal colon, often with mucosal edema and mild inflammation.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 1-year-old child with jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, and generalized lymphadenopathy is found to have congenital syphilis. Which of the following is associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Osteochondritis

The child has features of early congenital syphilis, which presents within the first 2 years of life. Typical manifestations include jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathy, snuffles (profuse nasal discharge), maculopapular rash involving palms and soles, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and skeletal lesions. The characteristic bony abnormalities are osteochondritis and periostitis, especially involving the long bones, causing pain, pseudoparalysis (Parrot's pseudoparalysis), and metaphyseal changes on X-ray. Intracranial calcifications are typical of congenital toxoplasmosis, bilateral cataracts of congenital rubella, and blueberry muffin rash is classically seen in congenital rubella (though it may occur in other TORCH infections).

| Condition | Characteristic Finding

| --------- | ----------------------

| Congenital Syphilis | Osteochondritis, periostitis, snuffles

| Congenital Rubella | Cataracts, PDA, blueberry muffin rash

| Congenital Toxoplasmosis | Intracranial calcifications, chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus

| Congenital CMV | Periventricular calcifications, sensorineural deafness

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-day-old neonate with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is hyperalert and shows hyperactive tendon reflexes, mydriatic pupils, clonus. Based on the clinical findings, what stage of HIE does this neonate currently have?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stage 1

Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is classified using the Sarnat staging system, which is based on the level of consciousness, muscle tone, reflexes, autonomic function, and seizures.

| Feature | Stage 1 (Mild) | Stage 2 (Moderate) | Stage 3 (Severe)

| ------- | -------------- | ------------------ | ----------------

| Level of consciousness | Hyperalert, irritable | Lethargic | Stupor / Coma

| Muscle tone | Normal or increased | Hypotonia | Flaccid

| Deep tendon reflexes | Hyperactive | Decreased | Absent

| Primitive reflexes (suck, Moro) | Strong | Weak | Absent

| Pupils | Mydriasis (dilated) | Miosis (constricted) | Variable, often poorly reactive

| Autonomic features | Tachycardia, dilated pupils | Bradycardia, constricted pupils | Severe autonomic dysfunction

| Seizures | Absent | Common | Rare or absent (due to severe depression)

| EEG | Normal | Abnormal | Severely abnormal / isoelectric

| Duration | < 24 hours | 2–14 days | Prolonged

| Prognosis | Good | Variable | Poor

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-minute-old boy is being evaluated in the delivery room. The patient was born at term to a 30-year-old primigravida woman. Pregnancy was unremarkable, but labor was complicated by recurrent late decelerations necessitating vacuum assistance for vaginal delivery. Apgar scores were 6 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 170/min, and respirations are 40/min. Scalp examination shows large, fluctuant swelling at the occiput that extends bilaterally to the ears, superiorly toward the crown, and inferiorly into the nape of the neck. This patient's hemorrhage is most likely located between which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Periosteum and galea aponeurosis

The newborn has a large, fluctuant scalp swelling that crosses suture lines and spreads widely over the scalp, which is characteristic of a subgaleal hemorrhage.

Subgaleal hemorrhage:

• Often associated with vacuum-assisted delivery
• Blood accumulates in the potential space between the periosteum of the skull and the galea aponeurotica
• The swelling is diffuse and crosses suture lines

Clinical importance:

• This space can hold a large volume of blood, leading to significant blood loss and hypovolemic shock in neonates.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-month-old baby is brought to the emergency room with bluish discoloration of the skin and rapid breathing. His mother reveals a history of congenital heart disease in the baby and adds that this episode was provoked by a fall leading to crying of the child. Which of the following is least likely to be used for managing this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Intravenous nitroglycerin

A child with cyanosis triggered by crying in the setting of congenital heart disease suggests a hypercyanotic (“Tet”) spell, commonly seen in Tetralogy of Fallot.

• Sudden increase in right ventricular outflow tract obstruction
• Increased right-to-left shunting across the VSD
• Reduced pulmonary blood flow → acute hypoxia and cyanosis

Management of a Tet spell includes:

• Knee-chest position → increases systemic vascular resistance (SVR)
• Oxygen administration
• Morphine → reduces agitation and catecholamine surge
• Propranolol → relieves RV outflow tract spasm
• Sodium bicarbonate → corrects metabolic acidosis

Nitroglycerin is least likely to be used because it decreases systemic vascular resistance, which would increase right-to-left shunting and worsen cyanosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-month-old infant is admitted with profuse diarrhea and vomiting for 3 days. On arrival the child is lethargic and poorly responsive. During examination, a skin pinch remains elevated for more than 2 seconds. While being evaluated, the child develops a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the seizure in this setting?
options: Rotavirus encephalitis is the commonest cause of seizures in diarrheal illness
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis secondary to severe dehydration
Acute bacterial meningitis due to ETEC infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis secondary to severe dehydration

The child has features of severe dehydration:

• Lethargy
• Very slow skin pinch (>2 sec)

Causes of seizures in a child with diarrhea include:

• Febrile seizure
• Cerebral venous/sagittal sinus thrombosis due to dehydration
• Electrolyte disturbances (hyponatremia, hypernatremia)
• Hypoglycemia

In a severely dehydrated infant, an important and frequently tested cause is cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy is brought with height below the 3rd percentile for age. He has a large head with frontal bossing, depressed nasal bridge, and disproportionately short limbs with a relatively normal trunk length. Hand X-ray shows a trident configuration. His upper segment: lower segment ratio is 1.3:1 (expected for age: 1:1). Father's height = 170 cm, mother's height = 155 cm. What is the most likely underlying mechanism?
options: Loss-of-function mutation in the growth hormone receptor gene
Gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3 causing impaired endochondral ossification
X-linked recessive mutation in the androgen receptor gene
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3 causing impaired endochondral ossification

• Mid-parental height for this boy = (170 + 155)/2 + 6.5 = 169 cm; his current stature is far below this genetic target, ruling out familial short stature as the primary cause.
• US:LS ratio elevated above the age-expected value (1.3:1 vs. expected 1:1 at 10 years) indicates short lower segment relative to upper segment — disproportionate short stature with rhizomelic limb shortening, while the trunk (upper segment) is relatively spared.
• Frontal bossing, depressed nasal bridge, and trident hand configuration are classic features of achondroplasia.
• Achondroplasia results from an activating (gain-of-function) mutation in FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3), which normally restrains chondrocyte proliferation. Constitutive activation leads to premature growth plate senescence and impaired endochondral ossification, selectively stunting long bone (limb) growth while intramembranous ossification (skull, flat bones) continues relatively normally — explaining the disproportion.
• Inheritance is autosomal dominant, though most cases arise from a de novo mutation, often associated with advanced paternal age.
• GH receptor defects (option A, Laron syndrome) cause proportionate short stature with normal US:LS ratio; UDP-GT deficiency (option C) relates to bilirubin conjugation, unrelated to growth; androgen receptor defects (option D) cause disorders of sexual differentiation, not short-limbed dwarfism.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 12-month-old infant presents with severe wasting, loss of subcutaneous fat, and no edema. The mother states she diluted cow’s milk due to poverty. Which statement best explains the metabolic state?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Deficient total calories (protein + calories)

Marasmus is a form of severe protein–energy malnutrition caused by deficiency of total calories (both protein and energy). It typically occurs due to prolonged inadequate intake, such as feeding diluted milk.

• Severe wasting
• Loss of subcutaneous fat
• No edema
• “Skin and bones” appearance
• Growth failure and irritability

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with complaints of sudden jerks in the morning causing him to drop objects. Identify the correct statements regarding this condition. 1. EEG shows generalized 4-5 Hz polyspike and slow-wave discharges 2. CACNB4, CLNC2 and EJM2 genes are mutated 3. Onset is classically during early infancy 4. KCNQ2 and SLC2A1 genes are mutated 5. Precipitated by sleep deprivation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 5

The presentation of sudden morning jerks causing the child to drop objects is characteristic of Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (JME).

• Typical onset: adolescence (around 12–18 years), not infancy.
• Seizure type: myoclonic jerks, usually soon after waking.
• EEG finding: generalized 4–6 Hz polyspike-and-slow-wave discharges.
• Triggers: commonly sleep deprivation, stress, or alcohol.
• Genetics: mutations reported in genes such as CACNB4, CLCN2, and EJM2.
• KCNQ2 and SLC2A1 mutations → False (associated with other epilepsies)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents for assessment of confusion and rapid breathing. Three days ago the patient developed rhinorrhea, cough, and fever, which have since resolved. The parents say that over the past 48 hours the patient has had increased urination, abdominal pain, and fatigue progressing to somnolence. On physical examination, she is ill-appearing with tachypnea, subcostal retractions, and dry mucous membranes. There is diffuse abdominal tenderness without rebound. Laboratory results are as follows: Hematocrit - 42% Leukocytes - 13,000/mm3 Serum Sodium - 129 mEq/L Potassium - 4.8 mEg/L Chloride - 98 mEq/L Bicarbonate - 9 mEq/L Blood urea nitrogen - 24 mg/dL Creatinine - 1.2 mg/dL Glucose - 450 mg/dL Which of the following is most likely decreased in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Total body potassium

This patient has diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), suggested by:

• Hyperglycemia (glucose 450 mg/dL)
• Metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate 9 mEq/L)
• Polyuria, dehydration, abdominal pain, and Kussmaul breathing

In DKA, insulin deficiency leads to:

• Increased lipolysis → elevated free fatty acids
• Increased ketone production → metabolic acidosis
• Osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia, causing loss of water and electrolytes in urine

Although serum potassium may appear normal or elevated, there is a significant depletion of total body potassium due to:

• Urinary potassium loss
• Shift of potassium from intracellular to extracellular space during acidosis

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 13-month-old girl is brought to the OPD by her mother due to concern about bruising. The mother first noticed bruising around her daughter's eyes 2 weeks ago after the patient returned from a weekend at her father's house. She recently started walking and falls frequently; the bruising was attributed to bumping her head on a coffee table. The bruising has since been persistent, and there is no other notable bruising on her body. The patient has no fever, vomiting, diarrhea, cough, or congestion. The girl's parents are divorced, and she spends most weekends with her father. Weight is 9 kg down from 9.5 kg a month ago. On examination, the patient has rapid, jerking movements of both eyes with infraorbital ecchymoses bilaterally. The abdomen is mildly distended with a 6-cm palpable, firm mass anterior to the left flank. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neuroblastoma

Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood, arising from neural crest cells of the sympathetic nervous system, often in the adrenal medulla.

• Abdominal mass (often firm and irregular)
• Periorbital ecchymosis (“raccoon eyes”) due to orbital metastasis
• Opsoclonus (rapid, chaotic eye movements) from paraneoplastic syndrome
• Weight loss and abdominal distension

Why not other options:

A. Child abuse: Periorbital bruising could occur, but opsoclonus (rapid jerky eye movements) and a firm abdominal mass strongly suggest a tumor.

B. Leukemia: Causes pallor, generalized bruising, hepatosplenomegaly, not a localized abdominal mass with raccoon eyes.

D. Von Willebrand disease: Causes mucocutaneous bleeding, not orbital ecchymosis with abdominal mass.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 14-month-old with acute diarrhoea has sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor with skin snapping back in 2 seconds, and is irritable but drinking eagerly. Weight is 10 kg. The total ORS required over 4 hours is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 750 mL

The child has some dehydration due to acute diarrhoea.

Key clues are:

• Sunken eyes
• Reduced skin turgor
• Skin pinch returns in \~2 seconds
• Irritable
• Drinks eagerly

This corresponds to WHO Plan B rehydration.

For some dehydration, ORS requirement is:

• 75 mL/kg over 4 hours

For a 10 kg child:

• 75 × 10 = 750 mL over 4 hours

After 4 hours, reassess hydration status and shift to Plan A, B, or C depending on response.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 14-month-old with febrile seizure is evaluated for recurrence risk. Which combination of risk factors would most increase the risk of recurrence?
options: Age >2 years + fever >39 degrees C at seizure onset
Age <1 year + fever duration <24 hours + temperature 38–39 degrees C at seizure onset
Complex seizure type alone + family history of epilepsy
No risk factors — all febrile seizures have equal recurrence
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Age <1 year + fever duration <24 hours + temperature 38–39 degrees C at seizure onset

The risk of febrile seizure recurrence is highest in children with younger age at first seizure (<1 year), short duration of fever (<24 hours) before the seizure, and lower fever (38–39°C) at the time of seizure. A lower temperature indicates a lower seizure threshold, making recurrence more likely. Additional risk factors include a family history of febrile seizures and recurrent febrile illnesses. Although complex febrile seizures increase the risk of subsequent epilepsy, they are not independent predictors of febrile seizure recurrence. Children with multiple recurrence risk factors may be considered for intermittent oral clobazam during febrile episodes, along with antipyretic measures.

High-Yield

• Biggest predictor: Age <1 year at first febrile seizure
• Recurrence risk increases with: Fever <24 hours, temperature 38–39°C, and family history of febrile seizures
• Complex febrile seizure → ↑ Risk of epilepsy, not necessarily recurrence

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy is brought by his parents with concern about short stature. His height is below the 3rd percentile. His father's height is 168 cm and mother's height is 154 cm. On examination, he has not yet entered puberty. Bone age on X-ray is delayed. His parents are of normal height. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and what is his mid-parental height?
options: Constitutional delay of growth; MPH = 161 cm
Constitutional delay of growth; MPH = 167.5 cm
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Constitutional delay of growth; MPH = 167.5 cm

Mid Parental Height (MPH): 168 + 154 / 2 + 6.5 for boys = 167.5

Constitutional Delay vs Familial Short Stature:

| | Constitutional Delay | Familial Short Stature

| --- | -------------------- | ----------------------

| Adult height | Normal | Short

| Puberty | Delayed | Normal for age

| Bone age | Delayed | Normal for age

| Parent's height | Normal | Short

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy presents with delayed puberty, decreased facial hair, and gynecomastia. Examination reveals small, firm testes. Which hormonal profile is expected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ↑ FSH, ↑ LH, ↓ testosterone

• A teenage boy with delayed puberty, gynecomastia, and small firm testes is suggestive of primary testicular failure, classically seen in Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY).
• Because the testes fail to produce adequate testosterone, there is loss of negative feedback on the hypothalamic–pituitary axis, leading to increased gonadotropins.

Hormonal profile:

• ↑ FSH
• ↑ LH
• ↓ Testosterone

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her mother for a yearly physical examination. The patient feels well but is worried that she has not yet started puberty. Temperature is 36.7 C (98 F), blood pressure is 152/91 mm Hg, pulse is 75/min, and respirations are 18/ min. Physical examination is significant for a lack of secondary sexual characteristics; a blind vagina is noted on pelvic examination. Laboratory studies reveal hypokalemia and low testosterone and estradiol levels. Cytogenetic analysis shows a 46, XY karyotype. This patient most likely has deficiency of which of the following enzymes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 17 alpha-hydroxylase

17α-hydroxylase deficiency is a rare form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia characterized by impaired synthesis of cortisol and sex steroids (androgens and estrogens).

Key features include:

• 46, XY individual with undervirilization → female or ambiguous external genitalia and lack of secondary sexual characteristics
• Blind vagina due to absence of androgen-driven male genital development
• Low testosterone and estradiol levels
• Hypertension and hypokalemia due to excess mineralocorticoid activity (↑ deoxycorticosterone)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 15-month-old infant is not yet walking independently. Examination and history are normal. Appropriate next step:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reassure and observe until 18 months

Independent walking normally develops between 9–18 months of age. Therefore, a 15-month-old child who is not yet walking but has otherwise normal development and examination can still fall within the normal range of motor milestone acquisition.

In such cases, the appropriate approach is reassurance and observation, with follow-up until 18 months, when delayed walking would warrant further evaluation.

Why not other options?

B. Immediate brain MRI: Not indicated because the child has normal history and neurological exam. Imaging is reserved if neurologic abnormalities or regression are present.

C. Start physiotherapy for cerebral palsy: CP would show abnormal tone, delayed milestones, or abnormal reflexes, which are not present here.

D. Genetic testing for SMA: SMA presents with hypotonia, weakness, and delayed motor milestones, usually with abnormal exam findings.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy is evaluated for poor scholastic performance and absence of secondary sexual characteristics. He is taller than his peers, has disproportionately long limbs, sparse facial hair, bilateral gynecomastia, and small firm testes. Serum testosterone levels are low. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?
options: Horseshoe kidney with coarctation of aorta
Extragonadal germ cell tumor in the mediastinum
Bicuspid aortic valve with webbed neck
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Extragonadal germ cell tumor in the mediastinum

• The stem points to Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY).
• High-yield association: Extragonadal germ cell tumors (mediastinum most common)
• Options A, B, and D are all Turner syndrome associations.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl presents with polyuria, polydipsia, progressive vision loss, and a history of recurrent urinary tract infections. Further evaluation reveals optic atrophy, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, and diabetes insipidus. Genetic testing confirms a diagnosis of DIDMOAD syndrome. Which of the following genes is most commonly associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. WFS1

• DIDMOAD syndrome (also known as Wolfram Syndrome) is a rare genetic disorder characterized by Diabetes Insipidus, Diabetes Mellitus, Optic Atrophy, and Deafness.
• It is most commonly caused by mutations in the WFS1 gene, which encodes wolframin, a protein involved in endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis.
• The syndrome typically presents in childhood or adolescence with diabetes mellitus and progressive optic atrophy.

Why not others (very brief):

• FOXP3: Causes IPEX syndrome (autoimmune disease).
• HNF1A: Causes MODY type 3 diabetes.
• PDX1: Causes pancreatic agenesis / MODY type 4.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 16-year-old male presents with subacute, painless, bilateral vision loss. Family history reveals his mother and maternal uncle had similar vision problems in their teens, but his father is unaffected and none of his father's relatives are affected. Which mitochondrial complex is implicated, and what inheritance pattern explains why only maternal relatives are affected?
options: Complex IV mutation; autosomal dominant inheritance
Complex III mutation; X-linked inheritance, explaining male predominance
Complex II mutation; autosomal recessive inheritance with consanguinity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Complex I mutation; mitochondrial (maternal) inheritance

Leber hereditary optic neuropathy = mutations in Complex I of the electron transport chain → neuronal death in retina/optic nerve → subacute bilateral vision loss in teens/young adults (males > females in expression, though inheritance is maternal). Mitochondrial DNA is transmitted only through the mother — explaining why maternal relatives (mother, maternal uncle) are affected while paternal relatives are entirely unaffected, regardless of the patient's own sex.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 19-month-old child is brought to the pediatric OPD for poor weight gain. Examination reveals severe wasting. Weight-for-height is −3.4 SD and MUAC is 11.1 cm. There is no pedal edema. The child eagerly accepts the test feed and finishes the entire portion. Temperature, blood glucose, hydration status, and systemic examination are normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Admit for 10-step inpatient management because weight-for-height is <−3 SD
Start therapeutic feeding at home with close follow-up
Begin iron therapy immediately and reassess after 1 month
Administer IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Start therapeutic feeding at home with close follow-up

The child has Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) because:

• Weight-for-height < −3 SD (−3.4 SD)
• MUAC < 11.5 cm (11.1 cm)

However, the child has uncomplicated SAM:

• No edema
• Good appetite (passes appetite/test feed)
• No hypoglycemia, hypothermia, dehydration, or severe illness

Management of uncomplicated SAM:

• Outpatient care with therapeutic feeding (RUTF/energy-dense therapeutic diet)
• Regular follow-up and monitoring

When is admission required?

• Failed appetite test
• Bilateral pedal edema
• Medical complications (hypoglycemia, hypothermia, severe infection, dehydration, shock, etc.)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-hour-old boy is evaluated in the newborn nursery due to cyanosis. The boy was born at 38 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery to a primigravida mother whose pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. When the mother attempted to breastfeed in the first hour of life, the patient latched and sucked well but began to appear blue around the lips and face. He began crying and turned pink when he was removed from the breast. He has voided and passed meconium. Heart rate and 4-extremity blood pressures are normal. Examination shows a non-dysmorphic neonate with mild cyanosis at rest. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Choanal atresia

Newborns are obligate nasal breathers during the first few months of life. Therefore, nasal obstruction can cause cyanosis that worsens during feeding and improves when the infant cries.

In choanal atresia, the posterior nasal choanae are blocked (by bone or membrane), preventing airflow through the nose.

• During feeding: the infant attempts to breathe through the nose while sucking → cyanosis develops.
• During crying: the mouth opens, allowing oral breathing → cyanosis improves.

This pattern of cyclical cyanosis relieved by crying is characteristic of choanal atresia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department for evaluation of cyanosis. He became fussy and sweaty while taking his bottle, and his lips "turned blue" for several minutes during the feeding. The infant has had similar episodes during feeding and crying, but these resolved quickly. The patient was born at 39 weeks gestation, and his birth weight was average for gestational age. His weight gain has been slow, currently at the 5th percentile. On examination, the infant is ill-appearing, agitated, cyanotic, and tachypneic. Cardiac auscultation reveals a grade 2/6 crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border and a single second heart sound. The patient is placed in a knee-chest position immediately. This maneuver improves the patient’s condition predominantly by which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased systemic vascular resistance

This infant’s episodic cyanosis during feeding or crying that improves with the knee-chest position is characteristic of a hypercyanotic (“tet”) spell seen in Tetralogy of Fallot.

During a tet spell:

• Increased right-to-left shunting across the ventricular septal defect occurs due to right ventricular outflow obstruction.
• This allows deoxygenated blood to bypass the lungs and enter systemic circulation, causing sudden cyanosis.

Knee-chest position mechanism:

• Compresses the femoral arteries → increases systemic vascular resistance (SVR).
• Higher SVR reduces right-to-left shunting across the VSD.
• More blood is directed toward the pulmonary circulation for oxygenation, improving cyanosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-month-old former 28-week preterm infant is admitted with cough, wheezing, and feeding difficulty. Examination shows moderate respiratory distress with nasal flaring and intercostal retractions. Nasopharyngeal swab is positive for RSV. The infant has a history of bronchopulmonary dysplasia and oxygen requirement at discharge. Which of the following is the most appropriate antiviral therapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ribavirin aerosol therapy

Severe RSV infection in high-risk infants (e.g., premature infants, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, congenital heart disease) may be treated with aerosolized ribavirin, an antiviral that inhibits viral RNA synthesis. It is reserved for severe RSV disease in hospitalized high-risk patients.

Key distinctions:

A. Nirsevimab: Long-acting monoclonal antibody for RSV prevention

C. Oseltamivir: Antiviral for influenza, not RSV

D. Palivizumab: Monoclonal antibody used for RSV prophylaxis, not treatment

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic because his parents are concerned about delayed speech and unusual behavior. He rarely responds when his name is called and spends long periods repeatedly spinning the wheels of his toy cars instead of playing with them normally. The child becomes distressed when his daily routine changes and frequently rocks back and forth while sitting. He can climb stairs and stack blocks appropriately for age. However, he speaks only a few single words and does not point to objects to share interest with others. During the examination, the child avoids eye contact and does not engage in pretend play. Audiology evaluation is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Autism spectrum disorder

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is characterized by:

1. Persistent deficits in social communication and interaction

• Poor eye contact
• Lack of joint attention (eg, not pointing to share interest)
• Delayed language development
• Limited pretend play

2. Restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior or interests

• Repetitive movements (rocking)
• Fixated behaviors (spinning wheels repeatedly)
• Distress with changes in routine

Symptoms typically become apparent in early childhood, and hearing evaluation is often normal despite poor response to name. Motor milestones may remain age appropriate.

Key differentiating points:

• ADHD → inattention/hyperactivity without core social deficits
• Intellectual disability → global developmental delay across multiple domains
• Childhood-onset fluency disorder → stuttering without impaired social interaction or repetitive behaviors.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-year-old child is evaluated for an abdominal mass detected incidentally. An intravenous pyelogram (IVP) is performed, but the left kidney is not visualized. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Multicystic dysplastic kidney

Multicystic dysplastic kidney (MCDK) is a congenital renal malformation in which the kidney is replaced by multiple nonfunctioning cysts with absent normal renal parenchyma.

• Presents in infancy or childhood as an abdominal mass
• The affected kidney is usually nonfunctional
• Therefore, it is not visualized on intravenous pyelogram (IVP)

Pathogenesis: Abnormal interaction between the ureteric bud and metanephric mesenchyme during renal development

Important associations:

• Contralateral renal anomalies (eg, vesicoureteral reflux)
• Usually unilateral with good prognosis if the opposite kidney is normal

Key distinctions:

• Polycystic kidney disease → bilateral enlarged kidneys with functioning renal tissue
• Renal hypoplasia → small but functioning kidney
• Duplicated collecting system → duplicated ureter/collecting structures, kidney still visualized on imaging.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-year-old child with severe marasmus is admitted for nutritional rehabilitation. The WHO cost sheet for management includes therapeutic feeds (F-75/F-100), antibiotics, vitamin A, zinc, potassium, magnesium, and folate supplements. Which of the following is not included, and for good physiologic reason?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Insulin administration

Insulin is not given in initial management of severe PEM because:

• Children are in a low-insulin catabolic state
• Refeeding → endogenous insulin rises naturally
• Exogenous insulin can precipitate refeeding syndrome → hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, arrhythmias, seizures
• WHO protocols focus on slow, safe anabolic transition rather than forcing insulin-driven anabolism

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-year-old child with unilateral Wilms tumor is found to have aniridia on exam. Which gene mutation is most commonly associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. WT1 gene on chromosome 11p13

The association of Wilms tumor with Aniridia suggests WAGR syndrome, which is caused by a deletion or mutation of the WT1 gene, located on chromosome 11p13.

WAGR syndrome features:

• W – Wilms tumor
• A – Aniridia (absence of iris)
• G – Genitourinary abnormalities
• R – Intellectual disability (previously termed mental retardation)

The WT1 gene is a tumor suppressor gene involved in kidney and gonadal development, and its mutation predisposes to Wilms tumor in early childhood.

Why not other options?

B. WT2 gene (11p15): Associated with Beckewith wiedeman syndrome, which presents with macroglossia, organomegaly, hemihypertrophy, and increased Wilms tumor risk but not aniridia.

C. TP53 gene (17p): Mutation seen in Li-Fraumeni syndrome, associated with multiple early-onset cancers.

D. RET proto-oncogene (10q): Mutation seen in Multiple endocrine neoplasia 1, associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after accidentally ingesting a household drain cleaner stored under the sink. Shortly afterward, she developed drooling, painful swallowing, and refusal to eat. Physical examination reveals erythema and ulceration around the mouth with blood-streaked saliva. Her clothing is soaked with the cleaning solution. Respiratory examination is normal without stridor or wheezing, and vital signs are stable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Placement of a nasogastric feeding tube
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Removal of contaminated clothing

In caustic ingestion with ongoing skin exposure, the first priority after airway and breathing assessment is immediate external decontamination, including removal of contaminated clothing and copious irrigation of exposed skin. Household drain cleaners commonly contain strong alkali agents that cause liquefactive necrosis and deep tissue injury.

Key points in management of caustic ingestion:

• Assess airway urgently for stridor, drooling, or respiratory distress
• Do not induce vomiting or attempt chemical neutralization
• Nasogastric tube placement is avoided initially due to risk of perforation
• Endoscopy is performed after stabilization to assess extent of esophageal injury

Alkali ingestion typically causes more severe esophageal damage than acid ingestion because of deeper tissue penetration.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician for a well-child visit. She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. Growth parameters are at the 60th percentile. Her parents report that she is active and plays well with other children. She walks up and down stairs with alternating feet, kicks a ball, and stacks six blocks. She feeds herself with a spoon and can help dress herself. However, her parents are concerned that she does not speak as much as children her age. She uses only about 10 single words and rarely combines them. She does point to objects she wants and follows 2-step commands such as “Pick up the toy and put it on the table.” She responds to her name, maintains eye contact, and engages in pretend play. Which of the following developmental milestones is likely delayed in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Language

This child has an isolated language delay. At 2 years of age, children are expected to:

• Use ≥50 words
• Form 2-word phrases (“more milk,” “mommy go”)

This patient uses only about 10 single words and rarely combines them, indicating delayed language development.

Other developmental domains are appropriate for age:

• Gross motor: walks stairs, kicks ball
• Fine motor/adaptive: stacks blocks, feeds self with spoon
• Social: eye contact, pretend play, responds to name

These preserved social interactions help distinguish isolated language delay from autism spectrum disorder, in which deficits in social communication and restricted/repetitive behaviors are present.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 20-month-old boy is brought by his parents with concerns about speech. He currently says only 4–5 words. He walks independently, builds a tower of 3 cubes, and plays alongside other children without interacting with them. His mother reports he does not yet have a vocabulary of sentences. Which of the following represents a red flag in this child's development?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vocabulary of only 4–5 words

Language Milestones:

| Age | Language

| --- | --------

| 6 months | Monosyllables

| 9 months | Bisyllables

| 1 year | 1–2 words

| 18 months | 8–10 words

| 2 years | 100 words, sentences

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2½-year-old boy is brought for evaluation of delayed speech. His parents report that he speaks only a few single words and does not combine words into phrases. He follows simple commands, shows appropriate eye contact, points to objects of interest, and engages in pretend play. His motor milestones were appropriate for age: he sat without support at 7 months, stood at 12 months, and walked independently by 14 months. There are no feeding issues or seizures. Hearing screening is normal. This clinical presentation most likely represents: This clinical presentation most likely represents:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Developmental dissociation

Developmental dissociation refers to uneven development in different developmental domains, where one area (e.g., language) is delayed while others such as social interaction, cognition, and motor development remain normal.

In this child Speech delay is present with Normal social interaction (eye contact, pointing, pretend play) and Normal motor milestones. This pattern indicates isolated language delay with otherwise normal development, which is characteristic of developmental dissociation.

Key distinctions:

B. Developmental delay: Delay in multiple developmental domains

C. Developmental regression: Loss of previously acquired skills

D. Developmental deviation: Abnormal pattern of development (e.g., autism spectrum behaviors)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 22-year-old primigravida develops fever and pruritic vesicular rash one day after delivering a full-term baby. The mother is diagnosed with varicella infection. What is the appropriate management for the neonate?
options: Acyclovir therapy should be started immediately
Wait and monitor the neonate for one week
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Administer varicella-zoster immunoglobulin

• If a mother develops varicella infection from 5 days before delivery to 2 days after delivery, the newborn is at high risk of severe neonatal varicella because transplacental maternal antibodies have not yet been transferred.
• In this situation, the recommended management for the neonate is administration of varicella-zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) to provide passive immunity and reduce the severity of infection.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Acyclovir → used if the neonate develops clinical varicella infection, not as first-line prophylaxis.
• Observation alone → not appropriate due to high risk of severe disease.
• Varicella vaccine → contraindicated in neonates and used only after 12 months of age.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman presents with weakness, lethargy, and hyperpigmentation. Laboratory findings show low cortisol, high ACTH, and elevated plasma potassium. Which of the following biochemical enzymes is most likely deficient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 21-hydroxylase

Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) presents with:

• Low cortisol
• High ACTH (loss of negative feedback)
• Hyperkalemia due to aldosterone deficiency
• Hyperpigmentation from excess ACTH stimulating melanocytes

The most common enzymatic defect causing impaired cortisol and aldosterone synthesis is 21-hydroxylase deficiency. 21-hydroxylase is required for:

• Progesterone → deoxycorticosterone (mineralocorticoid pathway)
• 17-hydroxyprogesterone → 11-deoxycortisol (glucocorticoid pathway)

Key differentiating points:

• 11β-hydroxylase deficiency → hypertension and hypokalemia
• 17α-hydroxylase deficiency → hypertension with sexual infantilism
• Aromatase deficiency affects estrogen synthesis, not cortisol production.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 27-week preterm neonate on CPAP for respiratory distress is examined: see-saw movement of chest and abdomen, marked lower chest wall and xiphoid retractions, marked nasal flaring, and grunting audible even without a stethoscope. FiO₂ requirement has risen to 45%. What is the Silverman score and the most appropriate next step?
options: Score 8 (severe); increase CPAP pressure alone, avoid ventilation
Score 4 (mild); no change in management, reassess in 6 hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Score 10 (severe); switch to mechanical ventilation

| Parameter | Finding | Score

| --------- | ------- | -----

| Upper chest retraction | See-saw | 2

| Lower chest retraction | Marked | 2

| Xiphoid retraction | Marked | 2

| Nasal flaring | Marked | 2

| Grunt | Audible without stethoscope | 2

| Total | | 10

• Score ≥7 = severe respiratory distress.
• Management is score-driven: mild-to-moderate → CPAP; severe → mechanical ventilation, not escalation of CPAP pressure alone.
• If already on CPAP with FiO₂ ≥40% and no improvement (or if score is severe), rescue surfactant is indicated — via INSURE (Intubate–Surfactant–Extubate) or LISA (Less Invasive Surfactant Administration, avoiding intubation).
• This infant, being extremely preterm (<28 weeks), would also have qualified for prophylactic surfactant at birth per current protocol, independent of the Silverman score.
• Continuing CPAP alone (option A/C) in a severe-score infant risks progression to respiratory failure; a mild score (option D) does not match the described findings.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 29-week preterm neonate develops respiratory distress at birth. On assessment: upper chest movement is see-saw, lower chest retractions are severe, xiphoid retractions are severe, nasal flaring is severe, and grunt is heard without a stethoscope. Chest X-ray shows ground glass appearance with air bronchogram sign. FiO₂ requirement is 0.35. What is the next best step in management?
options: CPAP alone as Silverman score is 4–6 indicating moderate distress
Prophylactic surfactant as gestational age is <34 weeks
Mechanical ventilation followed by surfactant within 2 hours via INSURE technique
CPAP initiation; surfactant not indicated as FiO₂ requirement has not reached 0.5
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mechanical ventilation followed by surfactant within 2 hours via INSURE technique

Silverman Scoring System — Revision Table:

| Parameter | Score 0 | Score 1 | Score 2

| --------- | ------- | ------- | -------

| Upper chest retractions | Synchronized | Lagging | See-saw

| Lower chest retractions | Nil | Mild | Severe

| Xiphoid retractions | Nil | Mild | Severe

| Nasal flaring | Nil | Mild | Severe

| Grunt | Absent | Heard with stethoscope | Heard without stethoscope

Silverman Score Interpretation:

| Score | Severity

| ----- | --------

| <3 | Mild

| 4–6 | Moderate

| ≥7 | Severe

Score of 10 → Severe RDS.

Management Protocol (≥28 weeks with respiratory distress):

| Silverman Score | Management

| --------------- | ----------

| Mild/Moderate | CPAP → if FiO₂ ≥0.3 → Surfactant within 2 hrs

| Severe | Mechanical ventilation → if FiO₂ ≥0.3 → Surfactant within 2 hrs

Surfactant administration:

• Route: Endotracheal tube
• Technique: INSURE — Intubation → Surfactant → Extubation
• Timing: Within 2 hours (Early surfactant)

FiO₂ of 0.35 (≥0.3) + Severe Silverman score → mechanical ventilation + surfactant within 2 hours via INSURE. Prophylactic surfactant is reserved for <28 weeks or those intubated at birth with incomplete antenatal steroids.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-day-old male neonate is brought to the neonatal intensive care unit due to progressive jaundice and poor feeding. He was born at 38 weeks gestation via normal vaginal delivery to a 24-year-old primigravida. Birth weight was 3.1 kg. Pregnancy was uncomplicated. The infant developed jaundice within 18 hours of life. Examination reveals lethargy, mild hypotonia, and scleral icterus extending to the lower limbs. Laboratory studies show: • Total bilirubin: 21 mg/dL • Direct bilirubin: 0.6 mg/dL • Hemoglobin: 11.2 g/dL • Reticulocyte count: Elevated • Peripheral smear: Spherocytes • Direct Coombs test: Negative Which of the following statements regarding this patient’s condition are correct? 1. Phototherapy converts bilirubin into water-soluble structural isomers excreted without conjugation 2. Exchange transfusion is indicated if signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy develop 3. Kernicterus most commonly affects the globus pallidus and subthalamic nuclei 4. Unconjugated bilirubin can be detected in urine in this patient 5. Deficiency of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase is the primary defect in this disorder 6. Early-onset jaundice in this infant is suggestive of hemolysis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3 and 6

This neonate likely has hereditary spherocytosis, causing severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to hemolysis.

• 1. Phototherapy converts bilirubin into water-soluble structural isomers excreted without conjugation — Correct: Phototherapy forms lumirubin and other isomers that can be excreted without hepatic conjugation.
• 2. Exchange transfusion is indicated if signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy develop — Correct: Exchange transfusion is indicated in severe hyperbilirubinemia or acute bilirubin encephalopathy.
• 3. Kernicterus most commonly affects the globus pallidus and subthalamic nuclei — Correct: Kernicterus classically involves basal ganglia, especially globus pallidus.
• 4. Unconjugated bilirubin can be detected in urine in this patient — Incorrect: Unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and not excreted in urine.
• 5. Deficiency of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase is the primary defect in this disorder — Incorrect: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase deficiency occurs in Crigler-Najjar and Gilbert syndrome, not hereditary spherocytosis.
• 6. Early-onset jaundice in this infant is suggestive of hemolysis — Correct: Jaundice within the first 24 hours strongly suggests pathologic hemolysis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-day-old neonate is brought with recurrent seizures. The baby has poor feeding and lethargy. There is no history of fever. On examination, the neonate is irritable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Check blood glucose level

Hypoglycemia is the most common and readily reversible metabolic cause of neonatal seizures, especially during the first week of life. A 3-day-old infant with recurrent seizures, poor feeding, lethargy, and irritability should therefore undergo an immediate bedside blood glucose estimation before initiating other investigations or treatment. Delayed recognition can lead to permanent neurological injury. If hypoglycemia is confirmed, IV 10% dextrose (2 mL/kg bolus) should be administered promptly, followed by a continuous glucose infusion. Antiepileptic drugs are considered only if seizures persist after correction of reversible metabolic abnormalities. Neuroimaging and antibiotics are guided by the clinical evaluation and suspected etiology.

• First investigation in any neonate with seizures: Blood glucose
• Other reversible causes: Hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hyponatremia
• Common causes of neonatal seizures: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE), hypoglycemia, intracranial hemorrhage, meningitis, metabolic disorders
• Management principle: Correct reversible metabolic causes before starting antiepileptic drugs.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-day-old neonate presents with severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (serum bilirubin = 28 mg/dL) requiring exchange transfusion. Genetic testing confirms absence of UGT1A1 enzyme activity. Which of the following correctly describes the urine and stool findings in this condition?
options: Urine bilirubin absent, Urine urobilinogen absent, Stool stercobilinogen absent
Urine bilirubin absent, Urine urobilinogen decreased, Stool stercobilinogen pale/decreased
Urine bilirubin absent, Urine urobilinogen normal/slightly decreased, Stool stercobilinogen normal/slightly decreased
Urine bilirubin present, Urine urobilinogen increased, Stool stercobilinogen normal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Urine bilirubin absent, Urine urobilinogen decreased, Stool stercobilinogen pale/decreased

| Parameter | Finding | Reason

| --------- | ------- | ------

| Urine bilirubin | ❌ Absent | Only conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and excreted in urine. CN has unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia → none reaches urine

| Urine urobilinogen | ⬇️ Decreased | Unconjugated bilirubin cannot enter bile → less reaches gut → less urobilinogen formed → less absorbed → less excreted in urine

| Stool stercobilinogen | ⬇️ Decreased/Pale stools | Less bilirubin reaching gut → less converted to stercobilinogen → pale stools

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-month-old exclusively breastfed infant is brought to the OPD. The mother asks about the nutritional adequacy of breast milk. She also mentions she expressed some milk in the morning and wants to know how long it can be safely stored at room temperature. A medical student accompanying you makes several statements about breast milk. All of the following statements are true except:
options: Colostrum contains IgA, anti-infective proteins, and Vitamin A
Lactoferrin and Bifidus factor in mature milk are protective against E. coli
Breast milk protein content is 3 times higher than cow's milk and is easily digestible
Low PABA content in breast milk is protective against malaria
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Breast milk protein content is 3 times higher than cow's milk and is easily digestible

Breast Milk Composition (vs Cow's Milk):

| Component | Breast Milk vs Cow's Milk

| --------- | -------------------------

| Carbohydrate | ↑↑ (Lactose)

| Protein | 3 times LOWER, easily digestible

| Fat | Same; rich in PUFA (DHA) → brain growth

| Calories | 67 kcal/100 mL

Breast milk protein is 3 times less than cow's milk — not higher. It is easily digestible, which is an advantage.

Immunological Properties:

| Component | Property

| --------- | --------

| Colostrum | IgA, anti-infective proteins, Vitamin A

| Mature milk (PLAB) | PABA (low) → protective against malaria

| | Lactoferrin + Bifidus factor → antibacterial against E. coli

| | IgA

Breast Milk Storage:

| Condition | Duration

| --------- | --------

| Room temperature | 6–8 hours

| Refrigerator | 24 hours

| Freezer (−20°C) | Up to 3 months

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-month-old infant presents with persistent jaundice, pale stools, and pruritus. Examination reveals a systolic murmur and butterfly-shaped thoracic vertebrae on X-ray. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alagille syndrome

Alagille syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder (JAG1 mutation) characterized by paucity of intrahepatic bile ducts, leading to chronic cholestasis in infancy.

Key Clinical Features (Classic clues):

• Persistent jaundice with pale stools and pruritus (cholestasis)
• Congenital heart defects (commonly pulmonary artery stenosis → systolic murmur)
• Butterfly vertebrae on X-ray
• Characteristic facies (broad forehead, deep-set eyes, pointed chin)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-week-old girl is brought to the emergency department due to lethargy. The patient was breastfeeding well until this morning when she became increasingly difficult to rouse. She was born at term to a 35-year-old woman who had a spontaneous vaginal delivery at home. The patient did not receive any vaccinations or medications after birth due to parental preference. Head circumference is at the 99th percentile. Weight and length are at the 25th percentile. Temperature is 37° C (98.6° F). Physical examination shows a large, bulging anterior fontanelle. The eyes are driven downward, and the patient does not appear to be able to look upward. No scalp swelling is present. Intracranial hemorrhage is confirmed on CT scan of the head. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin deficiency

Newborns are at risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) because they have:

• Low vitamin K stores at birth
• Poor placental transfer of vitamin K
• Sterile intestines (lack of gut flora to synthesize vitamin K)
• Low vitamin K content in breast milk

Infants who do not receive prophylactic vitamin K injection at birth are at risk of late VKDB (2–12 weeks of age), which commonly presents with intracranial hemorrhage.

Why not other options:

A. Germinal matrix fragility: Occurs in premature infants with IVH in the first few days of life. This baby is term and 3 weeks old.

B. Inherited hemophilia: X-linked, mainly affects males; this patient is female.

C. Birth trauma: Bleeding appears immediately after birth, not after 3 weeks.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy has weight-for-height > +3 SD. Which of the following cannot be a cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Edwards syndrome

A weight-for-height > +3 SD on WHO growth charts indicates severe overweight/obesity. Causes include genetic disorders (e.g., leptin or leptin receptor deficiency), endocrine disorders (e.g., growth hormone deficiency, hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome), and syndromic obesity such as Prader–Willi syndrome, which presents with hyperphagia and obesity after infancy. In contrast, Edwards syndrome (Trisomy 18) is characterized by severe intrauterine and postnatal growth restriction, failure to thrive, developmental delay, and congenital anomalies, not obesity. Therefore, it cannot be a cause of weight-for-height > +3 SD.

• Genetic obesity: Leptin deficiency, leptin receptor deficiency, MC4R mutation.
• Syndromic obesity: Prader–Willi syndrome (hyperphagia), Bardet–Biedl syndrome.
• Endocrine obesity: GH deficiency, hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome.
• Edwards syndrome (Trisomy 18): Growth restriction and failure to thrive, not obesity.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-year-old child presents with fast breathing and chest indrawing but no general danger signs. As per SAANS protocol, ASHA worker should:
options: Treat with oral amoxicillin and refer
Give pre-referral oral amoxicillin and refer
Hospitalize and treat per IMNCI guidelines
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Give pre-referral oral amoxicillin and refer

• Why: Chest indrawing in SAANS = severe pneumonia/very severe disease.
• ASHA role in severe pneumonia = give pre-referral oral amoxicillin then refer.
• ANM gives pre-referral oral amoxicillin + IM gentamicin then refers.
• Medical Officer = hospitalize + treat per IMNCI.
• Trap: chest indrawing alone (without general danger signs) = still severe per SAANS — differs from IMNCI where chest indrawing = pneumonia only.

| Classification | IMNCI signs | SAANS signs

| -------------- | ----------- | -----------

| No pneumonia | No severe signs | No severe signs

| Pneumonia | Fast breathing OR chest indrawing | Fast breathing only

| Severe/VSD | General danger signs | General danger signs OR chest indrawing

| Severity | ASHA | ANM

| No pneumonia | Home care | Home care

| Pneumonia | Refer after pre-referral oral amoxicillin | Oral amoxicillin + home care

| Severe | Pre-referral oral amoxicillin → refer | Pre-referral oral amoxicillin + IM gentamicin → refer

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-year-old child with cerebral palsy has involuntary writhing movements, choreiform activity, and fluctuating muscle tone. There is a history of severe neonatal jaundice requiring exchange transfusion. All of the following are true regarding this form of cerebral palsy except:
options: Chronic bilirubin encephalopathy is a recognized cause
Chorea and athetosis are characteristic manifestations
Periventricular leukomalacia is the characteristic neuropathological lesion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Periventricular leukomalacia is the characteristic neuropathological lesion

The diagnosis is Extrapyramidal cerebral palsy.

| Feature | Extrapyramidal CP

| ------- | -----------------

| Movement disorder | Chorea, athetosis

| Pathology | Basal ganglia lesions

| Etiology | Chronic bilirubin encephalopathy

Periventricular leukomalacia is seen in spastic diplegia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3.5-year-old child is evaluated for developmental concerns. On assessment, his developmental age is determined to be 2 years across gross motor, fine motor, language, and social domains. He was born at term with birth asphyxia. His DQ is calculated and further workup is planned. Which of the following statements regarding his condition is correct?
options: His DQ is 71, which is borderline and does not meet criteria for developmental delay
He has global developmental delay, and the most common cause in such cases is cerebral palsy
Global developmental delay is defined as DQ <70 in any one domain
His DQ is 57, which qualifies as developmental delay but not global developmental delay as only one domain is affected
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. He has global developmental delay, and the most common cause in such cases is cerebral palsy

Developmental Quotient (DQ):

| Term | Definition

| ---- | ----------

| Developmental delay | DQ <70
