| Global developmental delay | DQ <70 in ≥2 domains

| Most common cause of GDD | Cerebral palsy

DQ of 57 clearly meets criteria for developmental delay. The child has delay across all four domains with a history of birth asphyxia, satisfying the definition of global developmental delay. Option C is incorrect as GDD requires ≥2 domains (not just one). Option D is incorrect as the stem clearly states all four domains are affected. The most common cause of GDD is cerebral palsy, consistent with the history of birth asphyxia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 32-week preterm neonate on enteral feeds develops abdominal distension, vomiting, and bloody stools on day 5 of life. Abdominal X-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Stop feeds, start broad-spectrum antibiotics, gastric decompression
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stop feeds, start broad-spectrum antibiotics, gastric decompression

Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a serious gastrointestinal emergency seen mainly in preterm infants. The classic radiologic finding is pneumatosis intestinalis (gas within the intestinal wall).

Initial management:

• Stop enteral feeds (NPO)
• Nasogastric/gastric decompression
• Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
• Provide IV fluids and supportive care

Surgery is reserved for complications such as intestinal perforation or clinical deterioration.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 35-year-old primigravida comes to the labor and delivery unit at 36 weeks gestation with abdominal pain and blood-tinged vaginal discharge. She was diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus at 27 weeks but has not been compliant with diet or insulin therapy. Her family history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, coronary artery disease, and stroke in both maternal and paternal relatives. Monitoring shows regular uterine contractions and a normal fetal heart rate. Blood pressure is 135/86 mm Hg, and pulse is 100/min. BMI is 40 kg/m². Cervical examination shows 6 cm dilation and 100% effacement. Her blood glucose at admission is 290 mg/dL and is started on insulin. The patient has a spontaneous vaginal delivery of a boy. Which of the following examination findings would most likely be present in this neonate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Respiratory distress

Infants born to mothers with poorly controlled diabetes (especially gestational diabetes) are at increased risk of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS).

Mechanism:

• Maternal hyperglycemia → fetal hyperglycemia → fetal hyperinsulinemia.
• High insulin levels inhibit surfactant production by type II pneumocytes.
• This results in delayed lung maturation, increasing the risk of RDS, even in late preterm or term infants.

Other common findings in infants of diabetic mothers:

• Macrosomia
• Neonatal hypoglycemia
• Polycythemia
• Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 38-year-old woman undergoes first-trimester screening showing ↓β-hCG and ↓PAPP-A. Quadruple screening at 16 weeks (performed after she missed the first-trimester window) shows ↓hCG, normal-to-↓ inhibin A, ↓estriol, and ↓AFP. Which trisomy is most consistent with this combined pattern, and what skeletal/digit finding would you expect on prenatal ultrasound?
options: Trisomy 21 — single palmar crease and incurved 5th finger
Trisomy 18 — clenched fists with overlapping fingers
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trisomy 18 — clenched fists with overlapping fingers

The pattern described — ↓β-hCG, ↓PAPP-A in first trimester, and ALL quadruple markers decreased (hCG↓, inhibin A normal-or-↓, estriol↓, AFP↓) — is the signature of trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome), where "every prenatal screening marker decreases." The expected hand finding is clenched fists with overlapping fingers (part of "PRINCE Edward" mnemonic), distinct from trisomy 21's single palmar crease or trisomy 13's polydactyly.

| Trisomy | 1st trimester (β-hCG, PAPP-A) | Quad screen pattern | Hand finding

| ------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------- | ------------

| 21 | ↑, ↓ | hCG↑, inhibin A↑, estriol↓, AFP↓ | Single palmar crease

| 18 | ↓, ↓ | All decreased | Clenched fists, overlapping fingers

| 13 | ↓, ↓ | All unchanged (—) | Polydactyly

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-day old baby is active and feeding well. He has yellowish staining of face and upper trunk. What is the next step in the management of the baby?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Continue breastfeeding

Physiological jaundice is common in healthy newborns and usually appears after 24 hours of life, peaks around day 3–5 and resolves spontaneously.

Typical features include:

• Mild jaundice involving the face and upper trunk
• Infant is active and feeding well
• Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia within safe limits

Management in such cases is reassurance and continuation of breastfeeding, as frequent feeds help increase bilirubin excretion through stool.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-day-old term neonate is brought with yellowish discoloration of the body. On examination, jaundice is noted over the face, chest, and abdomen, with the limbs appearing normal. The baby is exclusively breastfed and the mother reports adequate latch. Serum bilirubin is 10.2 mg/dL. Which of the following correctly identifies this condition and its management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Physiological jaundice

| Feature | This baby

| ------- | ---------

| Age | 4 days old

| Onset | Not stated as <24 hrs

| Zone | Face + chest + abdomen (Kramer III)

| Bilirubin | 10.2 mg/dL

| Feeding | Exclusively breastfed, adequate latch

| Baby | Well, no pathological features

Kramer's zones:

| Zone | Area | Bilirubin

| ---- | ---- | ---------

| I | Head/face | 5–7

| II | Chest | 7–9

| III | Abdomen | 9–11

| IV | Limbs | 11–13

| V | Palms/soles | >13

Why NOT breastfeeding jaundice (option B):

• Breastfeeding jaundice = inadequate intake → dehydration → increased enterohepatic circulation. The question explicitly states adequate latch and adequate feeding. This rules out breastfeeding jaundice.

Why NOT breast milk jaundice (option A):

• Breast milk jaundice appears after Day 5–7, peaks at 2–3 weeks. This baby is only 4 days old.

Why NOT EHBA (option D):

• EHBA = conjugated jaundice, pale stools, dark urine, hepatomegaly. None present here.

Why Physiological jaundice:

| Criteria |

| -------- | ---

| Onset | After 24 hrs

| Day 4 | Within normal peak window (Day 3–5 in term)

| Bilirubin | 10.2 mg/dL — within physiological range for Day 4

| Zone | III — not palms/soles

| Well baby |

| Adequate breastfeeding |

Management = continue breastfeeding, reassure, recheck bilirubin at Day 5.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-day-old, full-term boy is brought to the OPD for his first visit after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. The patient's mother, gravida 1 para 1, has blood type A positive. Birth weight was 3.4 kg and length was 48.5 cm. He has been exclusively breastfed since birth and nurses for 10 minutes on each breast every 4 hours. The infant passed several dark brown, sticky, meconium stools during the first 2 days of life, but his last stool was yesterday and dark green. He has 2 wet diapers each day but has not voided today. The neonate's current weight is 3. He has scleral icterus and jaundice of the face, chest, and abdomen. The rest of his physical examination is normal. Laboratory results are as follows: Total bilirubin: 14 mg/dL Direct bilirubin: 0.9 mg/dL Which of the following is the most likely cause of this infant's hyperbilirubinemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Breastfeeding jaundice

Breastfeeding jaundice occurs in the first week of life due to inadequate breast milk intake, leading to dehydration and decreased bilirubin excretion.

Key features in this case:

• Day 4 of life (early onset)
• Poor feeding frequency (every 4 hours)
• Few wet diapers and decreased urine output → indicates dehydration
• Weight loss
• Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin elevated, direct bilirubin normal)

Mechanism:

• Inadequate milk intake → reduced intestinal motility
• Increased enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin
• Leads to indirect (unconjugated) hyperbilirubinemia

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-month-old infant has: • Failure to thrive • Tachypnea • Hyperdynamic precordium • Loud P2 • Pansystolic murmur at left lower sternal border • Mid-diastolic mitral flow murmur Which CXR finding is least likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pulmonary oligemia

The findings suggest a large ventricular septal defect (VSD) with pulmonary hypertension.

Key clues:

• Failure to thrive + tachypnea → significant left-to-right shunt
• Hyperdynamic precordium → volume overload
• Pansystolic murmur at left lower sternal border → VSD
• Mid-diastolic mitral flow murmur → increased flow across mitral valve due to large shunt
• Loud P2 → pulmonary hypertension

In a large VSD, chest X-ray usually shows cardiomegaly, left atrial and left ventricular enlargement, and pulmonary plethora/edema due to increased pulmonary blood flow.

Pulmonary oligemia means reduced pulmonary vascular markings and is seen in cyanotic heart diseases with decreased pulmonary blood flow, such as TOF, not large VSD.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-week-old term infant is brought with persistent jaundice. He is thriving, exclusively breastfed, and feeds well. Serum unconjugated bilirubin is 14 mg/dL. The most appropriate management is:
options: Admit for phototherapy and supplement with formula
Investigate for biliary atresia with HIDA scan
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Continue breastfeeding

This infant has breast milk jaundice, a benign cause of persistent unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that typically appears after the first week of life, peaks at 2–3 weeks, and may persist for 8–12 weeks. The baby is thriving, feeding well, exclusively breastfed, and has unconjugated bilirubin, all of which support the diagnosis. It is thought to result from β-glucuronidase and free fatty acids in breast milk, which increase enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin. Breastfeeding should be continued, as the condition is self-limiting and rarely requires treatment. Investigation for biliary atresia is indicated only in infants with conjugated jaundice, pale stools, or dark urine, while phototherapy is usually unnecessary at this bilirubin level in a healthy 4-week-old infant.

| Feature | Breastfeeding Jaundice | Breast Milk Jaundice

| ------- | ---------------------- | --------------------

| Onset | Day 2–5 | After Day 5–7 (peaks 2–3 weeks)

| Cause | Inadequate feeding → dehydration | β-glucuronidase in breast milk ↑ enterohepatic circulation

| Feeding | Poor | Good

| Weight gain | Poor | Normal (thriving infant)

| Management | Improve/increase breastfeeding | Continue breastfeeding

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with high-grade fever, poor oral intake, and increasing lethargy for the past 2 days. On examination, the child appears ill and has cold extremities with delayed capillary refill. Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring is initiated, as demonstrated in the accompanying video. Based on the vital parameters displayed in the video, which of the following best describes the child’s current hemodynamic status?
options: Compensated shock with maintained blood pressure
Isolated respiratory distress without circulatory compromise
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decompensated shock with hypotension

• The monitor in the video shows marked tachycardia (\~160/min) with a low blood pressure (\~66/33 mmHg). In a child with fever, poor intake, altered sensorium, cold extremities, and delayed capillary refill, these findings strongly suggest shock with cardiovascular decompensation.
• Children can initially maintain their blood pressure despite significant circulatory compromise through tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction. Therefore, hypotension is generally a late and concerning sign of pediatric shock.
• The combination of tachycardia + hypotension + clinical evidence of poor perfusion indicates decompensated shock and requires urgent resuscitation.
• Normal systolic BP for this age is roughly 90–100 mmHg; a systolic of 66 is well below the 5th percentile threshold for hypotension, which by the common formula is 70 + [2 × age in years] = 78 mmHg).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-year-old male child with a body weight of 15kg and height of 100cm is admitted with renal failure. His blood urea was 100 mg/dL and serum creatinine was 1 mg/dL. What is the closest calculated eGFR in the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 40 ml/min/1.73 m2 BSA

In children, glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is estimated using the Schwartz formula:

• k = 0.413 (for children)
• Height is in cm
• Height = 100 cm
• Serum creatinine = 1 mg/dL

Thus, the closest value is 40 ml/min/1.73 m².

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4.5-year-old child copies a figure with four equal sides and right angles. What is the next shape she should be able to copy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Triangle

The child has successfully copied a square, characterized by four equal sides and four right angles, indicating attainment of the 4.5-year developmental milestone for fine motor and visuospatial skills. The next expected milestone is the ability to copy a triangle at 5 years. This progression reflects increasing visuomotor integration and perceptual maturity. The sequence is best remembered by the mnemonic LOX STD: Line (2 years), Circle (3 years), Cross/X (4 years), Square (4.5 years), Triangle (5 years), Diamond (7 years). Thus, this child is developmentally appropriate for age, and the next expected achievement is copying a triangle.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-day-old term neonate is brought with jaundice noticed since 18 hours of life. On examination, jaundice involves the face, chest, abdomen, and palms and soles. The baby is lethargic with poor feeding, hypotonia, and intermittent arching of the back. Serum bilirubin is predominantly unconjugated. Which of the following regarding management is correct?
options: Phototherapy is the first step; blue light at 460–490 nm converts bilirubin to lumirubin by conjugation
Phototherapy is contraindicated as palms and soles involvement indicates conjugated hyperbilirubinemia
Phototherapy with blue light is initiated; bronze baby syndrome is an indication for phototherapy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Exchange transfusion is indicated

Pathological Jaundice: Criteria (any one):

| Criterion

| ---------

| Appearance <24 hrs

| Duration >3 weeks

| Palms and soles involvement

| Dark urine + clay stools

Palms and soles involvement → bilirubin 13–15 mg/dL (Kramer Zone V) → danger sign with risk of brain damage.

Features of Kernicterus/BIND (Acute):

| Feature

| -------

| Hypotonia → Hypertonia

| Lethargy

| ↓ Feeding

| Seizures

| Opisthotonus (arching of back)

Features of bilirubin encephalopathy are present → Exchange transfusion is indicated, not phototherapy alone.

Phototherapy:

| Detail | Fact

| ------ | ----

| Light wavelength | Blue light: 460–490 nm

| Mechanism | Structural isomerisation → Bilirubin → Lumirubin (NOT conjugation)

| Contraindication | Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia → Bronze baby syndrome

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-month-old girl is brought to the physician for a weight check. The patient has been evaluated several times for poor weight gain. Current weight is <5th percentile; length and head circumference have been tracking along the 25th percentile. The infant appears thin, but the remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Newborn screening results were normal. Laboratory results are as follows: Serum Chemistry: • Sodium: 140 mEq/L • Potassium: 3 mEq/L • Chloride: 121 mEq/L • Blood urea nitrogen: 10 mg/dL • Creatinine: 0.5 mg/dL • Calcium: 9 mg/dL • Glucose: 98 mg/dL Arterial Blood Gases: • pH: 7.21 • PaCO₂: 31 mmHg • Bicarbonate: 14 mEq/L Urinalysis: • pH: 7.9 • Potassium: Normal • Sodium: Normal Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's failure to thrive? Serum Chemistry: • Sodium: 140 mEq/L • Potassium: 3 mEq/L • Chloride: 121 mEq/L • Blood urea nitrogen: 10 mg/dL • Creatinine: 0.5 mg/dL • Calcium: 9 mg/dL • Glucose: 98 mg/dL Arterial Blood Gases: • pH: 7.21 • PaCO₂: 31 mm Hg • Bicarbonate: 14 mEq/L Urinalysis: • pH: 7.9 • Potassium: Normal • Sodium: Normal Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's failure to thrive?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fanconi disease

Failure to thrive with metabolic acidosis and electrolyte abnormalities in an infant suggests a renal tubular disorder.

• Metabolic acidosis: pH 7.21, HCO₃⁻ 14 mEq/L
• Hyperchloremia (Cl⁻ 121 mEq/L) → indicates normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis
• Hypokalemia (K⁺ 3 mEq/L)
• Alkaline urine (pH 7.9) despite systemic acidosis

These findings indicate renal tubular dysfunction, where the kidney fails to properly reabsorb bicarbonate and other solutes.

Fanconi syndrome is a proximal renal tubular disorder characterized by impaired reabsorption of:

• Bicarbonate
• Glucose
• Phosphate
• Amino acids
• Uric acid

Loss of these substances leads to metabolic acidosis, electrolyte abnormalities, and poor growth (failure to thrive).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presents with a persistent productive cough for the past 3 days, producing thick yellow sputum. He has a history of recurrent sinus infections and failure to thrive since infancy. Previous investigations revealed high sweat chloride content and pancreatic insufficiency. Which of the following findings is most consistent with this patient’s underlying disorder?
options: Abnormal post-translational processing of a transmembrane protein
Decreased transcription of a transmembrane protein
Increased conductivity of a transmembrane chloride channel
Presence of a truncated transmembrane protein on the cell surface
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Abnormal post-translational processing of a transmembrane protein

The child’s history of recurrent respiratory infections, productive cough, failure to thrive, pancreatic insufficiency, and elevated sweat chloride is characteristic of cystic fibrosis.

The most common mutation causing cystic fibrosis is ΔF508 in the CFTR gene, which results in misfolding of the CFTR protein during post-translational processing.

Mechanism:

• The misfolded CFTR chloride channel is recognized as defective in the endoplasmic reticulum.
• It undergoes degradation and fails to reach the cell membrane.
• This leads to defective chloride transport, producing thick mucus in the lungs and pancreas and high chloride levels in sweat.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old child is recovering from Haemophilus influenzae type B meningitis and is clinically stable for discharge. Which of the following investigations should be performed before discharge to detect the most important long-term complication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hearing test

In children recovering from Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis, the most important long-term complication is sensorineural hearing loss.

• Inflammation of the meninges can involve the cochlea and auditory nerve, leading to permanent hearing impairment.
• This complication may not be clinically obvious immediately after recovery.

Therefore, hearing assessment (audiological testing) should be performed before discharge or soon after recovery to allow early detection and intervention.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old girl has her first episode of febrile UTI. After treatment, USG KUB is normal. What is the next investigation required according to current guidelines?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. No further investigations

In a child >3 years with a first febrile UTI who responds well to treatment and has a normal ultrasonography (USG KUB), no further imaging is recommended according to current pediatric UTI guidelines. Micturating cystourethrogram (MCU/VCUG) is reserved for recurrent febrile UTIs, abnormal USG findings, atypical/non-E. coli infections, or suspected vesicoureteric reflux (VUR). A DMSA scan is not performed routinely after the first UTI; it is indicated 4–6 months later only when there is concern for renal scarring, such as after recurrent or atypical infections.

High-Yield

• First febrile UTI + Normal USG (>3 years) → No further imaging
• MCU (VCUG): Recurrent UTI, abnormal USG, atypical/non-E. coli UTI, suspected VUR
• DMSA scan: 4–6 months after infection to detect renal scarring, not acute pyelonephritis routinely.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old presents with persistent respiratory difficulty. Breath sounds reveal a localized, fixed, monophonic wheeze that does not vary with bronchodilator therapy. There is no history of recurrent cough or sputum. Which is the most likely underlying condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intraluminal airway obstruction

A localized, fixed, monophonic wheeze that does not improve with bronchodilators suggests focal airway obstruction, rather than diffuse airway disease like asthma.

Key reasoning:

• Monophonic wheeze → single airway segment involved
• Localized and persistent → structural or obstructive lesion
• No response to bronchodilator → not bronchospasm

Common causes:

• Intraluminal foreign body
• Endobronchial tumor or mucus plug
• Airway stenosis

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-day-old infant has a brisk Moro reflex. Which condition is likely responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypoglycemia

A brisk (exaggerated) Moro reflex in a neonate is most commonly associated with hypoglycemia, which causes neuronal hyperexcitability and may present with jitteriness, tremors, high-pitched cry, exaggerated primitive reflexes, seizures, or apnea. Prompt recognition is essential because prolonged hypoglycemia can result in permanent neurological injury. In contrast, kernicterus and Stage III hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) produce depressed or absent Moro reflexes due to severe CNS dysfunction, while Erb palsy causes an asymmetric Moro reflex with absent movement of the affected upper limb because of brachial plexus injury.

| Moro Reflex | Associated Condition

| ----------- | --------------------

| Brisk/Exaggerated | Hypoglycemia, neonatal drug withdrawal

| Absent bilaterally | Severe HIE, kernicterus, CNS depression

| Asymmetric | Erb palsy, clavicle fracture, humeral fracture

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant is being evaluated for delayed motor milestones. On examination, the child has poor head control and generalized hypotonia. Birth and immediate neonatal period were uncomplicated. Family history is unremarkable. The pediatric neurologist considers several differential diagnoses that can present with hypotonia in infancy. Which of the following conditions is least likely to present with hypotonia during infancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Periventricular leukomalacia

• Hypotonia (“floppy infant”) in early infancy is commonly seen in genetic, neuromuscular, and endocrine disorders, such as Prader–Willi syndrome, congenital myopathies, and congenital hypothyroidism, due to impaired muscle tone or neuromuscular function.
• In contrast, periventricular leukomalacia (PVL), a form of white matter injury seen in premature infants, typically evolves into spasticity and hypertonia (spastic cerebral palsy) rather than persistent hypotonia. Therefore, PVL is least likely to present with hypotonia in infancy.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant presents with recurrent seizures, irritability, poor feeding, and progressive microcephaly. Neuroimaging shows intracranial calcifications and white-matter abnormalities. CSF examination reveals elevated interferon-α levels. Genetic testing identifies a mutation in the TREX1 gene. Which of the following diagnoses best fits this clinical and genetic profile?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aicardi–Goutières syndrome

Aicardi–Goutières syndrome (AGS) is a rare genetic interferonopathy caused by mutations in genes involved in nucleic acid metabolism (commonly TREX1). It presents in infancy with features resembling congenital viral infection (TORCH-like syndrome).

• Early infancy onset
• Recurrent seizures and irritability
• Progressive microcephaly
• Intracranial calcifications and white-matter abnormalities on neuroimaging
• Elevated interferon-α in CSF (hallmark finding)

Why not the other options?

B. Leigh syndrome: Mitochondrial disorder with lactic acidosis and basal ganglia lesions, not intracranial calcifications or ↑CSF interferon-α.

C. Krabbe disease: Lysosomal leukodystrophy causing irritability, stiffness, and demyelination, but no intracranial calcifications or interferon-α elevation.

D. Zellweger syndrome: Peroxisomal disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial dysmorphism, liver dysfunction, not TORCH-like calcifications with TREX1 mutation.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-year-old child is brought with complaint of short stature. The height of the child corresponds to parent’s height and the chronological age of the child corresponds to bone age. What is the likely condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Familial short stature

Familial short stature is characterized by short height consistent with the genetic potential of the parents, with normal growth velocity and normal bone age.

• Height below average but appropriate for parental height (target height)
• Normal growth velocity
• Bone age equal to chronological age
• Normal onset of puberty

This distinguishes it from constitutional growth delay, where bone age is delayed compared to chronological age, and puberty is also delayed.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-year-old child with known Down syndrome presents for routine follow-up. The mother reports poor weight gain and chronic bloating. Examination shows midface hypoplasia and a large tongue. Which of the following conditions is NOT associated with an increased risk in Down syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. NF1

Children with Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) have an increased risk of several medical conditions due to immune dysregulation, craniofacial abnormalities, and genetic factors.

Common associations in Down syndrome:

• Celiac disease → autoimmune condition causing malabsorption, poor weight gain, bloating
• Infantile spasms → increased risk of epilepsy
• Obstructive sleep apnea → due to macroglossia, midface hypoplasia, and hypotonia

Not associated:

• Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) → caused by NF1 gene mutation on chromosome 17, unrelated to trisomy 21.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-year-old male child was presented with a past of persistent cough and foul-smelling stools. His sibling, who had experienced comparable symptoms, passed away a few years earlier. Tests including the sweat chloride test and CFTR gene analysis were conducted and cystic fibrosis was diagnosed. What will happen to the transport of Chloride ions in sweat gland and pancreatic ducts respectively?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decrease, decrease

Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in the CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator) gene, which encodes a chloride channel present in epithelial cells.

Defective CFTR leads to impaired chloride transport in multiple organs:

• Sweat glands: Normally, CFTR reabsorbs chloride (and sodium) from sweat. In cystic fibrosis, chloride reabsorption is decreased, resulting in high chloride levels in sweat (basis of the sweat chloride test).
• Pancreatic ducts: CFTR normally secretes chloride and bicarbonate into the ductal lumen to keep secretions fluid. In cystic fibrosis, chloride secretion is decreased, leading to thick pancreatic secretions and duct obstruction, causing malabsorption and steatorrhea.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-month-old child presents with fever and cough for 4 days. Respiratory rate is 54/min. SpO₂ is 97% on room air. There is no chest indrawing, cyanosis, lethargy, convulsion, or feeding difficulty. According to IMNCI guidelines, the child should be classified as:
options: Pneumonia requiring oral amoxicillin at home
Severe pneumonia requiring immediate referral and injectable antibiotics
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pneumonia requiring oral amoxicillin at home

For age 2–12 months, fast breathing = RR >50/min.

This child:

• RR = 54/min
• No danger signs
• Normal SpO₂

Thus, Pneumonia, managed with oral amoxicillin.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-month-old infant is brought with fever for 1 day and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 4 minutes. The child is alert after the event with no focal neurological deficit. Child is not immunized for age. Examination does not reveal neck stiffness or other meningeal signs. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure parents and discharge without further evaluation
Start oral clobazam prophylaxis for future febrile episodes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lumbar puncture should be considered

The seizure fulfills criteria for simple febrile seizure, but the question asks for the next step.

LP indications in febrile seizure:

• Age < 6 months
• Unimmunized child aged 6–12 months
• Pretreated with antibiotics
• Clinical features of meningitis

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy has had recurrent episodes of productive cough and pneumonia since infancy. He has poor weight gain despite a good appetite and passes bulky, foul-smelling stools. Examination reveals bilateral nasal polyps. Chest CT demonstrates bronchiectasis. Which of the following additional findings is most likely to be present?
options: Bilateral absence of vas deferens with azoospermia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bilateral absence of vas deferens with azoospermia

This child has classic cystic fibrosis (CF):

• Recurrent pneumonia
• Bronchiectasis
• Pancreatic insufficiency → steatorrhea
• Bilateral nasal polyps

A characteristic extra-pulmonary manifestation is congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens, leading to azoospermia and male infertility.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy is brought by his mother with complaints of bedwetting at night, occurring 3 times a week. She reports he has never had a dry night since birth. There is no daytime incontinence, no dysuria, and urine examination is normal. He is otherwise developmentally appropriate. The mother has tried fluid restriction at night but there has been no improvement. Which of the following represents the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Start oral desmopressin immediately as it is the first-line pharmacological agent
Initiate motivational therapy combined with alarm therapy
Treat with oxybutynin as anticholinergics are first-line for this condition
Reassure and advise regulated fluid intake in ratio of 40-20-40 across the day
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Initiate motivational therapy combined with alarm therapy

Nocturnal Enuresis — Classification:

| | Primary (m/c) | Secondary

| --- | ------------- | ---------

| Enuresis | Since birth, never dry | Previously dry period present

| Cause | Developmental/maturation delay of bladder | Stress / UTI

| Management | Improves with age, spontaneous resolution | Treat the cause

This child has primary nocturnal enuresis — never been dry since birth, no UTI, no daytime symptoms.

Treatment ladder for Primary Nocturnal Enuresis:

| Step | Treatment

| ---- | ---------

| Age <6 years | Behavioural therapy — avoid caffeinated drinks, regulated fluid intake (40% morning : 40% noon : 20% after 6pm), timed voiding

| 1st line (all ages) | Non-pharmacological — Motivational therapy + Alarm therapy

| No response to above | Pharmacological — Oral desmopressin (preferred) / Oxybutynin (anticholinergic)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old girl is brought with breast development and pubic hair noticed by her mother over the past 3 months. She also has irregular café-au-lait macules on her trunk and a history of a pathological fracture of the femur. Her LH and FSH levels are found to be suppressed. Which of the following statements about this condition is correct?
options: This is the most common cause of precocious puberty in girls and is gonadotropin dependent
The precocious puberty is driven by autonomous ovarian estrogen secretion and LH/FSH are expectedly low
Hypothalamic hamartoma is the most common cause of this specific syndrome
This condition involves monostotic fibrous dysplasia as its skeletal manifestation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The precocious puberty is driven by autonomous ovarian estrogen secretion and LH/FSH are expectedly low

The clinical triad of precocious puberty + polyostotic fibrous dysplasia + café-au-lait macules is diagnostic of McCune-Albright Syndrome.

McCune-Albright Syndrome features:

• Precocious puberty due to ↑ estrogen (autonomous ovarian secretion)
• Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (not monostotic)
• Café-au-lait macules
• LH and FSH are suppressed.

The suppressed gonadotropins confirm peripheral precocious puberty. Idiopathic is the most common cause for precocious puberty in girls overall, but it is gonadotropin dependent (elevated LH/FSH).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature. On examination, her upper segment to lower segment (US:LS) ratio is abnormal for age with relatively short limbs compared to the trunk. Skull X-ray shows a narrow foramen magnum. Which of the following conditions best explains this clinical picture, and what category of short stature does it represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Achondroplasia

Approach to Short Stature based on US:LS ratio:

| US:LS Normal for age | US:LS Abnormal — Short Trunk | US:LS Abnormal — Short Limbs

| -------------------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------

| Proportionate short stature | Disproportionate | Disproportionate

| Normal variants, Chronic malnutrition (Stunting), GH deficiency | Spondylo-epiphyseal dysplasia, Hemivertebrae, MPS, Pott's disease (TB spine) | Achondroplasia, Rickets, Congenital hypothyroidism

Achondroplasia presents with disproportionate short stature due to short limbs (rhizomelic shortening), with a characteristic narrow foramen magnum — a high-yield distinguishing feature. MPS and Pott's disease cause a short trunk pattern, not short limbs.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 9-month-old infant presents with 2 days of profuse diarrhea. On exam the child is lethargic, has delayed capillary refill, cool extremities, and weak pulses. The child has vomited multiple times in the ER and is noted to have a palpable sausage-shaped abdominal mass and currant-jelly stools. Which of the following clinical scenarios would still be an indication for ORS rather than a contraindication?
options: Depressed level of consciousness with aspiration risk
Mild dehydration with preserved thirst and oral intake
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mild dehydration with preserved thirst and oral intake

Oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the treatment of choice for mild to moderate dehydration when the child is alert and able to drink, as intestinal sodium–glucose cotransport allows effective fluid absorption even during diarrhea.

ORS is appropriate when:

• Mild dehydration
• Child is conscious and able to drink
• No intestinal obstruction
• Vomiting is mild and not persistent

Contraindications to ORS:

• Hypovolemic shock
• Severe dehydration requiring IV fluids
• Depressed consciousness/aspiration risk
• Intestinal obstruction (e.g., intussusception)
• Persistent severe vomiting preventing intake

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 9-month-old infant with known Tetralogy of Fallot suddenly becomes irritable and deeply cyanotic while crying. During the episode, pulse oximetry shows a drop in saturation and on auscultation the systolic murmur becomes faint. Which of the following is a clinical marker of a cyanotic spell?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Disappearance of murmur.

A cyanotic (hypercyanotic or “tet”) spell in Tetralogy of Fallot occurs due to sudden increase in right-to-left shunting across the VSD from worsening right ventricular outflow tract obstruction.

During a tet spell:

• Cyanosis worsens
• Oxygen saturation falls
• The systolic murmur becomes faint or disappears because less blood flows through the pulmonary outflow tract, reducing turbulence.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 9-year-old boy with known cystic fibrosis presents for routine follow-up. Despite pancreatic enzyme supplementation, he continues to have recurrent pulmonary exacerbations. Genetic testing reveals a CFTR mutation causing defective protein folding and impaired trafficking of the CFTR protein to the cell membrane. Which of the following drugs specifically targets this defect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lumacaftor

CFTR modulators are chosen based on the underlying molecular defect:

| Drug | Mechanism

| ---- | ---------

| Ivacaftor | CFTR potentiator; increases duration of chloride channel opening

| Lumacaftor | CFTR corrector; improves folding and trafficking of CFTR protein to the cell membrane

The stem describes a protein-folding defect (e.g., ΔF508 mutation), making Lumacaftor the appropriate therapy.

Ivacaftor works when the channel reaches the membrane but has defective gating.

• Dornase alfa reduces mucus viscosity but does not correct CFTR dysfunction.
• Azithromycin is used for chronic airway inflammation/infection control.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby born at 32 weeks is brought for developmental assessment at chronological age of 6 months. What age should be used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 16 weeks

Corrected (adjusted) age should be used = 16 weeks.

Why:

• Full term = 40 weeks. Baby born at 32 weeks → prematurity = 8 weeks
• Chronological age at assessment = 6 months = 24 weeks
• Corrected age = Chronological age – Degree of prematurity = 24 – 8 = 16 weeks

Key concept (high-yield):

• Corrected age is used for developmental assessment and growth monitoring in preterm infants
• Applied until 2–3 years of age (most texts say correct till 2 years for growth parameters, and up to 2–3 years for developmental milestones)
• Formula: Corrected age = Chronological age − (40 weeks − gestational age at birth)

Practical pearl: Always use corrected age (not chronological age) when plotting growth on charts or assessing milestones in a preterm baby until 2 years — prevents unnecessary labeling as "delayed" when the baby is actually appropriate for corrected age.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby has straw-yellow fluid staining clothes. Fluid comes out of the umbilicus when the child strains. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Urachal fistula

A patent urachus (urachal fistula) results from failure of obliteration of the urachus, which normally connects the fetal bladder to the umbilicus (allantois). It presents with continuous or intermittent leakage of straw-colored urine from the umbilicus, often becoming more obvious during crying, straining, or micturition due to increased intravesical pressure. The diagnosis is confirmed by ultrasonography and may be further evaluated with a sinogram or voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG). Definitive treatment is complete surgical excision of the urachal tract to prevent recurrent infection and potential malignant transformation later in life.

• Patent urachus → urine from umbilicus (straw-colored fluid).
• Leakage increases with straining/crying/micturition.
• Patent vitellointestinal (omphalomesenteric) duct → fecal or bilious discharge, not urine.
• Urachal cyst presents as an infected midline infraumbilical swelling without external discharge.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby is delivered at 32 weeks of gestation via normal vaginal delivery. The obstetrician clamps and cuts the cord immediately after birth. The neonatologist on call is counselling the residents about optimal newborn care practices. All of the following statements regarding immediate newborn care are true except:
options: Delayed cord clamping at 30–60 seconds after birth reduces the incidence of intraventricular hemorrhage in preterm babies
Vernix caseosa should be left on the skin and not cleaned at birth
Eye antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended routinely in all newborns to prevent ophthalmia neonatorum
Bathing should be deferred to beyond 24 hours of birth
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Eye antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended routinely in all newborns to prevent ophthalmia neonatorum

Care of Newborns — Key Practices:

| Practice | Detail

| -------- | ------

| Aseptic precautions | Clean hands, surface, cord cutting, clamp, cord

| Early skin-to-skin contact | Prevents hypothermia; establishes early breastfeeding

| Delayed cord clamping | 30–60 seconds after birth → ↓ anemia, ↓ IVH in preterm

| Cleaning | Meconium, secretions, blood cleaned; Vernix caseosa — NOT cleaned

| Bathing | Deferred to >24 hours

| Eye antibiotic prophylaxis | Not recommended

Normal Newborn Parameters:

| Parameter | Normal Range

| --------- | ------------

| Heart rate | 120–160/min

| Respiratory rate | 40–60/min

| BP | 60/40 mmHg

| Temperature | 36.5–37.5°C

| Meconium passage | Up to 48 hours after birth

| Urine passage | Up to 24 hours after birth

Eye antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended routinely. In this preterm baby, the cord was clamped immediately, which is suboptimal, delayed clamping at 30–60 seconds would have reduced the risk of IVH, a particularly important benefit in preterm neonates.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with a distinctive "elfin" facial appearance, excessive friendliness toward strangers, and well-preserved verbal abilities despite intellectual disability is found to have supravalvular aortic stenosis on echocardiography. Genetic testing reveals a microdeletion on a specific chromosome. Which structural protein's gene is deleted, and how does its loss directly explain the cardiovascular finding?
options: Fibrillin-1 deletion on chromosome 15, causing aortic root weakness
Elastin gene deletion on chromosome 7, causing loss of arterial wall elasticity and stenosis
Collagen type III deletion on chromosome 2, causing vascular fragility and rupture
Dystrophin deletion on the X chromosome, causing cardiomyopathy rather than stenosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Elastin gene deletion on chromosome 7, causing loss of arterial wall elasticity and stenosis

Williams syndrome = microdeletion of the long arm of chromosome 7, including the elastin gene. Loss of elastin reduces arterial wall elasticity/recoil, predisposing to stenotic lesions (supravalvular aortic stenosis, pulmonary artery stenosis, renal artery stenosis) rather than aneurysmal/rupture-prone lesions (which would be more typical of collagen defects like vascular EDS or fibrillin defects like Marfan syndrome, both causing dilation rather than narrowing).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with rickets has the following profile: Serum calcium: Normal Serum phosphate: Low PTH: Normal 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D: Low–normal Urinary phosphate excretion: Increased Which therapy directly targets the primary pathogenic mechanism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Burosumab

Rickets with normal calcium, low phosphate, normal PTH, low–normal 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and increased urinary phosphate excretion suggests FGF23-mediated hypophosphatemic rickets, most commonly X-linked hypophosphatemia. In this disorder, excess Fibroblast growth factor (FGF23) causes Renal phosphate wasting → hypophosphatemia and reduced renal 1-α hydroxylase activity → decreased production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D

The targeted therapy is Burosumab, a monoclonal antibody against FGF23 that:

• Inhibits excess FGF23 activity
• Increases renal phosphate reabsorption
• Raises 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels
• Improves bone mineralization and rickets

Why not the other options?

A. Ergocalciferol (Vitamin D₂): Used for nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets, not FGF23 excess.

B. Oral phosphate supplementation: Traditional therapy but does not address the underlying FGF23 excess.

D. Teriparatide: PTH analog used in osteoporosis; unrelated to phosphate-wasting rickets.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with rickets not responding to treatment is being evaluated. Investigations show a serum calcium level of 9 mg/dL, phosphate level of 2 mg/dL, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and normal parathyroid hormone levels with normal arterial blood gas levels. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypophosphatemic rickets

Hypophosphatemic rickets (most commonly X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets) is characterized by renal phosphate wasting, leading to defective bone mineralization.

• Normal serum calcium
• Low serum phosphate
• Elevated alkaline phosphatase
• Normal or mildly increased PTH
• Normal acid–base status

Rickets that does not respond to vitamin D therapy should raise suspicion for hypophosphatemic rickets.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with Tetralogy of Fallot develops hypercyanotic (Tet) spells while awaiting corrective open-heart surgery. Which of the following drugs would worsen the cyanosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Nicardipine

| Drug | Effect | Role in Tet Spell

| ---- | ------ | -----------------

| A. Sodium Bicarbonate | Corrects metabolic acidosis → ↓ respiratory drive → ↓ venous return | ✅ TREATS — breaks the vicious cycle

| B. Propranolol | β-blocker → ↓ HR + ↓ infundibular spasm (relaxes dynamic RVOTO) | ✅ TREATS — drug of choice for acute spell & long-term prophylaxis

| C. Phenylephrine | Pure α-agonist → ↑↑ SVR → forces blood through pulmonary circuit | ✅ TREATS — ↑ SVR reduces R→L shunt

| D. Nicardipine | Dihydropyridine CCB → vasodilation → ↓ SVR | ❌ WORSENS — ↓ SVR increases R→L shunt → ↑ cyanosis

Acute Tet Spell Management — Stepwise

| Step | Intervention | Mechanism

| ---- | ------------ | ---------

| 1 | Knee-chest position | ↑ SVR + ↓ venous return

| 2 | Calm the child, O₂ | ↓ O₂ demand, ↓ hypoxia

| 3 | Morphine IV/SC | ↓ Respiratory drive, ↓ infundibular spasm

| 4 | IV fluids | ↑ Preload → ↑ pulmonary flow

| 5 | Sodium bicarbonate | Correct acidosis

| 6 | Phenylephrine | ↑ SVR

| 7 | Propranolol IV | ↓ Infundibular spasm

| 8 | Ketamine | ↑ SVR + sedation

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child's height is measured at 87.5 cm. His arm span is measured and found to be 85 cm. His weight is appropriate. All of the following statements about this child are true except:
options: His current height represents half of his expected adult height
Arm span becomes equal to height at 11 years of age
His weight is approximately double his birth weight
He is gaining approximately 2 kg/year at this stage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. His weight is approximately double his birth weight

Height 87.5 cm = 2 years of age. Half of adult height is reached at 18–24 months.

| Age | Arm span vs Length

| --- | ------------------

| Birth | Arm span < Length (by 2.5 cm)

| 11 years | Arm span = Length

| >11 years | Arm span > Length (by >1 cm)

| Milestone | Age

| --------- | ---

| Weight doubles | 5–6 months

| Weight triples | 1 year

| Weight quadruples | 2 years

At 2 years, weight quadruples (not doubles) the birth weight. Weight gain of 2 kg/year is the correct rate between 1–7 years.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A clinician evaluates four patients with different trinucleotide repeat expansion diseases, each showing progressively earlier onset and more severe symptoms in their children compared to themselves. Which trinucleotide repeat and inheritance pattern correctly matches Friedreich ataxia, and how does its inheritance pattern affect the expected pattern of genetic anticipation compared to the autosomal dominant diseases in this category?
options: (CAG)n, autosomal dominant — anticipation prominent, similar to Huntington disease
(GAA)n, autosomal recessive — anticipation is less classically prominent compared to the autosomal dominant trinucleotide repeat diseases
(CTG)n, autosomal dominant — identical anticipation pattern to myotonic dystrophy
(CGG)n, X-linked dominant — anticipation occurs equally regardless of parental transmission
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. (GAA)n, autosomal recessive — anticipation is less classically prominent compared to the autosomal dominant trinucleotide repeat diseases

Friedreich ataxia = (GAA)n repeat, autosomal recessive inheritance (mnemonic: "Ataxic GAAit"). This is the only trinucleotide repeat disease in this group with autosomal recessive inheritance — Huntington disease (CAG, AD), myotonic dystrophy (CTG, AD), and Fragile X syndrome (CGG, X-linked) are all dominant patterns. Anticipation (earlier onset/worse severity in successive generations) is most classically described and pronounced in the dominant trinucleotide repeat diseases; its behavior in an autosomal recessive context is distinct since both parents must contribute an expanded allele, altering the inheritance dynamics compared to single-parent transmission in dominant conditions.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A father brings his child with a distended abdomen and poor feeding. Laboratory investigations show markedly low serum albumin levels. Which of the following findings are not consistent with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Simian facies

The clinical picture of distended abdomen, poor feeding, and markedly low serum albumin suggests kwashiorkor, a form of severe protein malnutrition.

Characteristic features of kwashiorkor include:

• Edema due to hypoalbuminemia
• Fatty liver from impaired lipoprotein synthesis
• Skin changes such as “flaky paint” dermatosis
• Hair changes like the “flag sign” (alternating bands of depigmented hair due to intermittent protein deficiency)

Simian facies, however, is typical of marasmus, which is caused by severe calorie deficiency and leads to loss of subcutaneous fat giving an “old man” or monkey-like appearance.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A full-term neonate develops tachypnea and central cyanosis within a few hours of birth. Pulse oximetry reveals an oxygen saturation of 96% in the right hand and 84% in the left foot. Femoral pulses are palpable with no brachiofemoral delay. Echocardiography shows a structurally normal heart but markedly elevated pulmonary artery pressures. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)

In persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), the normal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) after birth fails to occur. As a result:

• Pulmonary artery pressure remains abnormally high.
• Blood is shunted right-to-left through the patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and/or foramen ovale.
• The right upper limb (preductal) receives blood before it mixes with deoxygenated blood at the ductus, resulting in a higher oxygen saturation than the lower limbs (postductal).

This produces the characteristic finding of: Preductal SpO₂ > Postductal SpO₂

The presence of a structurally normal heart with elevated pulmonary pressures strongly supports the diagnosis of PPHN.

Why not the other options?

• A. Coarctation of the aorta: Typically presents with weak femoral pulses and radiofemoral/brachiofemoral delay, which are absent in this infant.
• B. Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR): Causes cyanosis but echocardiography would demonstrate anomalous pulmonary venous drainage rather than a structurally normal heart.
• D. Eisenmenger syndrome: Develops over years as a consequence of long-standing congenital left-to-right shunts and does not occur in the neonatal period.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A late preterm, asymptomatic neonate has a blood glucose of 18 mg/dL at 1 hour of life. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Feed orally and recheck in 1 hour
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Start IV 10% dextrose infusion immediately

Severe neonatal hypoglycemia (<25 mg/dL in the first 4 hours of life) requires immediate treatment with intravenous glucose, even if the infant is asymptomatic, because of the risk of acute neurologic injury and seizures.

Management:

• Severe hypoglycemia (<25 mg/dL in first 4 hours) → IV 10% dextrose bolus/infusion immediately
• Mild/moderate hypoglycemia → feeding or dextrose gel may be used

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A macrosomic infant of a poorly controlled diabetic mother develops lethargy and seizures on day 2 of life. Labs show hematocrit of 72%. Which complication is most likely due to fetal hyperinsulinemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Renal vein thrombosis

Infants of poorly controlled diabetic mothers often develop fetal hyperinsulinemia, which leads to macrosomia and chronic intrauterine hypoxia. Hypoxia stimulates increased erythropoietin production, resulting in polycythemia (hematocrit >65%).

Severe polycythemia causes hyperviscosity of blood, increasing the risk of thrombotic complications, most classically renal vein thrombosis in the neonate.

Why not the other options?

B. Adrenal hemorrhage: Usually due to birth trauma, asphyxia, or difficult delivery, not polycythemia from hyperinsulinemia.

C. Intracranial calcifications: Seen in congenital infections (TORCH), not in infants of diabetic mothers.

D. Periventricular leukomalacia: Occurs mainly in premature infants due to hypoxic-ischemic injury, not due to neonatal polycythemia/hyperviscosity.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A mother of a 2-month-old infant is concerned about her baby's slow weight gain. The baby is exclusively breastfed. The baby passes urine 6-8 times a day. What is the most likely explanation in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Insufficient intake of hindmilk

In an exclusively breastfed infant with slow weight gain but adequate urine output (6–8 times/day), the most likely cause is insufficient intake of hindmilk.

• Foremilk (initial milk during feeding) is low in fat and high in lactose, mainly satisfying thirst.
• Hindmilk (milk released later during feeding) is rich in fat and calories, which is essential for weight gain.

If the infant switches breasts too early or feeds for a short duration, they may receive mostly foremilk and not enough hindmilk, leading to poor weight gain despite adequate hydration.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A muscle biopsy from a patient with proximal weakness and recurrent episodes resembling strokes shows red-staining fibers with a trichrome stain, and electron microscopy reveals crystalline inclusions within abnormally proliferated organelles. Which underlying defect explains the compensatory change seen on light microscopy, and which specific syndrome (among mitochondrial myopathies) is most consistent with stroke-like episodes as a defining feature?
options: Defective oxidative phosphorylation → compensatory mitochondrial proliferation; MERRF
Defective oxidative phosphorylation → compensatory mitochondrial proliferation; MELAS
Defective glycolysis → compensatory mitochondrial proliferation; MELAS
Complex I mutation → neuronal death in retina; MELAS
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Defective oxidative phosphorylation → compensatory mitochondrial proliferation; MELAS

Ragged red fibers result from compensatory mitochondrial proliferation secondary to failed oxidative phosphorylation. Among mitochondrial myopathies, MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes) is specifically defined by the stroke-like episodes described in the vignette, distinguishing it from MERRF (myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers, no stroke-like component) — both share the ragged red fiber finding but differ in their defining clinical feature.

| Mitochondrial myopathy | Defining feature | Shared finding

| ---------------------- | ---------------- | --------------

| MELAS | Lactic acidosis, stroke-like episodes | Ragged red fibers

| MERRF | Myoclonic epilepsy | Ragged red fibers

| Leber hereditary optic neuropathy | Complex I mutation, optic neuropathy | Not ragged red fibers — distinct pathology

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A neonate born after prolonged rupture of membranes presents on day 2 of life with poor feeding and lethargy. Sepsis screen: TLC 4200/mm³, ANC 2000/mm³, I:T ratio 0.15, CRP 0.8 mg/dL, micro-ESR 10 mm in 1st hour. What is the correct interpretation and next step?
options: Sepsis screen positive; start Ampicillin + Gentamicin empirically based on screen alone
Sepsis screen negative; treatment decision should rest on clinical suspicion
Sepsis screen positive; proceed directly to lumbar puncture and start Ampicillin + Cefotaxime
Screen is indeterminate; repeat all 5 parameters after 24 hours before any decision
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sepsis screen negative; treatment decision should rest on clinical suspicion

| Parameter | Cutoff for positivity | This baby's value

| --------- | --------------------- | -----------------

| TLC | <5000/mm³ | 4200

| ANC | <1800/mm³ | 2000

| I:T ratio | >0.2 | 0.15

| CRP | >1 mg/dL | 0.8

| Micro-ESR | ≥15 mm in 1st hr | 10

• Screen is labeled positive only if ≥2 of 5 parameters are abnormal; here only 1 (TLC) is positive → screen is negative.
• A negative screen has good negative predictive value but does not exclude sepsis; blood culture remains the gold standard.
• Since the infant is symptomatic (poor feeding, lethargy) with a maternal risk factor (PROM), clinical judgment — not the screen result alone — should guide whether to start empirical antibiotics.
• LP is reserved for symptomatic/culture-positive neonates once a decision to treat has been made, not triggered by screen positivity per se.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A neonate born at 38 weeks weighs 2.1 kg with loose skin folds and is classified as SGA. Her head circumference is appropriate for gestational age but body weight is markedly reduced. Her Ponderal Index is 1.8. Which type of IUGR does she represent and what is its most likely aetiology?
options: Symmetric IUGR due to fetal chromosomal anomaly
Asymmetric IUGR due to uteroplacental insufficiency
Symmetric IUGR due to early TORCH infection
Asymmetric IUGR due to fetal metabolic disorder
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Asymmetric IUGR due to uteroplacental insufficiency

This term infant has low birth weight with a relatively preserved head circumference, indicating the brain-sparing effect, a hallmark of asymmetric IUGR. The Ponderal Index (PI) <2 supports this diagnosis, reflecting reduced soft tissue and fat mass with relatively normal linear growth. Asymmetric IUGR typically develops in the third trimester due to uteroplacental insufficiency, commonly associated with maternal conditions such as hypertension, preeclampsia, malnutrition, smoking, or placental disease. In contrast, symmetric IUGR presents with proportionately reduced head and body size (PI >2) and is usually caused by early fetal insults, such as chromosomal abnormalities, congenital infections (TORCH), or genetic syndromes.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A neonate born at term undergoes routine newborn metabolic screening. At which age is screening for congenital hypothyroidism ideally performed?
options: Within the first 6 hours of life
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Between 48–72 hours after birth

Screening for Congenital hypothyroidism should ideally be performed between 48–72 hours after birth using a heel-prick blood sample.

• Immediately after birth, there is a physiologic neonatal TSH surge that occurs within the first few hours of life.
• Testing too early (eg, within the first 6–24 hours) may give false-positive elevated TSH levels.
• Waiting 48–72 hours allow the transient TSH surge to settle, providing more accurate detection of persistent hypothyroidism.

Early detection through newborn screening allows prompt treatment with Levothyroxine, which prevents irreversible intellectual disability and growth failure associated with untreated congenital hypothyroidism.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A neonate is assessed at 5 minutes of life. The following findings are documented: limbs show some flexion, HR is 88 bpm, baby grimaces on stimulation, body is pink but extremities are blue, and breathing is irregular and slow. A second assessment at 10 minutes shows identical findings. Which of the following correctly interprets this clinical scenario?
options: APGAR score is 6 at 5 minutes; this is within normal limits and no further action needed
APGAR score is 5 at 5 minutes; persistent low score at 10 minutes is consistent with birth asphyxia
APGAR score is 7 at 5 minutes; persistently low score suggests birth asphyxia only if umbilical cord pH <7.0
APGAR score is 6 at 5 minutes; birth asphyxia is defined as APGAR 0–3 at >5 minutes only when accompanied by multiorgan damage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. APGAR score is 5 at 5 minutes; persistent low score at 10 minutes is consistent with birth asphyxia

APGAR Score Calculation:

| Sign | Finding | Score

| ---- | ------- | -----

| Activity (tone) | Some flexion | 1

| Pulse (HR) | 88 bpm (<100) | 1

| Grimace | Grimace | 1

| Appearance | Pink body, blue extremities | 1

| Respiratory effort | Irregular, slow | 1

| Total | | 5

APGAR Interpretation:

| Score | Interpretation

| ----- | --------------

| 7–10 | Normal

| <7 | Low → due to birth asphyxia

| 0–3 at >5 minutes | Birth asphyxia

Score of 5 is low (<7). The key two-step reasoning: score of 5 at 5 minutes is low but does not itself define birth asphyxia — birth asphyxia requires APGAR 0–3 at >5 minutes. However, a persistently low score at 10 minutes with score of 5 combined with other features (umbilical cord pH <7.0, HIE, multiorgan damage) is consistent with birth asphyxia.

Features of Birth Asphyxia:

| Feature | Threshold

| ------- | ---------

| APGAR | 0–3 at >5 minutes

| Umbilical cord pH | <7.0 (lactic acidosis)

| Neurological damage | HIE

| Other | Multiorgan damage

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn boy is brought to the nursery for evaluation after delivery. The mother received no prenatal care but reports that the pregnancy was uncomplicated and she was healthy. The infant was born via spontaneous vaginal delivery and required no resuscitation. On examination, the infant is below the 3rd percentile for weight, 25th percentile for length, and 50th percentile for head circumference. Hepatosplenomegaly is present on examination. Over the next 48 hours, the infant develops jaundice, clear rhinorrhea, and a maculopapular rash on the feet and buttocks that later desquamates. Which of the following congenital infections is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Syphilis

Congenital syphilis results from transplacental transmission of Treponema pallidum from an infected mother to the fetus.

Typical early features (within the first weeks of life) include:

• Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)
• Hepatosplenomegaly
• Jaundice
• “Snuffles” (profuse mucopurulent rhinorrhea) due to nasal mucosal inflammation
• Maculopapular rash involving palms, soles, buttocks, often followed by desquamation

These findings are characteristic of early congenital syphilis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn girl is evaluated in the delivery room for respiratory distress. The patient was born 15 minutes ago by spontaneous vaginal delivery at 37 weeks gestation to a mother who received no prenatal care. Temperature is 37°C (98.6°F) pulse is 176/min, and respirations are 70/min. Pulse oximetry is 82% on room air. Physical examination shows grunting; subcostal and suprasternal retractions; and cyanosis of the lips and tongue. The chest appears rounded and the abdomen appears flat. Auscultation reveals absent breath sounds on the left and clear breath sounds on the right. Heart sounds are loudest in the right chest. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endotracheal intubation

This neonate with severe respiratory distress, absent breath sounds on the left side, mediastinal shift (heart sounds louder on the right), and a scaphoid/flat abdomen is most consistent with congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH).

• A defect in the diaphragm allows abdominal organs to herniate into the thoracic cavity.
• This compresses the lungs and causes pulmonary hypoplasia and severe respiratory distress immediately after birth.

Immediate management:

• Endotracheal intubation with mechanical ventilation to stabilize the airway and oxygenation.
• Bag-mask ventilation must be avoided because it can inflate the stomach and intestines, worsening lung compression.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn infant develops nephrotic syndrome within the first two weeks of life. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s nephrotic syndrome?
options: Abnormality in the polycystin gene type
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Abnormality in the nephrin gene

•

Nephrotic syndrome presenting within the first 3 months (especially first few weeks) strongly suggests Congenital Nephrotic Syndrome (CNS).

•

The most classic form is Congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type, caused by mutation in the NPHS1 (nephrin) gene

This produces:

• Massive proteinuria
• Hypoalbuminemia
• Edema
• Progression to renal failure

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn infant fails to pass meconium for the first 48 hours. On examination, the abdomen is distended and emesis has occurred overnight. What should be the next diagnostic step?
options: Contrast imaging of the lower GI tract
Genotype of the child for cystic fibrosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Contrast imaging of the lower GI tract

Failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life with abdominal distension and vomiting suggests neonatal intestinal obstruction. The initial diagnostic step is contrast imaging of the lower gastrointestinal tract (contrast enema).

• It helps differentiate common causes of distal neonatal obstruction, such as:

o Hirschsprung disease (transition zone between dilated proximal bowel and narrow distal aganglionic segment)

o Meconium ileus (microcolon with inspissated meconium; often associated with cystic fibrosis)

o Small left colon syndrome

• It is both diagnostic and sometimes therapeutic (e.g., helps evacuate meconium in meconium ileus).

Why not the other options initially?

A. Anorectal manometry → used later to confirm Hirschsprung disease by demonstrating absence of the rectoanal inhibitory reflex.

B. CF genotype testing or D. Sweat chloride test → performed if meconium ileus is suspected after imaging findings.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn is brought with facial asymmetry. On examination, there is hemifacial hypoplasia, a small mandible, preauricular skin tags, and a limbal dermoid in the eye. Hearing impairment is also suspected. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Goldenhar syndrome

Goldenhar syndrome (oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum) is a congenital disorder involving abnormal development of the first and second branchial arches.

Classic features:

• Hemifacial microsomia/hypoplasia

• Mandibular hypoplasia

• Preauricular skin tags or malformed ears

• Ocular dermoids (especially limbal dermoids)

• Conductive hearing loss

Associated abnormalities:

• Vertebral anomalies

• Facial asymmetry

• Cleft lip/palate

• Cardiac and renal defects may occur

Pathogenesis: Defective development of first and second pharyngeal arches

Important differential diagnoses:

• Treacher Collins syndrome → bilateral facial abnormalities without limbal dermoids
• Pierre Robin sequence → micrognathia, glossoptosis, cleft palate
• Down syndrome → characteristic facies and hypotonia

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn presents with vomiting, dehydration, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypotension at 10 days of life. Physical exam shows 46,XY genitalia with female-appearing external genitalia. Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone, testosterone, and cortisol are all markedly low. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lipoid adrenal hyperplasia

Lipoid congenital adrenal hyperplasia (lipoid CAH) is caused by a defect in the StAR (steroidogenic acute regulatory) protein, which is required for transporting cholesterol into mitochondria for steroid hormone synthesis.

Key consequences:

• Failure of synthesis of all adrenal and gonadal steroids
• ↓ Cortisol, ↓ aldosterone, ↓ androgens/testosterone
• Leads to salt-wasting crisis in the neonatal period (vomiting, dehydration, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn screening test shows elevated immunoreactive trypsinogen. Sweat chloride testing confirms the diagnosis. Genetic analysis reveals a deletion causing loss of a single phenylalanine residue at position 508 of a chloride channel protein. Which downstream cellular event most directly explains the abnormally thick mucus secretions seen in this disease?
options: Misfolded CFTR protein is properly trafficked to the membrane but functions abnormally, directly increasing Cl- secretion
Misfolded CFTR protein fails proper trafficking, is absent from the membrane, causing ↓Cl- (and H2O) secretion with compensatory ↑Na+ reabsorption via ENaC, increasing H2O reabsorption
ΔF508 mutation directly increases ENaC channel density, independent of any CFTR trafficking defect
CFTR protein reaches the membrane normally, but ATP-gating is permanently locked open, causing excessive Cl- secretion and dehydrated mucus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Misfolded CFTR protein fails proper trafficking, is absent from the membrane, causing ↓Cl- (and H2O) secretion with compensatory ↑Na+ reabsorption via ENaC, increasing H2O reabsorption

ΔF508 (Phe508 deletion) → misfolded CFTR protein → improper trafficking → CFTR absent from cell membrane → ↓Cl⁻ (and H2O) secretion → compensatory ↑Na+ reabsorption via ENaC → ↑H2O reabsorption from the lumen → abnormally thick, dehydrated mucus in airways and thick secretions in GI tract/pancreatic ducts. This is a trafficking defect, not a gating or density defect — distinguishing it from other CFTR mutation classes.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A pediatrician is evaluating causes of refractory rickets in a child not responding to vitamin D therapy. All of the following statements are true except:
options: Familial hypophosphatemic rickets is inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern
Vitamin D–dependent rickets results from abnormalities in vitamin D metabolism
Chronic kidney disease is typically associated with elevated serum phosphate levels
Presence of metabolic acidosis with hypophosphatemia strongly favors vitamin D–dependent rickets
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Presence of metabolic acidosis with hypophosphatemia strongly favors vitamin D–dependent rickets

| Finding | Diagnosis favored

| ------- | -----------------

| Low phosphate + Acidosis | RTA

| Low phosphate + No acidosis + High PTH | VDDR

| Low phosphate + No acidosis + Normal PTH | Familial hypophosphatemic rickets

| High phosphate | CKD

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A pregnant woman at 10 weeks gestation is diagnosed with chickenpox. Her neonate is born with cicatricial skin lesions, limb hypoplasia, and eye abnormalities. Which intervention should be given to a neonate born to a mother who had varicella 3 days before delivery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. VZIG (Varicella Zoster Immunoglobulin)

A neonate whose mother develops varicella from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery is at high risk of severe neonatal varicella because there is insufficient time for maternal protective IgG antibodies to cross the placenta. Therefore, the recommended post-exposure prophylaxis is Varicella Zoster Immunoglobulin (VZIG), which should be administered as soon as possible after birth. If the neonate subsequently develops signs of varicella despite VZIG, intravenous acyclovir is indicated. The live varicella vaccine is contraindicated at birth and is administered routinely only after 12 months of age. The congenital findings described (cicatricial skin scars, limb hypoplasia, and ocular abnormalities) are characteristic of Congenital Varicella Syndrome, which occurs following maternal infection during early pregnancy (highest risk between 13–20 weeks gestation).

High-Yield

• Maternal varicella: 5 days before to 2 days after delivery → Give neonatal VZIG
• Neonatal varicella develops despite VZIG → IV acyclovir
• Congenital varicella syndrome: Cicatricial scars, limb hypoplasia, eye and CNS defects
• Varicella vaccine: Live vaccine, not given at birth; routine dose starts at 12 months

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A severely malnourished child in the stabilisation phase develops fever and poor feeding on day 3. The most likely infecting organism and appropriate empirical antibiotic are:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gram-negative Enterobacteriaceae — IV ampicillin + gentamicin

Children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) are profoundly immunocompromised due to impaired cell-mediated immunity, reduced complement activity, defective phagocyte function, and loss of mucosal barrier integrity. Consequently, they may have serious bacterial infections with minimal clinical signs, and Gram-negative enteric organisms (especially Enterobacteriaceae such as E. coli and Klebsiella) are the most common pathogens. Therefore, all children admitted in the stabilisation phase receive empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics, with IV ampicillin plus gentamicin as the recommended first-line regimen. Iron supplementation is withheld during the first week, as acute infection and poor intestinal absorption increase free radical generation and may promote bacterial growth; it is started only after stabilization and return of appetite.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A stable 1.8 kg LBW neonate develops cold extremities with a warm trunk. Axillary temperature is 36.2°C. The most appropriate immediate management is:
options: Kangaroo Mother Care with skin-to-skin contact — conduction mechanism
Warmed intravenous fluids to raise core temperature
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Kangaroo Mother Care with skin-to-skin contact — conduction mechanism

The neonate has cold stress (mild hypothermia), defined as an axillary temperature of 36.0–36.4°C, with cold extremities and a warm trunk indicating peripheral vasoconstriction. Since the infant is stable and weighs 1.8 kg, the recommended immediate management is Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC). KMC provides warmth through conduction via continuous skin-to-skin contact, while also promoting breastfeeding, cardiorespiratory stability, weight gain, and reducing neonatal morbidity. Radiant warmers (radiation) and incubators (convection) are preferred for unstable, critically ill, or extremely preterm infants, whereas warmed intravenous fluids are reserved for severe hypothermia or associated shock.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A term IDM (infant of a diabetic mother) presents with tachypnea and a harsh systolic murmur. Echocardiography reveals asymmetric septal hypertrophy with no outflow obstruction. What is the underlying mechanism?
options: Fetal hyperinsulinemia acting as a growth factor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fetal hyperinsulinemia acting as a growth factor

• In infants of diabetic mothers (IDM), maternal hyperglycemia leads to fetal hyperglycemia, which stimulates the fetal pancreas to produce excess insulin.
• Fetal hyperinsulinemia acts as a growth factor, causing myocardial hypertrophy, particularly asymmetric septal hypertrophy (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy). This may present with tachypnea and a systolic murmur in the neonate.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A term neonate becomes cyanotic shortly after birth. Saturations do not improve with 100% oxygen (hyperoxia test negative). Which lesion most likely benefits from maintaining ductal patency with prostaglandins?
options: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR) obstructed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Transposition of great arteries (TGA)

• A neonate with severe cyanosis that does not improve with 100% oxygen (negative hyperoxia test) suggests a cyanotic congenital heart disease with right-to-left shunt.
• In Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA), the systemic and pulmonary circulations run in parallel rather than in series, so survival depends on mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood through the ductus arteriosus, ASD, or VSD.
• Maintaining ductal patency with prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) allows mixing between the circulations and improves systemic oxygenation until definitive surgical correction (arterial switch operation).

Why not others?

A. Obstructed TAPVR: Requires urgent surgery; prostaglandin does not help much.

B. Tetralogy of Fallot: Cyanosis due to RV outflow obstruction; PDA not essential for survival.

D. Tricuspid atresia: PGE₁ may help but not the classic duct-dependent mixing lesion.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A term neonate delivered normally is being examined at birth. On turning the baby's head to the right, the right arm extends and the left arm flexes. At 5 months, the same reflex is still elicitable. The mother asks when the baby will start showing the parachute reflex. Which of the following is correct regarding these two reflexes?
options: ATNR should disappear by 6 months; parachute reflex appears at 7–8 months and persists throughout life
ATNR disappears by 6 months along with Moro reflex; parachute reflex appears at 4 months
Persistence of ATNR beyond 5 months is normal; parachute reflex disappears by 1 year
ATNR involves contralateral extension and ipsilateral flexion on head turning
questions.explanation:
