Correct answer: A. ATNR should disappear by 6 months; parachute reflex appears at 7–8 months and persists throughout life

Neonatal Reflexes:

| Reflex | Characteristics

| ------ | ---------------

| Moro reflex | Bilateral; disappears at 6 months

| ATNR | Head turn → ipsilateral extension, contralateral flexion; disappears around 6 months

| Parachute reflex | Extension of hands on falling forward; appears 7–8 months; persists throughout life

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A term neonate fails to pass meconium for 48 hours and develops progressive abdominal distension. Rectal biopsy shows hypertrophied nerve fibres with absent ganglion cells. The stain used and the IOC for Hirschsprung disease are:
options: Alcian blue stain; barium enema is IOC
Congo red stain; rectal biopsy is IOC
Haematoxylin and eosin; anorectal manometry is IOC
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Calretinin; rectal biopsy is IOC

• Hirschsprung disease = aganglionosis.
• Rectal biopsy is IOC.
• New stain = Calretinin (absent in aganglionic segment in Hirschsprung).
• Old special stain = Acetylcholinesterase (shows hypertrophied nerve fibres).
• Definitive surgery = pull-through procedure.

This neonate has classical Hirschsprung disease, presenting with delayed passage of meconium (>48 hours), progressive abdominal distension, and intestinal obstruction due to congenital aganglionosis of the distal bowel. The investigation of choice (IOC) is a full-thickness or suction rectal biopsy, which demonstrates absence of ganglion cells and hypertrophied nerve fibres. Calretinin immunohistochemistry is the preferred modern stain, showing absence of staining in aganglionic bowel, making diagnosis more accurate. The older acetylcholinesterase (AChE) stain demonstrates increased staining of hypertrophied nerve fibres. Although contrast enema and anorectal manometry are useful screening tests, histopathological confirmation by rectal biopsy remains the gold standard before definitive pull-through surgery.

High-Yield

• IOC (Gold standard): Rectal biopsy
• Modern stain: Calretinin (negative in aganglionic segment)
• Older stain: Acetylcholinesterase (positive in hypertrophied nerve fibres)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A term neonate is noted to have severe growth restriction, micrognathia, low-set ears, and a congenital heart defect. On examination, both hands remain tightly clenched with overlapping fingers despite repeated attempts to open them. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this infant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ventricular septal defect

| Clue | Diagnosis

| ---- | ---------

| Clenched fist | Trisomy 18

| Overlapping fingers | Trisomy 18

| Rocker-bottom feet | Trisomy 18

| Micrognathia | Trisomy 18

Now among the options:

• VSD is the most common cardiac defect in Edwards syndrome.
• Holoprosencephaly and post-axial polydactyly belong to Patau syndrome.
• Simian crease belongs to Down syndrome.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A term neonate with birth asphyxia is lethargic, has decreased activity, weak Moro, miosis, bradycardia, and frequent seizures. This corresponds to which stage of Sarnat staging?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stage 2 (Moderate)

This neonate has features of moderate hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) according to the Sarnat staging system. Hallmark findings include lethargy, decreased spontaneous activity, hypotonia, weak Moro and suck reflexes, miosis, bradycardia, and frequent seizures, which usually occur within the first 24 hours. Stage 2 HIE is the group that benefits most from therapeutic hypothermia, provided treatment is initiated within 6 hours of birth. In contrast, Stage 1 presents with hyperalertness, tachycardia, mydriasis, and no seizures, while Stage 3 is characterized by coma, absent reflexes, variable pupils, and severe autonomic dysfunction with a poor prognosis.

Sarnat Staging

| Stage 1 | Stage 2 | Stage 3

| ------- | ------- | -------

| Hyperalert | Lethargic | Coma

| Tachycardia, mydriasis | Bradycardia, miosis | Variable pupils

| Strong Moro | Weak Moro | Absent Moro

| No seizures | Seizures common | Seizures may be absent due to severe cerebral injury

| Excellent prognosis | Candidate for therapeutic hypothermia | High mortality and severe neurological sequelae

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Absence of the Landau reflex in an infant older than 6 months is suggestive of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Spastic cerebral palsy

• The Landau reflex appears at around 3–4 months of age and persists until about 12–24 months. When an infant is held in prone suspension, the normal response is extension of the head, trunk, and legs.
• Absence of the Landau reflex after 6 months suggests abnormal motor development, commonly seen in spastic cerebral palsy, due to impaired central motor control.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All of the following are contraindications of breastfeeding except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Metastatic malignancy in mother

Breastfeeding is contraindicated in certain maternal or infant conditions due to the risk of infection transmission or metabolic intolerance.

Absolute contraindications include:

• Maternal HIV infection (in settings where safe alternatives are available).
• Untreated active tuberculosis (breastfeeding may begin after treatment initiation and precautions).
• Congenital lactose intolerance / classic galactosemia in the infant because breast milk contains lactose.

Metastatic malignancy in the mother is not a direct contraindication to breastfeeding unless the mother is receiving chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or contraindicated medications.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All of the following genes have known associations with Down syndrome–related phenotypes except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. RB1

Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) results from an extra copy of chromosome 21, leading to overexpression of several genes that contribute to its characteristic clinical features.

Genes associated with Down syndrome phenotypes:

•

APP (Amyloid precursor protein) → Located on chromosome 21; responsible for early-onset Alzheimer disease seen in Down syndrome.

•

GATA1 → Mutations associated with transient myeloproliferative disorder and acute megakaryoblastic leukemia in Down syndrome.

•

CRELD1 → Associated with congenital heart defects (especially atrioventricular septal defects) seen in Down syndrome.

Not associated:

• RB1 → Located on chromosome 13; tumor suppressor gene linked to retinoblastoma, not Down syndrome.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All of the following milestones are delayed in a child with Down syndrome except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Personal and social development

Children with Down syndrome typically show global developmental delay, particularly affecting:

• Gross motor skills (due to hypotonia and ligamentous laxity)
• Fine motor skills
• Language development (often the most significantly delayed)

However, personal and social development is relatively preserved and may even be better compared to other developmental domains.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All the following are causes of neonatal hypocalcemia except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Maternal hypoparathyroidism in pregnancy

Neonatal hypocalcemia occurs due to immature parathyroid hormone (PTH) response, decreased calcium stores, or increased phosphate load in the newborn.

Common causes include:

• Prematurity → decreased transplacental calcium transfer in the third trimester.
• Infant of diabetic mother (IDM) → functional hypoparathyroidism and increased calcitonin levels lead to hypocalcemia.
• DiGeorge syndrome → congenital absence or hypoplasia of parathyroid glands causing low PTH and hypocalcemia.

Maternal hypoparathyroidism, however, usually leads to maternal hypocalcemia, which stimulates the fetal parathyroid glands and results in normal or even increased fetal calcium levels, making neonatal hypocalcemia unlikely.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An 11-year-old girl is brought to the physician for a physical examination prior to participating in sports. She is at the 50 percentile for height and weight. Physical examination shows a normal female body habitus, a slight increase in breast areolar diameter with nipple protrusion, and normal-appearing external genitalia with sparse straight hair on the labia majora. The physician concludes that the patient's breast and external genitalia are in the same stage of sexual development. Which of the following terms best describes the sexual development of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tanner stage 2

Tanner staging is used to assess sexual maturation during puberty based on breast development and pubic hair growth in girls.

Tanner Stage 2 (early puberty) features:

• Breast bud stage: small breast mound with enlargement of the areola and nipple.
• Pubic hair: sparse, lightly pigmented, straight hair along the labia majora.

This stage represents the earliest visible sign of puberty in girls, typically occurring around 10–11 years of age.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An 18-month-old known case of Tetralogy of Fallot becomes acutely more cyanotic and irritable after a bout of crying, breathing rapidly and deeply. On auscultation, the previously audible ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border has become noticeably softer during this episode. Which statement correctly explains this murmur change and the immediate management?
options: Increased flow across the pulmonary outflow tract produces a louder murmur; treat with immediate surgical shunt
Worsening infundibular spasm reduces flow across the right ventricular outflow tract, softening the murmur; place the child in knee-chest position and give oxygen and morphine
The VSD transiently closes during the spell, eliminating the murmur; no acute intervention is required
Increased pulmonary blood flow reduces right-to-left shunting, and the child should be given diuretics
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Worsening infundibular spasm reduces flow across the right ventricular outflow tract, softening the murmur; place the child in knee-chest position and give oxygen and morphine

• This is a hypercyanotic ("Tet") spell — precipitated by crying/agitation, which triggers infundibular (subpulmonic) muscular spasm, acutely worsening right ventricular outflow tract obstruction.
• As outflow obstruction worsens, less blood crosses the stenotic infundibulum into the pulmonary artery, causing the murmur (generated by flow through the stenotic RVOT) to become softer or even disappear.
• Simultaneously, obstructed right ventricular outflow diverts more blood right-to-left across the VSD, bypassing the lungs entirely — worsening systemic hypoxemia and cyanosis despite the softer murmur.
• Immediate management targets reducing right-to-left shunting and relieving infundibular spasm:

• Knee-chest position (or squatting in older children) — increases systemic vascular resistance, reducing right-to-left shunt and improving pulmonary flow.
• Oxygen supplementation.
• Morphine — sedates and reduces the hyperpnea/catecholamine drive.
• NaHCO₃ for correction of metabolic acidosis.
• IV propranolol (β-blocker) — relieves infundibular spasm directly.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An 18-year-old boy is brought to the clinic due to fatigue, malaise, fever, and sore throat for the past 6 days. He does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Temperature is 38.3°C (101°F), blood pressure is 115/70 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, and respirations are 18/min. Physical examination shows pharyngeal hyperaemia with exudates along with cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. Breath sounds are normal. Mild hepatosplenomegaly is present. Joints have a normal range of motion. There is no skin rash. A rapid streptococcal antigen test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?
options: Refrain from sports for at least 3-4 weeks
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Refrain from sports for at least 3-4 weeks

• The patient’s symptoms of fever, sore throat with exudates, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly are characteristic of infectious mononucleosis, most commonly caused by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV).
• A major complication of infectious mononucleosis is splenic enlargement, which increases the risk of splenic rupture, especially with physical trauma.
• Therefore, patients are advised to avoid contact sports and strenuous physical activity for at least 3–4 weeks or until splenomegaly resolves.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An 8-day-old neonate presents with jaundice. Which of the following is least likely to be the cause of jaundice after the first week of life?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Erythroblastosis fetalis

The timing of neonatal jaundice is important in determining the cause.

• Erythroblastosis fetalis (hemolytic disease of the newborn) causes severe hemolysis immediately after birth, leading to early-onset jaundice within the first 24–72 hours of life.

Jaundice appearing after the first week is more commonly due to other conditions such as:

• Breast milk jaundice – prolonged unconjugated jaundice starting around day 5–7.
• Cystic fibrosis – may cause neonatal cholestasis.
• Congenital biliary atresia – presents with persistent conjugated jaundice after 1–2 weeks.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An ultrasound shows a fetus with intrauterine growth restriction with head circumference at 75th percentile. All of the following could cause this pattern except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. TORCH infections

• Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) with normal or relatively preserved head circumference (e.g., head circumference at higher percentile than body size) suggests asymmetric IUGR, also called “head-sparing” growth restriction.
• In conditions causing uteroplacental insufficiency, the fetus redistributes blood flow preferentially to vital organs such as the brain, heart, and adrenals, preserving head growth while abdominal circumference and body weight decrease.

Common causes of asymmetric IUGR:

• Poor maternal nutrition
• Pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH)
• Placental insufficiency

TORCH infections typically cause symmetric IUGR, because infection occurs early in gestation, affecting overall cell division and growth, resulting in proportionately small head and body.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An unconscious child is brought to the casualty. What is the correct sequence of the management? 1. Assess breathing 2. Assess pulse 3. Assess response 4. Start compressions 5. Bag and mask ventilation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3-1-2-4-5

Initial management of an unconscious child follows the Pediatric Basic Life Support (PBLS) sequence, focusing on rapid assessment and initiation of resuscitation.

Correct sequence:

1. Assess response → Check if the child is conscious or responds to verbal/painful stimuli.
2. Assess breathing → Look for normal breathing.
3. Assess pulse → Check for a pulse (usually carotid or femoral) for ≤10 seconds.
4. Start chest compressions → If pulse is absent or <60/min with signs of poor perfusion.
5. Provide bag-mask ventilation → Deliver assisted ventilation along with compressions.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Anthropometric measurements for a 1-year-old child and corresponding values at birth are given below. Which of the following parameters indicates abnormal growth? 1. Weight - 6 kg; Birth weight - 3 kg 2. Length - 75 cm; Birth length - 50 cm 3. Head circumference (HC) - 47 cm; Birth HC - 34 cm 4. Chest circumference (CC) - 47 cm; Birth CC - 31 cm
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1

Evaluation of given parameters:

1. Weight: 6 kg (birth 3 kg) → only doubled, not tripled → abnormal growth
2. Length: 75 cm (birth 50 cm) → increase of 25 cm → normal
3. Head circumference: 47 cm (birth 34 cm) → normal
4. Chest circumference: 47 cm (birth 31 cm) → normal (equals head circumference at 1 year)

Therefore, the only abnormal parameter is weight.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Calculate the fluid requirement of a baby of 15 kg using Holliday and Segar formula.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1250 ml

Holliday-Segar formula is used to calculate daily maintenance fluid requirement in children.

Formula:

• First 10 kg = 100 mL/kg/day
• Next 10 kg = 50 mL/kg/day
• Above 20 kg = 20 mL/kg/day

For a 15 kg child:

• First 10 kg: 10 × 100 = 1000 mL
• Remaining 5 kg: 5 × 50 = 250 mL

Total fluid requirement: 1000 + 250 = 1250 mL/day

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Delayed puberty is seen in all of the following conditions except:
options: Constitutional delay in growth and puberty
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Familial short stature

Delayed puberty occurs when there is delayed activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis or gonadal failure.

Conditions associated with delayed puberty:

• Growth hormone deficiency → impaired growth and delayed sexual maturation
• Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP) → temporary delay in puberty with eventual normal development
• Turner syndrome → gonadal dysgenesis causing primary ovarian failure

Not associated:

• Familial short stature → children are short but have normal timing of puberty and bone age.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Failure of which mechanism is central to TTN?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ENaC-mediated alveolar sodium absorption

• Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn (TTN) occurs due to delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid after birth. Normally, during labor and shortly after delivery, epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the alveolar epithelium actively reabsorb sodium and water from the alveoli into the pulmonary circulation and lymphatics.
• Failure of ENaC-mediated sodium absorption leads to retained lung fluid, causing tachypnea and mild respiratory distress shortly after birth.

Why not the other options?

A. Surfactant production: Deficiency causes Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) in premature infants, not TTN.

C. Type II pneumocyte proliferation: Related to surfactant production; not the mechanism of TTN.

D. Pulmonary vasodilation: Failure causes Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: For a newborn with a cephalohematoma that is clinically uncomplicated, what is the next step in management?
options: Observe the child for neonatal jaundice
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Observe the child for neonatal jaundice

Cephalohematoma is a subperiosteal collection of blood that occurs due to birth trauma. It is confined by suture lines and usually appears hours after birth.

• Most cases are benign and self-resolving over weeks.
• As the blood within the hematoma breaks down, bilirubin levels can rise, increasing the risk of neonatal jaundice.
• Therefore, the appropriate management for an uncomplicated cephalohematoma is observation with monitoring for hyperbilirubinemia.

Why not the other options?

• Phototherapy → only if significant jaundice develops.
• Monitoring OFC and vitals → more relevant for subgaleal hemorrhage, which can cause significant blood loss.
• Incision and drainage → contraindicated due to risk of infection and because the condition resolves spontaneously.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Identify the correct statements: 1. Social smile – 2 months 2. Walk without support -12 months 3. Babbling gibberish-15 months 4. Walk upstairs with alternate foot – 4 years 5. Copy a circle-2 years
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3

Developmental milestones occur at predictable ages and are used to assess normal child development.

Evaluation of the statements:

1. Social smile – 2 months → Correct (appears around 6–8 weeks).
2. Walk without support – 12 months → Incorrect -> Independent walking is typically around 15months
3. Babbling gibberish – \~15 months → Correct (jargon speech with varied sounds appears around this age).
4. Walk upstairs with alternate feet – 4 years → Incorrect; alternating feet usually occurs around 3 years.
5. Copy a circle – 2 years → Incorrect; copying a circle occurs around 3 years (2 years: scribbling).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: In prenatal evaluation of congenital diaphragmatic hernia, which parameter is used to predict the severity of pulmonary hypoplasia and overall prognosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lung-to-Head Ratio

• In congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH), the major determinant of prognosis is the degree of pulmonary hypoplasia caused by herniation of abdominal contents into the thoracic cavity.
• The Lung-to-Head Ratio (LHR) measured on prenatal ultrasound estimates the size of the contralateral fetal lung relative to head circumference, helping predict lung development and survival.
• Low LHR → severe pulmonary hypoplasia → poor prognosis
• Higher LHR → better lung development → improved survival

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Match the following: Column A 1. 35-week preterm neonate 2. 33-week preterm neonate 3. 30-week preterm neonate 4. 27-week preterm neonate Column B a. OGT/NGT feeding b. Direct breastfeeding c. TPN and IV fluids d. Spoon/Paladai feeds
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1-b, 2-d, 3-a, 4-c

| Gestational age | Feeding modality

| --------------- | ----------------

| ≥34 weeks | Direct breastfeeding

| 32–34 weeks | Spoon/Paladai feeds

| 28–31 weeks | OGT/NGT

| <28 weeks | TPN/IV fluids

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Regarding vitamin D supplementation in an exclusively breast-fed newborn, which of the following is recommended?
options: Immediately, initially 200 IU and after 6 months 400 IU
To be started after breastfeeding is stopped
To be started 400 IU at the time of complementary feeding
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Immediately 400 IU

Exclusively breast-fed infants should receive vitamin D supplementation of 400 IU/day starting soon after birth.

• Human breast milk contains insufficient vitamin D (≈20–40 IU/L) to meet the infant’s requirement.
• Therefore, guidelines recommend 400 IU of vitamin D daily from the first few days of life, regardless of maternal vitamin D status.
• Supplementation should continue until the infant consumes adequate vitamin D from fortified formula or diet (≥400 IU/day).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: TIM1 and TAM-XL mutations are associated with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Congenital Zika virus infection

TIM1 (T-cell immunoglobulin mucin-1) and TAM receptors (Tyro3, AXL, Mer), particularly AXL, are host cell surface receptors that facilitate entry of certain viruses into cells.

In Zika virus infection:

• The virus uses AXL receptors on neural progenitor cells to enter the cells.
• Infection of these developing brain cells leads to impaired neurodevelopment.

Clinical consequence in congenital infection:

• Microcephaly
• Intracranial calcifications
• Developmental delay
• Ocular abnormalities

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the expected growth velocity in a child after 4 years?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 6 cms/year

Normal growth velocity varies with age in children. After the early childhood growth spurt, the rate of growth becomes relatively steady.

Typical growth velocities:

• Infancy (0–1 year): \~25 cm/year
• 1–2 years: \~10–12 cm/year
• 2–4 years: \~7–8 cm/year
• After 4 years until puberty: \~5–6 cm/year

Thus, the expected average growth velocity after 4 years is about 6 cm per year.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following can be a manifestation of endemic cretinism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Strabismus

Endemic cretinism results from severe maternal and fetal iodine deficiency during pregnancy, leading to congenital hypothyroidism and impaired neurodevelopment. Two major forms are recognized:

• Neurological cretinism: Characterized by deaf-mutism, spastic diplegia/quadriplegia, gait abnormalities, and strabismus (squint) with relatively preserved thyroid function.
• Myxedematous cretinism: Characterized by hypothyroidism, growth retardation, coarse facies, and delayed skeletal maturation.
• Among the options, strabismus is a classic manifestation of neurological endemic cretinism. Mental retardation due to endemic cretinism is irreversible if iodine deficiency is not corrected during fetal life.

| Neurological cretinism | Myxedematous cretinism

| ---------------------- | ----------------------

| Deaf-mutism | Hypothyroidism

| Strabismus (squint) | Growth retardation

| Spasticity | Myxedema

| Intellectual disability | Delayed bone age

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following criteria is common to both acute and chronic malnutrition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Weight for age

Acute malnutrition → assessed by weight for height and mid-arm circumference (reflect wasting)

Chronic malnutrition → assessed by height for age (reflect stunting)

Weight for age is influenced by both weight (acute) and height (chronic), so it becomes a combined indicator, making it common to both conditions.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following increase the risk of recurrence of febrile seizures? 1. Age < 1 year 2. Fever more than 102⁰F 3. Duration of fever < 24 h 4. Duration of fever > 48 h
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3

The risk of recurrence of febrile seizures is influenced by several clinical factors related to the child’s age and fever characteristics.

Established risk factors for recurrence include:

• Younger age (<1 year) at the first febrile seizure
• Short duration of fever (<24 hours) before seizure onset
• Low-grade fever at the time of seizure
• Family history of febrile seizures

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not a feature of severe dehydration in children?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thirsty child

Assessment of dehydration in children is based on clinical signs and is classified as no dehydration, some dehydration, and severe dehydration.

Features of severe dehydration include:

• Lethargy or drowsiness
• Very sunken eyes or sunken anterior fontanelle
• Skin pinch returning very slowly (>2 seconds)
• Poor drinking or inability to drink

A thirsty child who drinks eagerly is typically a sign of some (moderate) dehydration, not severe dehydration.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not a method of administering free-flow oxygen in a neonate?
options: Bag and mask ventilation with oxygen inlet
Bag and mask ventilation without oxygen inlet
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bag and mask ventilation without oxygen inlet

Free-flow oxygen in neonates refers to providing supplemental oxygen without delivering positive pressure ventilation.

Common methods of giving free-flow oxygen include:

• Face mask
• Oxygen tubing held near the mouth and nose (“blow-by oxygen”)
• Self-inflating bag and mask with an oxygen inlet (without squeezing the bag)

A self-inflating bag and mask without an oxygen inlet cannot deliver oxygen effectively and therefore cannot provide free-flow oxygen.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about breast milk jaundice?
options: Seen in 3-4% of exclusively breastfed children
Exclusive breastfeeding with total bilirubin more than 10 mg/dl after 3-4 weeks of birth
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia

Breast milk jaundice is a form of prolonged unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia seen in otherwise healthy exclusively breastfed infants, usually appearing after the first week of life and may persist for several weeks.

Key features:

• Occurs in about 3–4% of exclusively breastfed infants.
• Caused by substances in breast milk (e.g., β-glucuronidase) that increase enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin.
• Infants are well, feeding normally, and gaining weight.
• Phototherapy is rarely required because bilirubin levels are usually mild to moderate.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is seen in hyaline membrane disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. V/Q < 1 and low FRC

Hyaline membrane disease (neonatal respiratory distress syndrome) occurs due to surfactant deficiency, most commonly in premature infants.

• Surfactant deficiency → alveolar collapse (atelectasis)
• Decreased lung compliance
• Reduced functional residual capacity (FRC)
• Poor ventilation of perfused alveoli → V/Q mismatch

Because perfusion is relatively maintained but ventilation is reduced, this leads to:

• Low V/Q ratio (<1)
• Decreased FRC

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following statement is false in a 1-year-old child?
options: Chest circumference is equal to head circumference
Arm span is lesser than height
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Birth weight is quadrupled

Normal growth parameters at 1 year of age include characteristic changes in weight and body proportions.

Key developmental growth facts at 1 year:

• Birth weight is tripled (not quadrupled).
• Head circumference ≈ 46–47 cm.
• Chest circumference becomes approximately equal to head circumference around 1 year.
• Arm span is slightly less than height in infancy and early childhood.

Therefore, the statement “birth weight is quadrupled” is false because birth weight normally quadruples by about 2 years of age, not at 1 year.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect about breastmilk composition?
options: Polyunsaturated fatty acids help nerve myelination.
Breastmilk is deficient in vitamin C
Exclusive breastfeeding may cause vitamin D deficiency.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Breastmilk is deficient in vitamin C

Human breast milk provides adequate amounts of vitamin C, so it is not deficient in vitamin C. Vitamin C in breast milk helps with iron absorption and immune function in the infant.

Important components of breast milk include:

• Polyunsaturated fatty acids (DHA, ARA) → essential for brain development and nerve myelination.
• Lactoferrin → an iron-binding protein with antimicrobial properties, inhibiting bacterial growth.
• Vitamin D → present in low amounts, which is why exclusively breastfed infants require vitamin D supplementation.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the subsequent options is non-essential in the evaluation of mosaic Turner syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anti-nuclear antibodies

Evaluation of Turner syndrome (including mosaic Turner syndrome) focuses on identifying common associated systemic complications, as the condition can affect multiple organs.

Important investigations include:

• Echocardiography → to detect congenital heart defects such as coarctation of the aorta or bicuspid aortic valve.
• Audiometry → due to increased risk of sensorineural hearing loss.
• Glucose tolerance test → because patients have a higher risk of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) testing is not routinely required in the evaluation of Turner syndrome, although autoimmune disorders can occur.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of these is incorrect about Wilms’ tumor?
options: Presents in children < 5 years of age
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lung metastasis is rare

Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) is the most common renal malignancy in children, typically presenting between 2–5 years of age with an asymptomatic abdominal mass.

Important features include:

• It may invade the renal vein and extend into the inferior vena cava (IVC).
• Calcification is uncommon on imaging, which helps differentiate it from neuroblastoma, where calcification is common.
• Lungs are the most common site of metastasis, followed by the liver.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: While you are evaluating a baby, you show him a bright pink teddy bear that he reaches out to with both hands. What is the earliest age by which this milestone is typically achieved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 4 months

Reaching out for an object with both hands is an early gross motor and visual–motor coordination milestone that typically appears by 4 months of age.

At this age:

• Infants develop improved head control and upper limb coordination.
• They begin to visually track objects and voluntarily reach for them with both hands.
• This marks the transition from reflexive grasping to purposeful reaching.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: ΔF508 mutation has a functional defect on the CFTR channel. It leads to:
options: Defective regulation: CFTR not activated by adenosine triphosphate or cyclic adenosine monophosphate
Reduced chloride transport through CFTR at the apical membrane
Defect in protein trafficking with ubiquitination and degradation in the endoplasmic reticulum/Golgi body
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Defect in protein trafficking with ubiquitination and degradation in the endoplasmic reticulum/Golgi body

The ΔF508 mutation is the most common mutation causing cystic fibrosis. It results in misfolding of the CFTR protein, leading to defective trafficking from the endoplasmic reticulum to the cell membrane. The abnormal protein is recognized as defective, ubiquitinated, and degraded in the ER/Golgi, preventing it from reaching the apical membrane.

Why not the other options?

A. Defective regulation: Seen in Class III CFTR mutations (gating defect), not ΔF508.

B. Lack of protein production: Seen in Class I mutations due to nonsense/frameshift mutations.

C. Reduced chloride transport at membrane: Seen in Class IV mutations (conductance defect).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with recurrent episodes of cough and cold is diagnosed with an acyanotic congenital heart disease suggestive of a ventricular septal defect (VSD). Which type of murmur is most commonly heard?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pansystolic

Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most common congenital heart disease and classically produces a harsh pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur, best heard at the left lower sternal border due to left-to-right shunting across the ventricular septum.

Key clinical features:

• Small VSD: Loud, harsh pansystolic murmur with a palpable thrill.
• Large VSD: Softer murmur (due to equalization of ventricular pressures), recurrent respiratory infections, failure to thrive, and signs of congestive heart failure.

Exam Pearl:

• VSD → Pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border.
• Large left-to-right shunts may produce an apical mid-diastolic flow murmur due to increased mitral inflow, but the characteristic murmur of VSD remains the pansystolic murmur.
• Untreated large VSDs can progress to pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger syndrome, resulting in reversal of the shunt (right-to-left) and cyanosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A one-month-old child presents with recurrent pneumonia and no cyanosis. On examination, a continuous murmur is heard below the left clavicle and a bounding pulse is present. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. PDA (Patent Ductus Arteriosus)

Patent ductus arteriosus is a congenital left-to-right shunt in which the ductus arteriosus fails to close after birth, leading to continuous blood flow from the aorta to the pulmonary artery.

• Continuous “machinery” murmur best heard below the left clavicle
• Bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure due to runoff of blood into pulmonary circulation
• Recurrent respiratory infections and signs of heart failure due to increased pulmonary blood flow
• Usually no cyanosis initially (acyanotic congenital heart disease)

Pathophysiology:

• Persistent connection between aorta and pulmonary artery → left-to-right shunt
• Increased pulmonary blood flow → pulmonary congestion → recurrent pneumonia

Contrast:

• ASD: fixed split S2, no continuous murmur
• VSD: pansystolic murmur at left lower sternal border
• Coarctation of aorta: radio-femoral delay, upper limb hypertension, weak lower limb pulses

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A patient has cyanosis in the lower extremities, but examination reveals that the upper extremities are pink and well oxygenated. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Large Patent Ductus Arteriosus

Differential cyanosis (cyanosis of the lower extremities with pink upper extremities) is a classic finding in large Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) with Eisenmenger syndrome. Progressive pulmonary hypertension causes reversal of the shunt (right-to-left) across the PDA, allowing deoxygenated blood to enter the descending aorta distal to the origin of the subclavian arteries, thereby affecting the lower limbs while sparing the upper limbs.

• In a large PDA with Eisenmenger physiology:

• Initial shunt: Left → Right
• With pulmonary hypertension: Right → Left
• Deoxygenated blood enters the descending aorta distal to the branches supplying the upper limbs.
• Upper extremities remain pink, while the lower extremities become cyanotic (differential cyanosis).

Why not the other options?

• A. Severe peripheral vascular disease: Causes ischemia but does not produce differential cyanosis.
• C. Atrioventricular septal defect: Eisenmenger syndrome causes central cyanosis, not differential cyanosis.
• D. Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome: Causes hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia with recurrent epistaxis and AVMs, not differential cyanosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Eisenmenger Syndrome: 1. In patients with severe and prolonged pulmonary hypertension, the right-to-left shunt gets reversed to a left-to-right shunt. 2. There is marked cyanosis, which may be more apparent in the feet and toes than in the upper part of the body. 3. Antihypertensives which cause peripheral vasodilatation can exacerbate the shunting and worsen the symptoms. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2 and 3

• 1. Right-to-left shunt reverses to left-to-right: Incorrect

• The sequence is the opposite.
• Initially, a congenital left-to-right shunt causes increased pulmonary blood flow.
• Prolonged pulmonary hypertension increases pulmonary vascular resistance until it exceeds systemic resistance, causing the shunt to reverse from left-to-right → right-to-left.
• This is Eisenmenger syndrome.

• 2. Cyanosis may be more prominent in the feet and toes: Correct

• This is differential cyanosis, classically seen when Eisenmenger syndrome develops due to a PDA.
• Deoxygenated blood enters the descending aorta distal to the branches supplying the upper limbs → lower limbs become more cyanotic than upper limbs.

• 3. Peripheral vasodilators can worsen shunting: Correct

• Systemic vasodilation decreases systemic vascular resistance (SVR).
• This favors right-to-left shunting, increasing the amount of deoxygenated blood entering systemic circulation and worsening cyanosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding the murmur of Patent Ductus Arteriosus: 1. It is a continuous ‘machinery’ murmur. 2. There is a late diastolic accentuation. 3. It is maximal in the second left intercostal space below the clavicle. 4. With the development of Eisenmenger Syndrome, the murmur becomes louder and rumbling in character. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 3

• 1. Continuous “machinery” murmur: Correct

• PDA produces a continuous murmur because blood flows from the aorta to the pulmonary artery during both systole and diastole.
• It is classically described as a machinery murmur.

• 2. Late diastolic accentuation: Incorrect

• The murmur is generally continuous with systolic accentuation, rather than specifically late-diastolic accentuation.

• 3. Maximal at the second left intercostal space below the clavicle: Correct

• The murmur is best heard at the left upper sternal border / second left intercostal space, beneath the left clavicle.

• 4. Becomes louder and rumbling with Eisenmenger syndrome: Incorrect

• As pulmonary vascular resistance rises and the shunt decreases or reverses, the PDA murmur becomes softer and may eventually disappear.
• A prominent continuous murmur requires a significant left-to-right pressure gradient.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Cyanosis is most likely to be seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Eisenmenger syndrome

Eisenmenger syndrome is the most common cause of cyanosis in patients with congenital heart disease due to reversal of a long-standing left-to-right shunt into a right-to-left shunt following the development of severe pulmonary arterial hypertension. Cyanosis appears because deoxygenated blood bypasses the lungs and enters the systemic circulation.

Why is D correct?

• Eisenmenger syndrome results from irreversible pulmonary vascular disease causing right-to-left shunting, leading to:

• Central cyanosis
• Digital clubbing
• Secondary polycythemia
• Exertional dyspnea

Why not the other options?

• A. Atrial septal defect (ASD): Typically produces a left-to-right shunt and is acyanotic unless Eisenmenger physiology develops.
• B. Partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection (PAPVC): Usually causes a left-to-right shunt and is an acyanotic congenital heart disease.
• C. Advanced aortic stenosis: Causes obstruction to left ventricular outflow with syncope, angina, and heart failure but does not cause cyanosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Nadas criteria include all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Raised Troponin T level

• Nada's criteria are used for clinical diagnosis of congenital heart disease in children.
• They include features like congestive cardiac failure, diastolic murmur, and abnormal chest X-ray findings.
• They rely on clinical findings + basic investigations, not cardiac biomarkers.

Major Criteria

Presence of any one major criterion strongly suggests organic heart disease.

1. Diastolic murmur
2. Grade ≥ 3/6 systolic murmur
3. Cyanosis
4. Congestive heart failure

Minor Criteria

1. Abnormal ECG
2. Abnormal chest X-ray
3. Abnormal blood pressure (hypertension or significant discrepancy)
4. Systolic murmur of grade <3/6
5. Abnormal second heart sound (S2)
6. Abnormal precordial activity (thrill/heave)
7. Abnormal cardiac examination (e.g., clicks, gallops)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ASD, left ventricular hypertrophy

Tetralogy of Fallot is a cyanotic congenital heart disease characterized by four structural abnormalities resulting in right-to-left shunting. Right ventricular outflow obstruction leads to right-to-left shunt and cyanosis

Severity of pulmonary stenosis determines clinical presentation

Components (remember: PROV):

• Pulmonary stenosis
• Right ventricular hypertrophy
• Overriding aorta
• Ventricular septal defect (VSD)

Why option A is incorrect:

• ASD is not a component of TOF
• Left ventricular hypertrophy is not seen; instead, right ventricular hypertrophy occurs

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with fever, hoarse voice, and a barking cough for 2 days. On examination, the child has inspiratory stridor that worsens at night. There is no drooling, and the child is able to swallow. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Parainfluenza virus

• Barking cough + stridor + hoarseness → classic triad
• Age: 6 months – 3 years
•

No drooling → rules out epiglottitis

•

Most common cause of croup = Parainfluenza virus (Type 1)

• X-ray: Steeple sign
• Treatment: Steroids (dexamethasone) ± nebulized adrenaline

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-week-old infant is brought to OPD with complaints of cough and sore throat. The mother reports that the infant develops a paroxysm of cough followed by apnea. Blood investigations reveal total leucocyte count to be >50,000 cells/L. Which of the following drugs is appropriate for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Azithromycin

This 3-week-old infant has classical pertussis (whooping cough) caused by Bordetella pertussis. In young infants, the disease often presents with paroxysmal cough followed by apnea, while the characteristic "whoop" may be absent. A marked leukocytosis (>50,000 cells/µL) with absolute lymphocytosis is a hallmark laboratory finding due to the effect of pertussis toxin. The drug of choice is azithromycin, a macrolide that eradicates the organism, reduces transmission, and is preferred in infants <1 month because it has a lower risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis than erythromycin. Close contacts should also receive macrolide chemoprophylaxis, regardless of vaccination status.

High-Yield

• Organism: Bordetella pertussis
• Classic triad: Paroxysmal cough + inspiratory whoop + post-tussive vomiting
• Infants: Apnea may be the presenting feature; whoop may be absent.
• Laboratory clue: Marked leukocytosis with absolute lymphocytosis
• DOC (<1 month): Azithromycin
• Post-exposure prophylaxis: Macrolide for all household contacts, irrespective of immunization status.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with a respiratory rate of 66 breaths per minute, along with chest indrawing and nasal flaring. There are no other significant findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pneumonia

According to IMNCI guidelines, a 2–12 month old infant with fast breathing (respiratory rate ≥50/min) is classified as pneumonia. In this case, a respiratory rate of 66/min indicates fast breathing for age.

• Age-specific fast breathing:
• <2 months: ≥60/min
• 2–12 months: ≥50/min
• 1–5 years: ≥40/min
• Chest indrawing in infants may be present due to compliant chest wall and does not always indicate severe disease
• Severe pneumonia is diagnosed when there are danger signs such as inability to feed, lethargy, convulsions, or central cyanosis

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant presents with recurrent respiratory infections, persistent wheezing, failure to thrive, and hyperviscous secretions due to dysfunction of a transmembrane regulator channel. Which ion channel is primarily affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chloride channel

The clinical presentation is consistent with cystic fibrosis (CF), an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene.

The CFTR protein is a chloride channel located on the apical surface of epithelial cells in the:

• Respiratory tract
• Pancreas
• Intestine
• Sweat glands
• Hepatobiliary system
• Reproductive tract

Defective chloride transport leads to:

• Decreased chloride secretion
• Increased sodium and water reabsorption
• Thick, dehydrated mucus causing airway obstruction and recurrent infections.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sodium channel: ENaC activity is secondarily increased, but the primary defect is in the CFTR chloride channel.
• B. Potassium channel: Not involved in cystic fibrosis.
• D. Calcium channel: Not involved in cystic fibrosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby is diagnosed with a mutation in the CFTR gene. Which ion channel is directly affected by this mutation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chloride

Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene on chromosome 7. The CFTR protein functions as a chloride ion channel on epithelial cells.

Defective CFTR leads to:

• Decreased chloride secretion
• Increased sodium and water absorption
• Thick, dehydrated secretions affecting the lungs, pancreas, intestines, and sweat glands.

Key differentiating features:

• Lungs: Recurrent respiratory infections, bronchiectasis (commonly Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa)
• Pancreas: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency → steatorrhea, malabsorption, failure to thrive
• GI tract: Meconium ileus in newborns
• Sweat glands: Elevated sweat chloride concentration
• Reproductive system: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens causing male infertility

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with recurrent sinusitis and repeated lung infection. Genetic testing shows a mutation in CFTR gene. Which test is considered gold standard to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sweat Chloride Test

A child with recurrent sinopulmonary infections and a CFTR gene mutation is suspected to have cystic fibrosis. The gold standard test for confirming the diagnosis is the sweat chloride test, which demonstrates elevated chloride levels due to defective chloride transport.

• Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutation in the CFTR gene leading to thick, viscous secretions
• Common features include recurrent sinusitis, chronic lung infections, malabsorption, and failure to thrive
•

Sweat chloride test:

•

≥60 mmol/L is diagnostic

• 30–59 mmol/L is intermediate
• Newborn screening and genetic testing support diagnosis but confirmation is by sweat test

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: According to the WHO clinical criteria, which of the following clinical signs are indicative of ‘severe pneumonia or very severe disease’ in children aged 2 months to 5 years? 1. Convulsions 2. Lower chest indrawing 3. Inability to feed 4. Stridor Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

According to the WHO IMCI classification, a child aged 2 months to 5 years has severe pneumonia or very severe disease if there is any general danger sign or stridor in a calm child.

General danger signs include:

• Convulsions
• Inability to drink/feed
• Lethargy or unconsciousness
• Vomiting everything

Thus:

• 1. Convulsions ✔️
• 3. Inability to feed ✔️
• 4. Stridor ✔️

Why not statement 2?

• Lower chest indrawing was previously classified as severe pneumonia, but in the current WHO IMCI guidelines, chest indrawing alone is classified as pneumonia, while danger signs or stridor indicate severe pneumonia/very severe disease.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All are seen in Cystic fibrosis except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Biliary atresia

Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by CFTR gene mutation leading to thick, viscous secretions affecting multiple organs.

• Gastrointestinal: meconium ileus in neonates, pancreatic insufficiency causing malabsorption
• Respiratory: recurrent infections, bronchiectasis, nasal polyps
• Hepatobiliary: can cause biliary cirrhosis but not biliary atresia
• Hematological: fat-soluble vitamin (vitamin K) deficiency → bleeding tendency

Why biliary atresia is not seen:

• Biliary atresia is a separate obstructive condition of the extrahepatic bile ducts, not related to CFTR dysfunction (bile duct obstruction is seen in CF, not atresia)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: At what cut-off respiratory rate will you consider “fast breathing” in a 2-year-old child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ≥40 per minute

Fast breathing (tachypnea) is an important clinical sign used in the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI/IMCI) to identify possible pneumonia. The respiratory rate cut-off varies with age. In a 2-year-old child (12–59 months), a respiratory rate of ≥40 breaths/minute is considered fast breathing.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. ≥60 per minute: Cut-off for young infants <2 months.
• B. ≥50 per minute: Cut-off for infants 2–12 months.
• D. ≥30 per minute: Below the diagnostic threshold for fast breathing in a 2-year-old.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Choose the true statement regarding CF (Cystic Fibrosis) :
options: Chloride secretion is decreased in sweat and increased in pancreatic fluid
Chloride secretion is increased in sweat and decreased in pancreatic fluid
Chloride secretion is decreased in both sweat and pancreatic fluid
Chloride secretion is increased in both sweat and pancreatic fluid
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chloride secretion is increased in sweat and decreased in pancreatic fluid

Cystic fibrosis is caused by CFTR channel dysfunction leading to abnormal chloride transport in different tissues, producing opposite effects in sweat glands and exocrine organs.

• In sweat glands: defective reabsorption of chloride → increased chloride in sweat (basis of sweat chloride test)
• In pancreas and other exocrine glands: decreased chloride secretion → thick, viscous secretions causing ductal obstruction

Clinical correlation:

• High sweat chloride is diagnostic
• Pancreatic insufficiency leads to malabsorption and failure to thrive

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: For a sick child aged 4 years, which of the following are signs of “severe pneumonia or very severe disease”, as per IMNCI (Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness) Program? I. Fast breathing (≥40 breaths/minute) II. Child vomits everything III. Stridor in a calm child IV. Chest indrawing Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. II and III

According to the IMNCI (Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness) guidelines, a child aged 2 months to 5 years is classified as having severe pneumonia or very severe disease if any general danger sign is present or if there is stridor in a calm child.

• I. Fast breathing (≥40 breaths/minute) ✘

• Fast breathing alone is classified as pneumonia, not severe pneumonia or very severe disease.
• For children 12 months to 5 years, fast breathing is ≥40 breaths/minute.

• II. Child vomits everything ✔

• This is a general danger sign in IMNCI and indicates severe pneumonia or very severe disease.

• III. Stridor in a calm child ✔

• Stridor at rest (in a calm child) indicates upper airway obstruction and is classified as severe pneumonia or very severe disease.

• IV. Chest indrawing ✘

• According to the revised IMNCI/WHO guidelines, chest indrawing alone is classified as pneumonia, not severe pneumonia (provided there are no danger signs).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: In which disease among the following, Chloride level in sweat is evaluated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cystic fibrosis

Sweat chloride test is the gold standard diagnostic test for cystic fibrosis, reflecting defective chloride transport due to CFTR mutation.

• CFTR dysfunction → impaired chloride reabsorption in sweat glands → increased chloride concentration in sweat
• Sweat chloride level >60 mmol/L is diagnostic (in appropriate clinical setting)

Clinical relevance:

• Used in children with recurrent respiratory infections, failure to thrive, or steatorrhea
• Helps confirm diagnosis early and guide management

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The recommended dose of cotrimoxazole for treatment of pneumonia in a child weighing 16 kg is:
options: One paediatric tablet twice a day
Two paediatric tablets twice a day
Three paediatric tablets twice a day
Four paediatric tablets twice a day
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Two paediatric tablets twice a day

Under the IMNCI/F-IMNCI guidelines, cotrimoxazole was recommended for the treatment of non-severe pneumonia in children. The dose is based on body weight (or age).

For a child weighing 16 kg, the recommended dose is:

• Two paediatric tablets twice daily for 5 days

Hence, the correct answer is B. Two paediatric tablets twice a day.

Note: Current WHO and Indian guidelines now recommend oral amoxicillin as the first-line antibiotic for uncomplicated childhood pneumonia. Cotrimoxazole is of historical importance and may still appear in older examination questions.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Under the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI), caretakers are advised to return immediately to a health facility if: 1. Any sick child is not able to drink or breastfeed. 2. Fast breathing or difficult breathing, in a child who has no pneumonia. 3. Blood in stool, in a child with diarrhoea. 4. Conjunctivitis in a child with measles. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

The Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) strategy emphasizes caregiver counselling to recognize danger signs that require immediate return to a health facility. Early identification of these warning signs helps reduce morbidity and mortality from common childhood illnesses.

Why is A correct?

• 1. Any sick child is not able to drink or breastfeed. ✅

• This is a general danger sign requiring urgent medical evaluation.

• 2. Fast breathing or difficult breathing\, in a child who has no pneumonia. ✅

• Development of fast or difficult breathing after initial assessment may indicate progression to pneumonia and requires immediate reassessment.

• 3. Blood in stool\, in a child with diarrhoea. ✅

• Suggests dysentery (Shigella until proven otherwise) and requires prompt medical attention.

• 4. Conjunctivitis in a child with measles. ❌

• Conjunctivitis is a common feature of measles and, by itself, is not an indication for immediate return unless associated with severe eye complications (e.g., corneal clouding).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which one of the following correctly denotes the inheritance pattern of cystic fibrosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Autosomal Recessive

Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene located on chromosome 7. The most common mutation is ΔF508 (deletion of phenylalanine at position 508).

The defective CFTR protein results in impaired chloride and bicarbonate transport, leading to thick, viscous secretions in multiple organs, particularly the lungs, pancreas, gastrointestinal tract, and reproductive system.

Cystic fibrosis follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, meaning:

• Both parents are typically asymptomatic carriers.
• The child must inherit two mutated CFTR alleles to develop the disease.
• Each pregnancy carries:

• 25% affected
• 50% carrier
• 25% unaffected

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 20-month-old child started walking without support at 15 months, scribbling at 15 months, and obeys one-step commands, but speaks only one meaningful word till now. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Detailed speech and hearing evaluation

Speech delay in a toddler should always be evaluated promptly, with hearing assessment as the first priority. A 20-month-old child who speaks only one meaningful word has isolated expressive language delay, despite otherwise appropriate gross motor, fine motor, and social development. The next step is a detailed speech and hearing evaluation to identify potentially reversible causes, particularly hearing impairment.

• The child has significant speech delay for age.
• Hearing loss is the most common reversible cause of speech delay and must be excluded before considering other developmental disorders.

Why not the other options?

• A. Reassurance and follow-up at 5 years: Inappropriate; speech delay requires early evaluation and intervention.
• C. Diagnose as autism immediately: Autism requires persistent deficits in social communication and restricted/repetitive behaviors, which are not described in this child.
• D. Start antiepileptics: There is no history of seizures or epilepsy to justify treatment.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the outpatient department with complaints of developmental delay. He can feed himself a biscuit, can draw a line, can climb steps, and only says bisyllables. Which one of the following developmental screening tools is not suitable for him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phatak’s Baroda Screening Test

The child is 3 years old, so Phatak’s Baroda Development Screening Test (BDST) is not suitable because it is designed for children 0–30 months (2.5 years).

The other tools can be used at this age:

• Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ): 1 month–5½ years.
• Denver II: 0–6 years.
• Trivandrum Development Screening Chart (TDSC): Primarily designed for early childhood screening; the commonly described original chart is for younger children.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy has recently started telling his full name, although he cannot recite a poem. His Developmental Quotient (DQ) in the language sphere is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 50%

Developmental Quotient (DQ) is used to assess a child’s developmental progress and is calculated as:

DQ = (Developmental Age ÷ Chronological Age) × 100

A 6-year-old child (72 months) who has just started telling his full name has a language developmental age of approximately 3 years (36 months). Therefore:

DQ = (3 ÷ 6) × 100 = 50%

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 9 months old infant is brought for a routine check-up. The infant is able to sit without support and transfer objects. Which of the following developmental milestones is most likely to be present at this age?
options: Creeps well on hands and knees
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Creeps well on hands and knees

At 9 months of age, infants typically achieve gross motor milestones such as sitting without support and beginning to creep or crawl on hands and knees. Fine motor development at this stage includes transferring objects from one hand to another and developing an immature pincer grasp.

• Gross motor: sits without support, creeps/crawls
• Fine motor: hand-to-hand transfer of objects, immature pincer grasp
• Advanced milestones like mature pincer grasp (12 months), running (18–24 months), and hopping (4 years) occur later

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 9-month-old infant is able to roll over, babble ‘mama’ and ‘dada,’ and exhibits stranger anxiety but is unable to sit without support. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reassurance

Developmental milestones can show normal variation, and a single mildly delayed milestone in the presence of otherwise appropriate development does not necessarily indicate pathology.

• At 9 months, expected milestones include babbling (“mama/dada”), stranger anxiety, and rolling over, all of which are present in this child
• Sitting without support typically develops around 8–9 months, but slight delay can still fall within normal variation
• Absence of red flag signs (loss of milestones, global delay, abnormal tone) supports reassurance

Clinical approach:

• If development is normal in other domains (social, language, fine motor), isolated borderline delay can be observed
• Regular follow-up is important to ensure progression

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child can make a tower of 3 blocks, runs, copies his mother while sweeping and has a vocabulary of 8–10 words. His developmental age is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 18 months

Developmental milestones are assessed across four domains: gross motor, fine motor, language, and social/adaptive skills. The combination of milestones in this child corresponds most closely to a developmental age of 18 months.

Why is C correct?

The child demonstrates several classic 18-month milestones:

• Tower of 3 blocks ✔ (Fine motor)
• Runs ✔ (Gross motor)
• Copies mother while sweeping (imitative play) ✔ (Social/adaptive)
• Vocabulary of 8–10 words ✔ (Language)

These milestones are characteristic of an 18-month-old child.

Why not the other options?

• A. 12 months ✘

• Walks with support or independently
• Says 1–2 meaningful words
• Tower of 2 blocks

• B. 15 months ✘

• Walks well
• Scribbles
• Tower of 2 blocks
• Vocabulary around 3–5 words

• D. 24 months ✘

• Tower of 6 blocks
• Runs well and climbs stairs
• Vocabulary >50 words
• Uses 2-word sentences
• Copies a vertical line

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child can ride a tricycle, copies a circle, knows name and gender. The developmental age of this child is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3 years

Developmental milestones are assessed in four domains: gross motor, fine motor, language, and personal-social skills. The combination of riding a tricycle, copying a circle, and knowing one’s name and gender are classic milestones of a 3-year-old child.

Why is B correct?

The child demonstrates the following 3-year milestones:

• Rides a tricycle ✔ (Gross motor)
• Copies a circle ✔ (Fine motor)
• Knows own name and gender ✔ (Language/Personal-social)

These milestones correspond to a developmental age of 3 years.

Why not the other options?

• A. 2 years ✘

• Runs well
• Climbs stairs with both feet on each step
• Tower of 6 blocks
• Uses 2-word sentences
• Vocabulary >50 words

• C. 4 years ✘

• Hops on one foot
• Copies a cross
• Draws a person with 3 parts
• Knows 4 colors

• D. 5 years ✘

• Skips
• Copies a triangle
• Draws a person with 6 parts
• Knows full address and can count to 10

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child develops ‘stranger anxiety’ at:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 6–7 months

Stranger anxiety is a normal developmental milestone that typically appears at 6-7 months as the infant begins to recognize familiar caregivers and differentiate them from strangers. It reflects normal cognitive and emotional development, including object permanence and attachment.

High-yield developmental milestones (Ghai)

• Around 6 months: Stranger anxiety appears
• 8–9 months: Stranger anxiety becomes more pronounced (peaks)
• 10–18 months: Separation anxiety is also prominent
• By 2–3 years: Stranger anxiety gradually decreases as the child becomes more socially adaptable

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child who can make a cross, tell stories make tower of 6 cubes and goes to toilet alone, what is the age of the child:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4 years

A 4-year-old child demonstrates advanced fine motor, language, and social independence milestones.

• Fine motor: able to copy a cross and build a tower of about 6 cubes
• Language: can tell simple stories and use well-formed sentences
• Social/adaptive: goes to the toilet independently

Age correlation:

• 1 year: basic motor skills like standing, few words
• 2 years: 2-word phrases, stacks 4–6 cubes
• 3 years: copies a circle, partial toilet training
• 4 years: copies a cross, storytelling, complete toilet training

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with developmental delay has absence of the developmental milestone of social smile by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3 months

The social smile normally appears at 6–8 weeks (around 2 months). Failure to develop a social smile by 3 months is considered abnormal and is an early marker of developmental delay, warranting further evaluation for visual impairment, hearing impairment, autism spectrum disorder, or global developmental delay.

Why not the other options?

• A. 6 weeks ❌: Social smile is just beginning to appear; absence is still within normal limits.
• B. 10 weeks ❌: Many infants develop it by this age, but the upper limit of normal is 3 months.
• C. 3 months ✔️: Correct. Absence beyond this age is abnormal.
• D. 4 months ❌: Delay should be recognized earlier, by 3 months.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Consider the following statements with respect to developmental milestones at 9 months of age: 1. At this age, child develops immature pincer grasp. 2. At this age, child can say bisyllables (mama, dada, etc.). 3. At this age, child can wave bye-bye. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

At 9 months, infants achieve several important developmental milestones:

• Immature pincer grasp develops (thumb and index finger).
• Can say bisyllables such as “mama” and “dada” (usually nonspecific).
• Can perform simple gestures such as waving bye-bye and playing peek-a-boo, indicating improving social interaction.

Why are the statements correct?

• 1. At this age, child develops immature pincer grasp✔️: Immature pincer grasp develops at 9 months.
• 2. At this age\, child can say bisyllables (mama\, dada\, etc.)✔️: Bisyllables (“mama”, “dada”) are spoken around 9 months.
• 3. At this age\, child can wave bye-bye✔️: Waving bye-bye is a typical 9-month social milestone.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: For developmental assessment of a baby, grasp is best assessed by offering the child:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A red cube

For developmental assessment of grasp, the standard object used is a red cube (approximately 2.5 cm). Offering a red cube allows assessment of the progression of grasp:

• Palmar grasp (5–6 months)
• Radial palmar grasp (6–7 months)
• Inferior pincer grasp (9 months)
• Mature pincer grasp (10–12 months)

Why not the other options?

• A. A red ring: Used more for assessing visual fixation and reaching, not grasp.
• C. Red pellets: Used specifically to assess pincer grasp in older infants (9–12 months), not general grasp.
• D. Multicoloured pellets: Not the standard object for developmental assessment.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The upper limit of age for attainment of visual fixation or following is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3 months

Visual fixation and following should be attained by 3 months of age. Although many infants begin to fix and follow faces or objects by 6–8 weeks, failure to achieve this by 3 months is abnormal and warrants evaluation for visual impairment or neurodevelopmental disorders.

Why not the other options?

• A. Birth: Newborns can briefly fix on faces but consistent fixation/following is not expected.
• B. 1 month: Visual tracking is still developing and may be inconsistent.
• C. 2 months: Many infants achieve fixation by this age, but the upper limit of normal is 3 months.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What are the upper age limits by which a child should start walking alone, and be able to speak single words?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 18 months, 18 months respectively

The upper limit of normal for developmental milestones is:

• Walking alone: 18 months
• Speaking single meaningful words: 18 months

Failure to achieve these milestones by 18 months warrants evaluation for developmental delay, hearing impairment, neuromuscular disorders, or autism spectrum disorder.

Why not the other options?

• A. 12 months, 15 months respectively: These are the average ages at which many children achieve these milestones, not the upper limit of normal.
• C. 15 months, 15 months respectively: Delay beyond this age alone does not necessarily indicate abnormal development.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of these milestones is correctly matched with the corresponding age?
options: Stacking two cubes in a tower 2 years
Transferring the object from one hand to another hand by 6 months
Reaching out to the object with one hand by the age of 8 months
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Transferring the object from one hand to another hand by 6 months

Object transfer from one hand to another is a key fine motor developmental milestone achieved at \~6 months of age.

• It reflects improving hand coordination and bilateral integration.

Why other options are incorrect:

• A. Stacking two cubes → occurs at \~15 months, not 2 years
• B. Mature pincer grasp → develops at \~12 months, not 9 months
• D. Reaching with one hand → seen earlier (\~5 months), not 8 months

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which one of the following can be used for developmental screening for use in community to identify children (aged 0–6 years) with developmental delay?
options: Revised Denver Development Screening Test (Denver II)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Trivandrum Development Screening Chart

The Trivandrum Development Screening Chart (TDSC) is a simple, rapid developmental screening tool designed for community use to identify developmental delay in children aged 0–6 years. It is easy to administer by primary healthcare workers and is widely used in community screening programs in India.

Why not the other options?

• A. Revised Denver Development Screening Test (Denver II): Comprehensive developmental screening test but not specifically designed for community-level screening.
• B. Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ-3): Parent-completed screening tool; not the standard community screening tool used in India.
• C. Phatak’s Baroda Development Screening Test: Used for developmental assessment but TDSC is the preferred community screening tool for children 0–6 years.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which one of the following fine motor milestones will appear ahead of others?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Copies a circle

Fine motor development follows a predictable sequence, progressing from simple imitation (copying) to independent drawing, and from simpler shapes to more complex figures. Copying a circle is achieved earlier than drawing or copying a cross and is an important developmental milestone.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Copies a cross: Usually achieved at 4 years.
• C. Draws a circle: Drawing a circle independently is a more advanced skill than copying one.
• D. Draws a cross: An independent drawing task that develops later than copying a circle.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding a normal newborn’s growth?
options: Weight loss may be 8–10% of birth weight in the initial two weeks of life
Birth weight is regained by 7–10 days of age
Birth weight is regained within the first week of life
Weight loss may be 12–15% of birth weight in the initial two weeks of life
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Weight loss may be 8–10% of birth weight in the initial two weeks of life

Normal newborns lose up to 8–10% of their birth weight during the first few days of life due to physiological diuresis and limited initial feeding. This weight is usually regained by 10–14 days (2 weeks) of age.

Why not the other options?

• B. Birth weight is regained by 7–10 days of age: Birth weight is usually regained by 10–14 days, not 7–10 days.
• C. Birth weight is regained within the first week of life: Birth weight is not regained within the first week in normal newborns.
• D. Weight loss may be 12–15% of birth weight in the initial two weeks of life: A weight loss of 12–15% is excessive and should prompt evaluation for dehydration, inadequate feeding, or illness.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10 year old boy was brought for psychiatric evaluation for intellectual disability. On examination, his IQ was 45. He has a long face, large ear ,large testis and a cardiac murmur and A history of poor intellectual function is present in the paternal family.What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fragile X syndrome

The given clinical vignette along with the family history is suggestive of fragile X syndrome.

* Fragile X syndrome is the second most common genetic cause of mental retardation (Down syndrome being the most common).

* It is caused by a trinucleotide mutation in the familial mental retardation-1 (FMR1) gene.

* When the cells were cultured in a folate-deficient medium, the cytogenetic alteration was discovered as a break in the staining in the long arm of the X chromosome. As it appeared that the chromosome was “broken” at this locale, it was named as a fragile site.

* In fragile X syndrome, the affected males are mentally retarded, with an IQ in the range of 20 to 60.

* The characteristic phenotypic features includes:

* Long face with a large mandible

* Large everted ears

* Large testicles (macro-orchidism)

* In some cases, hyperextensible joints, a high arched palate, and mitral valve prolapse may also be noted.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 22-year-old mother presented with her 3 week-old newborn who had a large tongue and a umbilical hernia. Which of the following investigations has to be done in view of congenital hypothyrodism?
options: A fresh blood sample and screen first for TSH levels
A fresh blood sample and screen first for T4 levels
A dried blood sample and screen first for TSH levels
A dried blood sample and screen first for T4 levels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A dried blood sample and screen first for TSH levels

The most commonly followed strategy for newborn screening of congenital hypothyroidism is using a dried blood sample and screening it first for TSH.

Screening for children for congenital hypothyroidism is very important, as early diagnosis and treatment can help in normal intellectual development. Otherwise, congenital hypothyroidism is known as the most common preventable cause of mental retardation. Children diagnosed beyond the neonatal period have a poor outcome.

Screening is usually done on day 2-day 4 postnatally, and programs usually use dried blood samples for this. The most commonly used strategy screens for TSH first as they have higher sensitivity compared to the T4-based approach. Although the TSH-based approach is better, it doesn't identify central hypothyroidism, which can be identified by the T4-first approach. But, the T4-based approach misses out on the cases of compensated hypothyroidism.

The incidence of congenital hypothyroidism seems to be 4 times higher in India compared to western countries. Thyroid dysgenesis has emerged as the most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism in India accounting for about 75% of all cases. Interestingly, an Increased incidence of thyroid dysgenesis is noted in Down syndrome.

Clinical features of hypothyroidism:

Congenital
Acquired

Open posterior fontanel
Growth retardation

Umbilical hernia
Delayed skeletal maturation

Characteristic edematous facies
Delayed dental development

Constipation
Delayed puberty

Pallor
Myopathy and pseudohypertrophy

Hypothermia
Enlarged sella

Large tongue
Pseudotumor cerebri

Rough dry skin

Hypotonia

Large abdomen
