Management: Thyroid replacement soon after the diagnosis. Thyroxine of dose 10-15 μg/kg/day should be started and adjusted to achieve normal free T4 range. TSH may be elevated up to 2 years of age with reset of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy had a fever, a rash on his hand along with painful sores in his mouth as shown below. What is the causative agent of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Coxsackie virus

The diagnosis of the above clinical condition is hand-foot-mouth disease (HFMD) caused by coxsackievirus.

It is caused by the coxsackievirus and enterovirus. The serotypes commonly involved are coxsackievirus A16 and enterovirus 71. It spreads by droplets or faecal contamination. It can also lead to aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, polio-like syndrome, acute transverse myelitis, and Guillain-Barre syndrome.

HFMD is characterised by multiple vesicles surrounded by a halo of erythema. These vesicles usually rupture leading to superficial ulcers with a grey-yellow base and an erythematous rim. The lesions can be macular, papular, or vesicular. They are generally non-pruritic and non-painful, involving the dorsum of the hand, feet, buttocks, legs, and arms.

Treatment for HFMD is supportive. Pain and fever can be treated with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents. The patient should be adequately hydrated.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presented with hematemesis and was found to have splenomegaly, on examination. There was a past history of exchange transfusion in this child for neonatal jaundice. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Portal Vein thrombosis

As the child has a history of neonatal blood transfusion, along with hematemesis and splenomegaly this is a case of portal vein thrombosis.

Neonatal blood transfusion is done via the umbilical vein and as the umbilical vein drains into the portal vein, thrombosis of the portal vein might have occurred leading to portal hypertension.

A child presenting with hematemesis and splenomegaly is presumed to have variceal bleeding unless proved otherwise. Bleeding from esophageal varices is the most common presentation of portal hypertension.

Pearl PF0077: Etiology of portal hypertension

Pre hepatic

* Portal vein thrombosis

* Splenic vein thrombosis

* Splenomegaly

Intrahepatic - This is further classified as

* Presinusoidal -

* Schistosomiasis

* Sarcoidosis

* Primary biliary cholangitis

* Noncirrhotic portal fibrosis (NCPF)

* Sinusoidal - Cirrhosis due to various causes

* ALD and NAFLD

* Viral hepatitis

* Postsinusoidal - sinusoidal obstruction syndrome

Post hepatic

* Budd Chiari syndrome

* Veno-occlusive disease

* Chronic right-sided cardiac congestion

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old child brought to the hospital with a history of loose stools. The mother says he is irritable and drinks water hastily when given. On examination, eyes are sunken and during the skin pinch test, the skin retracted within two seconds but not immediately. What is the treatment for the child?
options: Administer the first dose of IV antibiotic and immediately refer to a higher center
Give oral fluids and ask the mother to continue the same and visit again the next day
Give zinc supplementation and oral rehydration solution only and ask mother to come back if some danger signs develop
Consider severe dehydration, start intravenous (IV) fluids, IV antibiotics, and refer to a higher center
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Give zinc supplementation and oral rehydration solution only and ask mother to come back if some danger signs develop

The child in this scenario has some degree of dehydration, since the child is restless and irritable, drinks water readily, has sunken eyes, and the skin goes back slowly on the skin pinch test (<2 seconds) with sunken eyes.

Treatment includes oral rehydration therapy, zinc supplementation, and continued breastfeeding according to WHO Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Diseases (IMNCI) Protocol, Plan B.

WHO IMNCI PLANS:

Pearl PF0049: Symptoms associated with different levels of dehydration

Symptoms

Mild to moderate dehydration

Loss of body weight

Mental status

Fatigued or irritable
Lethargic or unconscious

Thirsty; eager to drink

Normal
Normal to increased
Tachycardia

Quality of pulse
Normal
Normal to decreased
Weak, thready or impalpable

Skin turgor test

Recoil in <2 sec
Recoil in >2 sec

Capillary refill

Prolonged

Pearl PF0283: Treatment of dehydration based on severity

Plan A: For no dehydration or minimal dehydration. ORS is administered after each loose stool.

Age

>10 years

Plan B: For moderate dehydration.

The amount of oral rehydration solution (ORS) to be given is 75 mL/kg body weight (wt × 75).

Plan C: Severe dehydration

Age

Followed by 70 mL/kg in

Note: Ringer lactate (ideal) or normal saline is used as intravenous fluids.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-month-old child was brought by her mother with complaints of diarrhoea and mucocutaneous lesions as shown in the image. The symptoms have been present since weaning was started. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acrodermatitis enteropathica

A child with eczematous rash typically in the perioral and perineal region is characteristic of acrodermatitis enteropathica which is due to secondary zinc deficiency.

Acrodermatitis enteropathica:

* autosomal recessive disorder seen in infants due to a defect in the intestinal zinc-specific transporter gene.

* classically presents while weaning from breast milk to formula, which has lower zinc bioavailability than breast milk.

* symptoms are perioral and perineal rashes, periungual dermatitis- Beau’s lines on nails, chronic diarrhea, and alopecia.

* present with symmetrical, eczematous plaques that become vesicular, bullous, pustular, or erosive with characteristic crusting at the edges.

* perioral eruption usually spares the upper lip, giving it a U‐shaped or horseshoe‐shaped appearance.

* Investigations would reveal low serum zinc.

* Oral zinc therapy is the preferred management.(3 mg/kg/24 hour)

Option A: Wiskott Aldrich syndrome is the classical triad of thrombocytopenia, eczema and recurrent pyogenic infections. No history of bleeding rules out this option.

Option C: Epidermolysis bullosa presents as bullous lesions in pressure handling areas.

Option D: In atopic dermatitis usually the lesions will be itchy and distributed in extensor aspects (flexural in adults).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby assessed five minutes after birth is found to be blue with irregular gasping respiration. The heart rate is 50 beats/min, and a grimace is seen in response to stimulation with a catheter in the nostrils. On assessing the baby's muscle tone, you note that there is some flexion of the extremities. The APGAR score for this newborn is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4

The APGAR score of this newborn is 4.

In this baby:

* Colour blue - score 0

* HR < 100/min - score 1

* Grimace - score 1

* Some flexion of extremities - score 1

* Irregular respiration - score 1

Thus total score in this patient is 4

SIGN
0
1
2

A: Appearance (Colour)
Blue, pale
Body pink, extremities blue
Completely pink

P: Pulse (Heart rate)
Absent
Below 100
Over 100

G: Grimace
(Response to catheter in nostril)
No response
Grimace
Cough or sneeze

A: Activity(Muscle tone)
Limp
Some flexion of extremities
Active motion

R: Respiratory effort
Absent
Slow, irregular
Good, crying

* At 1 minute and 5 minutes after complete birth of the infant (disregarding the cord and placenta), the 5 objective signs listed here are evaluated, and each is given a score of 0, 1, or 2.

* A total score of 10 indicates an infant in the best possible condition.

* An infant with a score of 0-3 requires immediate resuscitation.

Pearl PF1658: APGAR score

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child in your unit is admitted with acute bronchiolitis. Which of the following is the most common etiological agent responsible for this condition during infancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Respiratory syncytial virus

Acute bronchiolitis is predominantly a viral disease in children younger than 2 years. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is responsible for more than 50% of cases.

Acute bronchiolitis refers to airway inflammation and obstruction of the lower respiratory tract. Commonly, symptoms of bronchiolitis begin with rhinitis or congestion and cough and may progress to signs of increasing respiratory distress (tachypnea, wheezing, and accessory muscle use). Management is mainly conservative.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child is brought to the pediatrician with short stature. On evaluation, growth hormone levels are found to be high and Insulin-like growth factor(IGF-1) levels are low. Which among the following could be a cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Laron dwarfism

The presence of high growth hormone levels and low Insulin-like growth factor(IGF-1) levels point towards Laron syndrome/dwarfism. It is caused by end-organ resistance to growth hormone(GH insensitivity) due to the mutation of the growth hormone receptor.

Here, growth hormones are produced, but not able to act on the target tissues as growth hormone receptors in the target tissue are not responding to growth hormones. So, the resting and stimulated growth hormone levels are high and insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) levels are low.

It is an autosomal-recessive disorder with clinical features that are the same as those seen in pituitary dwarfism.

Other options:

Pituitary dwarfism is a condition with growth hormone deficiency. Maternal deprivation dwarfism is due to psychosocial causes such as emotional deprivation and neglect. Turner syndrome is a chromosomal disorder in which a female is born with only one X chromosome.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with continuing seizures for the past 30 minutes. The relatives say that there had been no seizure-free intervals in the past 30 minutes. After stabilizing the vitals of the patient, the first drug the patient should be started upon is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diazepam

This scenario described above is of status epilepticus. The first line drug used is Diazepam/Lorazepam.

Status epilepticus refers to continuous or repetitive, discrete seizures with impaired consciousness which lasts for more than 5 minutes.

The duration of seizure activity to meet the definition of status epilepticus has traditionally been specified as 15–30 min. However, a more practical definition is to consider status epilepticus as a situation in which the duration of seizures prompts the acute use of anticonvulsant therapy, i.e., more than 5 minutes.

Management of status epilepticus:

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A male infant was brought to the emergency pediatric unit with abdominal distention. There was a history of recurrent urinary tract infections. On examination, he was found to have urinary retention. Imaging showed bilateral hydronephrosis. What could be the probable diagnosis of his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior urethral valves

The given clinical scenario with USG finding of bilateral hydronephrosis is suggestive of posterior urethral valve.

Posterior urethral valve:

* The valves are membranes that have a small posterior slit within them, which typically lie just distal to the verumontanum

* They function as flap valves and are obstructive to antegrade urinary flow. A urethral catheter can be passed retrogradely.

* Diagnosis is most commonly made antenatally with ultrasound, which demonstrates bilateral hydronephrosis above a distended bladder

* If the diagnosis is not made antenatally, then babies typically present with urinary infection in the neonatal period or with uraemia and renal failure

* The investigation of choice is micturating cystourethrography

* Definitive treatment is by urethroscopic destruction of the valves with continuing lifelong supportive treatment of the dilated urinary tract, the recurrent urinary infections and the uraemia.

Vesicoureteric reflux would present with unilateral hydronephrosis, on the affected side.

Pearl PF1540: Causes of Hydronephrosis

Unilateral hydronephrosis

Extramural obstruction

* Tumor from adjacent structures, e.g., cervix, prostate, rectum, colon, or cecum

* Retrocaval ureter

Intramural obstruction

* Congenital stenosis

* Ureterocele

* PUJ obstruction

* Congenital small ureteric orifice

* Inflammatory stricture following removal of ureteric calculus, repair of a damaged ureter, or tuberculous infection

* Neoplasm of the ureter or bladder cancer involving the ureteric orifice

Intraluminal obstruction

* Calculus in the pelvis or ureter

* Sloughed papilla in papillary necrosis (especially, in patients with diabetes, analgesic abuse, or sickle cell disease)

Bilateral hydronephrosis

Congenital:

* Posterior urethral valves (associated with pulmonary hypoplasia)

* Urethral atresia

* PUJ obstruction

Acquired:

* Benign prostatic hypertrophy or carcinoma of the prostate

* Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis (Ormond's disease)

* Postoperative bladder neck scarring

* Urethral stricture

* Phimosis

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A one-and-half-year-old child was brought to the hospital with a history of breathlessness, fever, cough, and cold. On examination, respiratory rate was 46/min with chest retractions and no danger signs. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Give IV antibiotics and refer to higher centre
Oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home
No need of treatment only home remedies
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute respiratory illness. According to the recent WHO guidelines,  this child can be classified as having 'Pneumonia'. The treatment is oral amoxicillin and home care advice.

Three key clinical signs are used to assess a sick child with cough or difficult breathing:

* Respiratory rate

* Which distinguishes children who have pneumonia from those who do not

* > 50 for infants 2 months to 12 months

* > 40 for children 12 months to 5 years of age

* Lower chest wall indrawing

* Which indicates pneumonia

* Stridor

* Which indicates those with severe pneumonia who require hospital admission.

The following table gives the classification for cough / difficult breathing from 2 months to 5 years of age:

The recent WHO guidelines state that chest indrawing and fast breathing are in the category of pneumonia.

Signs of severe pneumonia are :

* Not able to drink

* Persistent vomiting

* Convulsions

* Lethargic or unconscious

* Stridor in a calm child

* Severe malnutrition

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A patient has bruising, petechiae, and occasional minor epistaxis without any significant impairment in his daily activities. On further workup, a diagnosis of a mild case of ITP is made. How will you manage the patient?
options: A single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Education, counseling and watchful expectancy

In this patients with mild ITP, the next step in management is education, counselling, and watchful expectancy.

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura or idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is an acquired disorder in which there is immune-mediated destruction of platelets. The antibodies formed in the spleen against the cell-surface antigens GpIIb/IIIa or GpIb/IX, cause increased peripheral destruction of platelets. It can be

* Asymptomatic.

* Mild symptoms- bruising and petechiae, and occasional minor epistaxis which has very little interference with daily living.

* Moderate symptoms- more severe skin and mucosal lesions, more troublesome epistaxis, and menorrhagia.

* Severe symptoms- bleeding episodes - menorrhagia, epistaxis, and melena - requiring transfusions or hospitalization, symptoms interfering seriously with quality of life.

Treatment of ITP:

* Mild to moderate bleeding symptoms- watchful expectancy, education, and counselling.

* Platelet count < 30,000 + risk factors for bleeding (antiplatelet drugs/anticoagulants or concomitant bleeding disorders)- oral glucocorticoids or intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or IV anti-D

* Severe bleeding symptoms- IV methylprednisolone ± IVIG or IV anti-D

* Life-threatening bleeding (eg. intracranial haemorrhage)- platelet transfusion + IV methylprednisolone + IVIG or IV anti-D

The role of splenectomy in ITP should be reserved for 2 circumstances:

* The older child (≥4 yr) with severe ITP that has lasted >1 year (chronic ITP) and whose symptoms are not easily controlled with medical therapy

* When life-threatening hemorrhage (ICH) complicates acute ITP and the platelet count cannot be corrected rapidly with transfusion of platelets and administration of IVIG and corticosteroids.

Pearl PF1322: Idiopathic/Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)

It is characterized by

* Isolated thrombocytopenia—the presence of antibody against platelet membrane glycoprotein and subsequent destruction in reticuloendothelial system

* Normal bone marrow—normal or even increased number of megakaryocytes

* Absence of other causes of thrombocytopenia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All of the following are features of tetralogy of Fallot except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Atrial septal defect

An atrial septal defect is not seen in a patient with tetralogy of Fallot.

The primary defect gives rise to the 4 anatomical components of TOF which are:

* Ventricular septal defect (VSD)

* Obstruction to right ventricular outflow - Pulmonic stenosis (PS)

* Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)

* Overriding (or dextroposition) of the aorta

Tetrology of Fallot(TOF):

* TOF is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease

* The primary defect is an anterior deviation of the infundibular septum (the muscular septum that separates the aortic and pulmonary outflows).

* Obstruction to pulmonary arterial blood flow is usually at both the right ventricular infundibulum (subpulmonic area) and the pulmonary valve.

* The degree of pulmonary outflow obstruction determines the degree of the patient’s cyanosis and the age of first presentation.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: New A 6-year-old child presents to the OPD with nausea, vomiting, fatigue, with oliguria. On examination, swelling around the eyes and both ankles was noticed. Urine output measured was 0.5 ml/kg/hour for last 8 hours and serum creatinine was found to be 1.5 times the normal levels. The patient comes under which stage of AKI by KDIGO criteria?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stage 1

The patient comes under acute kidney injury stage 1 of the KDIGO classification as the serum creatinine is increased 1.5 times the normal value and urine output is <0.5 mL/kg/hour for last 8 hours.

KDIGO criteria classify AKI on the basis of an increase in serum creatinine and/or decrease in urinary output.

* Stage 1 – Increase in serum creatinine to 1.5 to 1.9 times baseline, or increase in serum creatinine by ≥0.3 mg/dL or reduction in urine output to <0.5 mL/kg/hour for 6 to 12 hours.

* Stage 2 – Increase in serum creatinine to 2.0 to 2.9 times baseline, or reduction in urine output to <0.5 mL/kg/hour for ≥12 hours.

* Stage 3 – Increase in serum creatinine to 3.0 times baseline, or increase in serum creatinine to ≥ 4.0 mg/dL or reduction in urine output to <0.3 mL/kg/hour for ≥24 hours, or anuria for ≥12 hours, or the initiation of renal replacement therapy.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The mother of a newborn in your unit is extremely sick and is unable to feed her baby. The relatives have arranged a breast milk donor and wish to feed the baby using the device shown in the image. This method of primary feeding can be recommended in newborns with a gestational age of _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 32-34 weeks

The given image shows paladai. It can be used as a primary feeding method during routine feeding in neonates born at gestational age 32-34 weeks only. Sick mothers or mothers with contraindications to breastfeeding can feed their child using paladai. The milk can either be expressed breastmilk or they can resort to using undiluted cow milk or formula feeds.

Newborns with a gestational age of <32 weeks will not have the coordination between swallowing and breathing. So, paladai can only be used occasionally.

Newborns with a gestational age >34 weeks will have a completely mature sucking pattern when breastfeeding becomes more preferred.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the diagnosis of the patient having the following type of karyotype as shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Down’s syndrome

The given karyotyping suggest a diagnosis of Trisomy 21 or Down syndrome.

* Down syndrome is the most common of the chromosomal disorders and is a major cause of mental retardation.

PATHOGENESIS:

* Maternal age has a strong influence on the incidence of trisomy 21.

* In most cases, themeiotic nondisjunction of chromosome 21 occurs in the ovum.

* In about 4% of cases, Robertsonian translocation of the long arm of chromosome 21 to another acrocentric chromosome (e.g., 22 or 14) is seen.

CLINICAL FINDINGS:

* Mental retardationis seen.

* Flat facial profile, oblique palpebral fissures, and epicanthic folds are seen.

* Approximately 40% of the patients have congenital heart disease; the most common defects are of the endocardial cushion, including ostium primum, atrial septal defects, atrioventricular valve malformations, and ventricular septal defects.

* Cardiac problems are responsible for the majority of the deaths in infancy and early childhood.

* Congenital malformations, including atresias of the esophagus and small bowel.

* Patients older than age 40 develop neuropathologic changes characteristic of Alzheimer disease.

* Increased risk of developing acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AML-M7)

* Predisposition to autoimmune diseases and serious lung infections is seen.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets?
options: It is the most common cause of rickets
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. PHEX gene is affected

In X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets,(vitamin D resistant rickets) the gene PHEX is affected.

* X-linked dominant hypophosphatemic rickets is the most common genetic cause of rickets (overall, the most common is nutritional vitamin D deficiency).

* PHEX gene (phosphate-regulating endopeptidase on x chromosome) products are responsible for inactivation of phosphatonin. Mutation of PHEX leads to increased phosphatonin (FGF 23) levels, and hence, the excretion of phosphorus through renal tubules is increased.

* Treated with oral phosphorus and 1,25-D (calcitriol).

Evaluation of Vit D-resistant rickets:

Pearl PF1529: Vitamin D activation and Rickets

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old child is brought to the OPD with a history of repeated fractures for the past 2 years. On examination, there is the presence of blue sclera and dental abnormalities. There is a positive family history. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Osteogenesis imperfecta

Positive family history and clinical features such as blue sclera with dental abnormalities are suggestive of Osteogenesis imperfecta.

Osteogenesis imperfecta occurs due to the abnormality in Type 1 collagen. It is characterized by increased fragility of bones, dental anomalies, and lax joints. Skin, sclera, and cornea are also involved.

It is classified into different types based on their characteristic features, severity, and mode of inheritance.

Type 1

* The most common and mildest form of the disease.

* Autosomal dominant inheritance.

* The presentation can be a young child with a history of recurrent fractures.

* Blue sclera and dental abnormalities are seen.

* The radiograph may show osteoporosis, cortical thinning with thin and gracile bones. Wormian bones are seen.

Type 2

* Most lethal variant

* Infants have deep blue sclera with short and deformed limbs due to multiple fractures.

* Pulmonary insufficiency is the usual cause of death due to rib fractures.

* Ribs having a beaded appearance may be seen in the radiograph.

* Intrasutural bones may be seen in the occipital and parietal regions.

Type 3

* Autosomal recessive inheritance

* Fractures of the long bones are present at birth.

* Deformity increases with the growth of the child.

* Progressive kyphoscoliosis is seen from childhood due to vertebral fractures.

* The radiograph shows abnormal epiphysis with islands of calcified cartilage.

Type 4

* Autosomal dominant inheritance

* Severity varies and hence can be confused with type 1 and type 3 disease.

* Short stature is seen and basilar invagination occurs in a large number of cases

Type 5

* It is similar to type 4 disease

* Autosomal dominant inheritance is seen but it can occur spontaneously.

* Hypertrophic callus formation at sites or fracture or surgical intervention is a typical finding.

Image showing wormian bones-

1. Collagen backbone
Preprocollagen - Glycin-proline-lysine

Deficiency of Vit C causes Scurvy.

3. Glycosylation
Formation of procollagen and resulting triple helix

4. Cleavage of terminals of procollagen
Resulting in the formation of tropocollagen

5. Cross-linking by lysyl oxidase (copper-containing enzyme)

Formation of mature collagen.

Defect causes Menkes disease and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old male child presents with a history of spontaneous excessive bruising and haemarthrosis. On investigation, he has a normal platelet count, prolonged PTT, and a normal PT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hemophilia A

The most likely diagnosis is Haemophilia A. Bleeding into joints (hemarthrosis) following minor trauma is particularly characteristic of hemophilia.

* Hemophilia A, the most common hereditary disease associated with life-threatening bleeding, is caused by mutations in factor VIII, an essential cofactor for factor IX in the coagulation cascade.

* Hemophilia A is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait and thus affects mainly males and homozygous females.

* About 30% of patients have no family history; their disease is caused by new mutations.

* Hemophilia A -  clinical severity correlates well with the level of factor VIII activity.

* Those with less than 1% of normal levels have a severe disease; those with 2% to 5% of normal levels have moderately severe disease, and those with 6% to 50% of normal levels have mild disease.

* A tendency toward easy bruising and massive hemorrhage after trauma or operative procedures.

* Spontaneous hemorrhages frequently occur in regions of the body that are susceptible to trauma, particularly the joints, where they are known as hemarthroses.

* Recurrent bleeding into the joints leads to progressive deformities that can be crippling.

* Petechiae are characteristically absent.

* Patients with hemophilia A have a prolonged PTT and a normal PT results that point to an abnormality of the intrinsic coagulation pathway.

* Factor VIII-specific assays are required for diagnosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy presents with recurrent episodes of urinary tract infection. His mother says that he urinates frequently but has a poor urinary stream along with dribbling of urine. On examination, he has a palpable bladder. What investigation can be used to find out the underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Micturating cystourethrography

The clinical scenario is suggestive of the posterior urethral valve which affects only males and MCU is the investigation of choice.

Posterior urethral valves:

Features:

* Posterior urethral valves are the most common cause of severe obstructive uropathy in children.

* The valves are membranes that have a small posterior slit within them, which typically lie just distal to the verumontanum

* They function as flap valves and are obstructive to antegrade urinary flow. A urethral catheter can be passed retrogradely.

* 15% of boys with posterior urethral valves have unilateral reflux into a nonfunctioning dysplastic kidney, termed the VURD syndrome (valves, unilateral reflux, dysplasia)

* Diagnosis is most commonly made antenatally with ultrasound, which demonstrates bilateral hydronephrosis above a distended bladder

* Antenatal USG would also demonstrate oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia.

* If the diagnosis is not made antenatally, then babies typically present with urinary infection in the neonatal period or with uremia and renal failure

* Clinically a poor urinary stream, dribbling, and palpable bladder (due to diverticula) can be present.

* The investigation of choice is micturating cystourethrography

* The ultrasound shows the typical 'key-hole sign in which the bladder and the proximal urethra is dilated

* Definitive treatment is by urethroscopic destruction of the valves with continuing lifelong supportive treatment of the dilated urinary tract, recurrent urinary infections, and uremia.

The given image below shows the 'key-hole sign seen in USG.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy weighing 30 Kgs has been posted for surgical resection of a tumor. What is the daily maintenance fluid required for this child while he’s NPO?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1700 mL

The daily maintenance fluid required for a child weighing 30 Kg is 1700 ml.

Bodyweight method for calculating the daily maintenance fluid volume (also known as Holliday-Segar method) is used.

Bodyweight
Fluid required per day

0–10 Kg
100 mL/Kg

11–20 Kg
1000 mL + 50 mL/Kg for each Kg >10 Kg

>20 Kg
1500 mL + 20 mL/Kg for each Kg >20 kg

Calculation:

In the question, the weight of the child is given as 30 Kgs.

So, the formula for >20 Kg is used.

1500 mL + (20 mL x weight more than 20 Kgs)

Since the child weight is 30 Kgs, he/she is 10 Kgs more.

Therefore, fluid required is

= 1500 mL + (20 mL x 10)

= 1500 mL + 200 mL

= 1700 mL.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old child from a poor family is brought with complaints of fever, convulsions, and abnormal behaviour for the last 2 months and has not been responding to the parents for the past 2 days. On examination, neck rigidity is seen with CSF showing increased lymphocytes, glucose-30mg% and proteins 300mg%. The diagnosis is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tubercular meningitis

Fever, convulsions, and signs of meningeal irritation (nuchal rigidity) in a child, with CSF showing reduced glucose, increased protein, and increased lymphocytes levels is a typical presentation of tubercular meningitis.

Other options:

*

Viral meningitis: Viral meningitis can present with similar symptoms, such as fever and abnormal behavior. However, in viral meningitis, the CSF findings typically show a lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose levels, and mildly elevated protein levels.

*

Bacterial meningitis: Bacterial meningitis can also present with fever, convulsions, and altered consciousness. However, the CSF findings in bacterial meningitis usually show a predominance of neutrophils, low glucose levels, and significantly elevated protein levels.

*

Partially treated bacterial meningitis: This option is less likely, as partially treated bacterial meningitis would usually have a different clinical course and CSF findings. In this scenario, the CSF findings and clinical presentation are more consistent with tubercular meningitis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A mother with her preterm newborn is worried as the newborn hasn't passed the meconium till now. What is the maximum time to wait for meconium to pass in this infant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 48 hours

Meconium is normally evacuated within 6 hours of birth( or earlier), but it can be delayed up to 24-48 hours and the maximum time to wait in a pre-term infant is 48 hours, however, in a term infant, it is 24 hours.

Meconium found in the intestine of a neonate consists of succus entericus (bile salts, bile acids, and debris from the intestinal mucosa).

Meconium ileus occurs in the first 24-48 hours of life when meconium becomes inspissated and obstructs the distal ileum causing abdominal distension and emesis. Abdominal radiographs show dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels and, frequently, a collection of granular, “ground-glass” material in the lower central abdomen.

Meconium ileus may also be seen with pancreatic atresia or pancreatic duct stenosis.

Radiological image shows contrast enema in a newborn infant with abdominal distention and failure to pass meconium. Several air-fluid levels in the small bowel are visible on the upright lateral view.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn at birth was noticed to have a herniated liver and small intestine via the umbilicus. The herniated mass was covered with membranes. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Omphalocele

A newborn with a herniated liver and small intestine via the umbilicus and the herniated mass being covered with membranes are both indicative of an omphalocele.

Failure of the intestinal loops to return to the abdominal cavity results in omphalocele or exomphalos which is covered with a membrane.

Omphalocele is a congenital malformation in which the abdominal viscera protrudes through a wide umbilical defect. The defect arises due to failure of the intestinal loops in the physiological umbilical hernia to return to the body cavity during the 6th to 10th weeks. The bowel loops are covered by amnion.

A small omphalocele contains only the intestines. A large omphalocele may contain other viscera such as stomach, liver, spleen, and large intestine, along with the small intestine. Omphalocele is commonly associated with other congenital anomalies (e.g., trisomy 13, trisomy 18, or Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome) and causes increased levels of α-fetoprotein.

Other options:

Option B: Gastroschisis should be ruled out while evaluating an omphalocele. Unlike an omphalocele, it lacks a covering membranous sac. It is typically found in a paraumbilical position, most often to the right of the umbilicus.

Option C: In a persistent vitellointestinal duct, the vitelline duct remains patent over its entire length. This results in the formation of direct communication between the umbilicus and the intestinal tract. A fecal discharge may then be found at the umbilicus.

Option D: Bochdalek hernia (posterior) is the most common type of diaphragmatic hernia. Herniation occurs through the pleuroperitoneal foramen.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A patient presents with chronic small bowel diarrhea and says that he is allergic to wheat. Duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy. Anti-endomysial antibodies and tTG IgA antibodies are positive. What is the diagnosis? tTG - tissue transglutaminase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Celiac sprue

Villous atrophy on duodenal biopsy together with a positive serological test for anti-endomysial antibodies and IgA anti-TTG antibodies suggests the diagnosis of celiac sprue.

Celiac disease is triggered by the ingestion of gluten, which is the major storage protein of wheat and similar grains. It usually affects the second portion of the duodenum or proximal jejunum. Antibodies associated with celiac disease are anti-gliadin antibodies, anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies, and anti-endomysial antibodies.

The histopathology is characterized by villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial CD8+T lymphocytes. An increase in the number of intraepithelial lymphocytes is a sensitive marker of celiac disease, even in the absence of epithelial damage and villous atrophy. MARSH's Score is used to assess celiac disease histologically.

Dermatitis herpetiformis can occur in as many as 10% of patients.

The main stay of treatment is a gluten-free diet.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The X-ray image of a child with muscle weakness and failure to thrive is attached below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rickets

The clinical vignette with the above X-ray image shows fraying and cupping of the metaphysis, suggestive of rickets.

Radiological features in rickets:

* Fraying (Widening and irregularity of the growth plate)

* Cupping (Concavity of the metaphysis)

* Splaying at metaphysis (widening of metaphyseal ends)

* Generalized rarefaction

Pearl PF0381: Radiological features of rickets

Radiological features of rickets:

* Delayed appearance of the epiphysis.

* Widening of growth plate: normal width of growth is 2-4mm. It is increased in cases of rickets due to excessive accumulation of uncalcified osteoid at the growth plate.

* Cupping of metaphysis: normally metaphysis meets epiphysis as a smooth line of sclerosis. But in rickets the line is absent and the metaphyseal ends appear irregular and the cartilage accumulating in the growth plate creates a depression in the metaphysis causing cupping.

* Fraying: indistinct margins of the metaphysis

* Bowing of diaphysis, with thinning of cortices.

* Loss of provisional zone of calcification (becomes denser in healing rickets, known as the white line of Frenkel).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: While performing surgery for acute appendicitis on a 2 year old child the following structure was found 2 feet proximal to ileocaecal junction and it was 2 inches long. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Meckel's diverticulum

The given clinical viignette and image is suggestive of Meckel's diverticulum which extends from the antimesenteric side of the small bowel.

The most common true diverticulum is Meckel's diverticulum, which occurs in the ileum.

A true diverticulum is a blind outpouching of the alimentary tract that communicates with the lumen and includes all three layers of the bowel wall. Meckel diverticulum occurs as a result of the failed involution of the vitelline duct, which connects the lumen of the developing gut to the yolk sac.

Meckel’s Diverticulum:

* Meckel’s diverticulum is caused by a failure of normal regression of the vitelline duct that develops during weeks 5 to 7 of gestation.

* The rule of 2s (Mnemonic for Meckel’s diverticulum) :

* 2 types of heterotopic mucosa (gastric & pancreatic)

* 2% incidence

* located within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve

* approximately 2 inches in length

* Usually symptomatic by 2 years of age

* Most common presentation is painless, massive, lower GI bleed in children younger than 5 years.

* A Meckel's can be the lead point for ileoileal or ileocolic intussusception.

* The bleeding Meckel's diverticulum may be confirmed by a 99 mTc-pertechnetate isotope scan to detect gastric mucosa.

* Surgical treatment is the definitive therapy for Meckel’s diverticulum. A simple V-shaped diverticulectomy with transverse closure of the ileum is the ideal surgical approach.

Pearl PF0287: Rule of two’s in Meckel's diverticulum

* 2% prevalence

* 2:1 male predominance

* Location 2 feet (60 cm) proximal to the ileocecal valve in adults

* 2 inches in length

* Half of those who are symptomatic are under 2 years of age.

Pearl PF0326: Zenker’s Diverticulum

* Hypopharyngeal diverticulum

* False diverticulum

* Pulsion diverticulum

* Acquired diverticulum, seen in the elderly (>60 years)

* Herniation is through the Killian’s triangle (a weak area between two parts of the inferior constrictor) in the posterior pharyngeal wall

* Clinical features:

* Dysphagia

* Regurgitation

* Halitosis

* Aspiration

* Gurgling sound during swallowing

* Investigation of choice: Barium swallow (Lateral X rays)

* Treatment

* Cricopharyngeal myotomy

* Surgical diverticulectomy

* Marsupialization

* Dohlman’s procedure

Zenker’s diverticulum

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-month-old child undergoes treatment for diarrhoea with hypokalemia but the child does not respond to the treatment appropriately and on examination muscular weakness is noted, What is the most likely cause of treatment failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypomagnesemia

The given clinical scenario of a child with diarrhea, muscular weakness, and hypokalemia not responding to treatment is most likely due to hypomagnesemia.

The major cause of hypomagnesemia in this scenario is severe diarrhoea/gastrointestinal loss which in turn worsens the hypokalemia. In such cases, hypokalemia can not be corrected unless the underlying hypomagnesemia is addressed.

Treatment failure in hypokalemia due to hypomagnesemia is mediated by two mechanisms:

* ↓ Magnesium → inhibits Na+/ K+ - ATPase activity → ↓ influx of potassium into the cell → secondary kaliuresis.

* ↓ Magnesium → decreased block of ROMK (renal outer medullary K+ channel) potassium efflux channels → increased potassium secretion by distal nephron

Therefore in the presence of hypomagnesemia, hypokalemic patients are clinically refractory to potassium supplementation therapy.

Hypokalemia is defined as a plasma concentration of K+ <3.5 meq/L. The following are various causes of hypokalemia:

* Inadequate intake

* Diet, potassium-free intravenous fluids, potassium deficient TPN

* Excessive potassium excretion

* Hyperaldosteronism

* Medications

* Potassium losses

* Direct loss of potassium from GI fluid (diarrhea)

* Renal loss of potassium (to conserve sodium in response to gastric losses)

* Metabolic

* Intracellular potassium shifts from metabolic alkalosis or insulin therapy

Clinical features

* Weakness and paralysis

* Intestinal ileus

* Risk of atrial and ventricular arrhythmias

* Broad flat T waves, ST depression, and QT prolongation are most marked when serum K+ <2.7 mmol/L

* Sodium chloride and bicarbonate retention lead to metabolic alkalosis

Management includes potassium supplementation with concurrent cardiac monitoring. Treat hypomagnesemia by supplementation. High dose propranolol if due to excess sympathetic activity

Other options:

Option B: The clinical features of hyponatremia are predominantly neurological as a result of the development of cerebral edema. Patients usually present with nausea, headache, vomiting, seizure, brainstem herniation, and coma.

Option C: The clinical features of hypermagnesemia are dose-dependent.

* >2 mmol/L - vasodilation and neuromuscular blockade.

* >4 mmol/L - refractory hypotension, progressive weakness leading to respiratory paralysis and coma. Although hypermagnesemia causes muscle weakness, the question asked is the cause of treatment failure in hypokalemia.

* >10mmol/L - dilated pupils, bradycardia, PR, QRS, and QT prolongation.

Option D: The clinical features of hypernatremia are neurological. The most frequent manifestation is altered mental status ranging from confusion and lethargy to deep coma.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-day old male neonate who has not yet passed meconium developed abdominal distension. There is no history of fever. On rectal examination, forceful expulsion of stool was observed. A barium enema is performed and the findings are shown in the image below. Which of the following is the gold standard for the diagnosis of the above condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rectal biopsy

The clinical scenario of a newborn presenting with failure to pass meconium, abdominal distension, forceful expulsion of stools on rectal examination, and barium enema showing dilated right colon with a transition zone in the mid-descending colon is suggestive of Hirschsprung's disease. The gold standard for the diagnosis of Hirschprung's disease is a rectal biopsy.

Hirschsprung disease or congenital aganglionic colon is characterized by the absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus and submucosal (Meissner) plexus of the distal intestinal segment. This is because of the premature arrest of normal migration of neural crest cells from the cecum to the rectum.

They are predominantly seen in boys and are associated with Down syndrome. Most cases present during the neonatal period with abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, and failure to pass meconium. Later they may also have poor feeding and severe constipation. Forceful expulsion of stools is observed on rectal examination as the stools accumulate in the distal colon.

A barium enema is obtained on all suspected cases. This demonstrates the location of the transition zone between the dilated ganglionic colon and the distal aganglionic rectal segment.  In older children, anorectal manometry shows a high internal sphincter pressure due to the absence of normal inhibitory reflex.

Rectal biopsy is the gold standard investigation shows the following:

* Absent ganglia

* Hypertrophied nerve trunks

* Positive immunostaining for acetylcholinesterase

* Calretinin immunostaining (superior to acetylcholinesterase staining)

The definitive surgeries are the Swenson procedure, Duhamel procedure, and Soave's procedure

The most common cause of death in uncorrected Hirschprung's disease is enterocolitis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 31-year-old lady with diabetes mellitus delivers a term neonate. Which of the following problems is associated with a baby born to this lady?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypoglycemia

The condition associated with an infant born to a mother with diabetes mellitus is hypoglycemia.

In pregestational diabetes and gestational diabetes mellitus, maternal hyperglycemia causes a higher amount of blood glucose to pass through the placenta into the fetal circulation. It results in fetal hyperglycemia leading to fetal hyperinsulinism. These increased insulin levels continue to persist after delivery which leads to hypoglycemia. Extra glucose in the fetus is stored as body fat causing macrosomia. These newborns are at risk of developing various complications due to fetal hyperglycemia. They are:

* Gastrointestinal: These infants may demonstrate abdominal distention caused by a transient delay in the development of the left side of the colon due to fluctuations in maternal and fetal glucose resulting in small left colon syndrome.

* Metabolic: Hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia

* Neural: Neural tube defects like caudal regression syndrome, encephalocele, anencephaly

* Respiratory: Respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnea of newborn, persistent pulmonary hypertension

* Cardiac: Cardiomegaly, cardiac malformations like a ventricular or atrial septal defect, transposition of the great vessels(most specific), truncus arteriosus, double-outlet right ventricle, tricuspid atresia, coarctation of the aorta

* Haematological: Polycythemia, renal vein thrombosis

* Others: Hyperbilirubinemia, insulin resistance, diabetes, sudden intrauterine death

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old male with known history of asthma developed sudden onset breathlessness, and wheezing . He was rushed to the emergency, where the preliminary assessment was done. The pulse is 140/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and the FEV1 is 40% of the predicted value. Which of the following is the best next step in treatment in this case?
options: A high concentration of oxygen should be given by a face mask + Salbutamol nebulisation
High doses of SABA to be given by a nebulizer only
Sedatives should be added to alleviate anxiety
Nebulized anticholinergics to be added immediately as the mainstay of treatment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A high concentration of oxygen should be given by a face mask + Salbutamol nebulisation

The clinical scenario given above is suggestive of severe, acute attack of asthma. The best next step in the treatment would be to give a high concentration of oxygen should be given by a face mask + Salbutamol nebulisation .

Management of acute attack of asthma:

* A high concentration of oxygen should be given by face mask and oxygen saturation should be maintained at >90%.

* The mainstay of treatment are high doses of SABA given either by nebulizer or via a metered-dose inhaler (MDI) with a spacer.

* In severely ill patients with impending respiratory failure, IV β2-agonists may be given.

* A nebulized anticholinergic may be added if there is not a good response to β2-agonists alone.

* In patients who are refractory to inhaled therapies, a slow infusion of aminophylline can also be given.

Features of Acute severe attack of asthma include:

* Inability to speak a complete sentence in one breath

* Pulse >120/min

* Respiratory rate >25/min

* FEV1 between 33 to 50% of predicted

* Pulsus paradoxus of >10 mmHg

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-year-old child was brought to her pediatrician for routine well-child care. Her physical examination is normal except for a systolic murmur and a widely split-second heart sound that does not vary with respiration. She has no family history of heart disease. Which among the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Atrial septal defect

The age of the patient, normal physical findings except for a systolic murmur, and wide and fixed (does not vary with respiration) splitting of S2 are all in favor of a diagnosis of atrial septal defect.

ASDs are abnormal, fixed openings in the atrial septum caused by incomplete tissue formation that allows communication of blood between the left and right atria. The ASD creates a left to right shunt that increases the blood flow to the right side of the heart. This causes the pulmonary valve to close later than the aortic valve. Since the two atria are linked, inspiration does not produce any net pressure changes between them abolishing respiration-related changes in venous return hence causing fixed S2.

Other options:

Option A: TAPVC patients usually present with cyanosis and congestive cardiac failure around 4-10 weeks of age. This is when the fetal pulmonary vasculature regresses and there is increased pulmonary blood flow which results in early-onset cardiac failure. The physical findings are identical to ASD.

Option B: Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is typically associated with a pan-systolic murmur best heard in the left lower sternal border.

Option C: Pulmonic stenosis is an acyanotic heart disease and physical findings include an ejection systolic murmur and a thrill in the left second intercostal space and a wide and variable split S2 because of delayed closure of P2.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy has non-blanching rashes on the legs and buttocks as seen in the picture. He also complains of joint pains, abdominal pain, vomiting, and blood in the stool. Lab investigations revealed normal platelet count and urine analysis shows haematuria +++ and proteinuria +. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Henoch Schonlein purpura (HSP)

This clinical scenario describes Henoch Schonlein purpura.

Features of Henoch Schonlein purpura (HSP):

* Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP) is a common small vessel vasculitis in childhood.

* It is characterized by a purpuric rash and commonly accompanied by arthritis and abdominal pain.

* About half of the patients with HSP develop renal manifestations, which vary from asymptomatic microscopic hematuria to severe, progressive glomerulonephritis: The pathogenesis of HSP nephritis appears to be mediated by the deposition of polymeric immunoglobulin A (IgA) in glomeruli.

* Laboratory studies generally show a mild leukocytosis, a normal platelet count, and occasionally eosinophilia. Serum complement components are normal.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child is brought to the pediatrician with short stature. On evaluation, growth hormone levels are found to be high and Insulin-like growth factor(IGF-1) levels are low. Which among the following could be the abnormality here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. GH receptor anomaly

The presence of high growth hormone levels and low Insulin-like growth factor(IGF-1) levels point towards Laron syndrome/dwarfism. It is caused by end-organ resistance to growth hormone(GH insensitivity) due to the mutation of the growth hormone receptor.

Here, growth hormones are produced, but not able to act on the target tissues as growth hormone receptors in the target tissue are not responding to growth hormones. So, the resting and stimulated growth hormone levels are high and insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) levels are low.

It is an autosomal-recessive disorder with clinical features that are the same as those seen in pituitary dwarfism. The primary clinical symptom associated with this condition is short stature.

Treatment is by subcutaneous injections of insulin-like growth factor 1 (a growth-promoting hormone), often called IGF-1.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child who was fed only on rice water presents with a swollen belly and dull face. His appearance is of a 'fat sugar baby' and is found to have low serum protein and low albumin. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kwashiorkar

A swollen belly with a dull face,appearance of 'fat sugar baby',low serum albumin, and protein are suggestive of Kwashiorkor.

Kwashiorkor is a form of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) characterized by oedema and apathy.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn baby presents with irritability and cyanosis which subsides on crying. On examination, you are unable to pass a nasogastric tube and no mist formation is noted on the laryngeal mirror test. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Oro pharyngeal airway

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of choanal atresia, the best next step would be to provide an oropharyngeal airway.

Choanal atresia is the persistence of the bucconasal membrane, unilateral is more common and may remain undiagnosed until adult life, bilateral atresia will present as a respiratory obstruction in the newborn. The initial clinical evaluation consists of placing a large laryngeal mirror under each nostril and checking for fogging, this is known as the laryngeal mirror test.

Diagnosis can be made by:

* Presence of mucoid discharge in the nose

* Absence of air bubbles in the nasal discharge

* Failure to pass a catheter from the nose to the pharynx

* Putting methylene blue dye into the nose and checking its passage to the pharynx

* Putting a radio-opaque dye into the nose and taking a lateral radiograph

* CT in the axial plane

Management: In bilateral atresia, emergency treatment is to provide an airway, which is done by McGovern's technique- (a feeding tube with a large hole that provides a good oral airway), this removes the need for tracheostomy. Definitive treatment is correcting the atresia either by transpalatal or transnasal approach, which is usually done at one and a half years of age.

Pearl PF1080: Choanal atresia

* It is due to the persistence of bucconasal membrane which separates primitive oropharynx from the primitive nasopharynx

* Unilateral > bilateral

* 30% of cases are bony and 70% are mixed

* Unilateral cases may be asymptomatic and present in adult life

* Bilateral cases are life-threatening and present with respiratory distress

* Associated with CHARGE syndrome

* C- Coloboma of the eye

* H- Heart defects

* A- Atresia of choana

* R- Retarded growth and development

* G- Genital anomalies

* E- Ear anomalies and hearing loss.

* CT scan is the best investigation

Image: Membranous, bilateral choanal atresia in a newborn

* McGoverns technique- A feeding nipple with a large hole provides a good oral airway

* Definitive treatment consists of correction of atresia by a trans-nasal or trans-palatal approach.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy presented with dark-colored urine as shown below, oliguria, hypertension, and facial puffiness for 3 days. The urine test is positive for albumin. He had a history of throat infection 2 weeks back. On microscopic examination, enlarged, pale glomeruli and epithelial humps are seen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

The clinical scenario given in the question is suggestive of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN).

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis(PSGN) is characterized by the sudden onset of gross hematuria, oedema, hypertension, and renal insufficiency. It usually occurs following a throat infection by nephritogenic strains of group A β-hemolytic streptococci. It can also occur after streptococcal skin infection or pyoderma.

The typical patient develops an acute nephritic syndrome following 1 to 2 weeks after antecedent streptococcal pharyngitis or 3 to 6 weeks after streptococcal pyoderma. The pathogenesis involves circulating antibodies elicited by streptococcal antigens reacting with normal glomerular antigens, and complement activation by directly deposited streptococcal antigens causing the immunologic injury.

In this immune complex-mediated APSGN, we see a decrease in the serum complement (C3) level (levels normalise in 6 to 8 weeks), and ASO titer is increased (the titers decrease to low levels within 4 to 6 weeks).

Microscopic Findings in PSGN include

* Light microscopy: Enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with diffuse mesangial proliferation and leukocyte infiltration.

* Immunofluorescence: Granular deposits of IgG and complement C3 along the glomerular basement membrane(GBM)and in the mesangium.

* Electron microscopy: Electron-dense deposits, or humps, are observed on the epithelial side of the GBM.

Below is the image showing light microscopy findings of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Other options:

Option A: Post-staphylococcal glomerulonephritis is a kidney condition that occurs after a Staphylococcus infection, leading to immune complex deposition in the glomeruli. It presents with hematuria, proteinuria, oedema, and hypertension, often seen in adults with underlying health conditions.

Option C: Nephrotic syndrome is a kidney disorder characterized by massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminemia, oedema, and hyperlipidemia. It results from increased glomerular permeability, leading to fluid retention and other systemic complications.

Option D: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) is the most common type of glomerulonephritis worldwide. It is characterized by recurrent hematuria/ nephritic syndrome and the presence of prominent IgA deposits in the mesangium. Clinically, children and young adults present with gross or microscopic hematuria within 1-2 days of onset of an upper respiratory (synpharyngitic presentation) or gastrointestinal infection.

The below image is an immunofluorescence study of IgA nephropathy showing the characteristic IgA deposition in the mesangial regions.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Dystrophin protein is absent completely in which of the following diseases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy

Dystrophin protein (a sarcolemmal protein), is absent in patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) due to a mutation in the dystrophin gene. Lack of dystrophin leads to cellular instability, which leads to progressive leakage of intracellular components.

Dystrophin connects actin filaments to the transmembrane protein β-dystroglycan in the sarcolemma by the smaller proteins syntrophins in the cytoplasm.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy:

* Most common hereditary neuromuscular disease

* It is an X-linked recessive disorder, and the causative gene is located at Xp21.

* Clinical features

* Progressive weakness with developmental delay occurs.

* Pseudohypertrophy of calves and wasting of thigh muscles is seen.

* Trendelenburg gait or hip waddle is characteristic.

* Gower’s sign: Indicates weakness of proximal muscles: The patient has to use hands and arms to "walk-up" their own body from a squatting position.

* Dilated cardiomyopathy

* Diagnosis

* Elevated serum creatine kinase levels

* Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis for the dystrophin gene

* If PCR is normal, but clinical suspicion is high, muscle biopsy with dystrophin immunocytochemistry is done.

* Treatment: Treatment of cardiac decompensation, nutritional management, physiotherapy, and glucocorticoids.

* Prognosis: Death occurs usually at about 18 to 20 years of age due to respiratory failure, intractable heart failure, pneumonia, or aspiration.

Other options:

Option A: Becker's muscular dystrophy(BMD) leads to abnormal dystrophin formation, whereas the dystrophin gene mutation in DMD leads to dystrophin deficiency.

Option C: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a neuromuscular disorder that is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles, due to a decrease in the number of available acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at neuromuscular junctions as a result of antibody-mediated autoimmune attack.

Option D: Lambert Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome is a neuromuscular junction disorder associated with the reduced acetylcholine (Ach) release from the presynaptic nerve terminals, despite normal ACh vesicle numbers, ACh presynaptic concentration, and postsynaptic ACh receptors.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Tetralogy of Fallot is most commonly associated with which of the following:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Down syndrome

Tetralogy of Fallot is most commonly associated with Down syndrome among the given options.

Tetralogy of Fallot: It is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease.

* The primary defect is an anterior deviation of the infundibular septum (the muscular septum that separates the aortic and pulmonary outflows).

* The primary defect gives rise to the 4 anatomical components of TOF which are:

* Ventricular septal defect (VSD) ( NOT ASD)

* Obstruction to right ventricular outflow - Pulmonic stenosis (PS)

* Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)

* Overriding (or dextroposition) of the aorta

* Obstruction to pulmonary arterial blood flow is usually at both the right ventricular infundibulum (subpulmonic area) and the pulmonary valve.

* The degree of pulmonary outflow obstruction determines the degree of the patient’s cyanosis and the age of first presentation.

The heart is typically enlarged and is classically “boot-shaped” due to marked right ventricular hypertrophy.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Vitamin K supplementation is given to neonates to prevent ___.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hemorrhagic disease of newborn

Intramuscular injection of 0.5-1 mg of phytonadione(Vitamin K)  is given to all newborn infants to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

Hemorrhagic disease of the newborn is caused by a transient deficiency of vitamin K–dependent factors, factors II, VII, IX, and X.

Causes include:

* Lack of free vitamin K from the mother

* Absence of the bacterial intestinal flora normally responsible for the synthesis of vitamin K.

It is responsive to and prevented by vitamin K therapy (0.5-1 mg of phytonadione).

However, for newborns with vitamin K deficiency, the dose of vitamin K administered is 1–5 mg intravenously.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is the first-line drug used to control seizures in a child presenting with febrile seizures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Midazolam

The first-line drug to control the seizures in febrile seizures is a benzodiazepine like midazolam or lorazepam.

Febrile seizures occur in children of the age of 6-60 months with a high-grade fever of 38°C (100.4 F) or higher without underlying CNS infections, metabolic abnormality, or prior afebrile seizures.

Risk factors:

Major:

* Age less than 1 year

* Duration of fever less than 24 hr

* Fever range: 38-39°C (100.4-102.2°F)

Minor:

* Family history of epilepsy

* Daycare

* Male gender

* Complex febrile seizure

* Family history of febrile seizures

* Lower serum sodium at the time of presentation

Types of febrile seizures:

Simple febrile seizures
Complex (atypical) febrile seizures

Occurs within 24 hours of the onset of fever
Can occur at any time during a fever

Generalized seizures
Focal seizures

Duration is <15 min
Prolonged (>15 min)

No recurrence within 24 hrs of seizures
Recurrent within 24 hours

Chances of going into epilepsy 1%
Chances of going into epilepsy 6%

Investigations:

* Lumbar puncture should be performed in the first episode of seizures with fever, for all infants <6 months age (to exclude meningitis).

* EEG and neuroimaging are advised for children with atypical febrile seizures.

Acute treatment of febrile seizures includes lorazepam and midazolam for seizures lasting more than 5 minutes. Rectal diazepam is prescribed to use at home as rescue medication if febrile seizures last more than 5 minutes. The use of antipyretics can decrease the discomfort of the child but does not reduce the risk of having a recurrent febrile seizure.

Prophylaxis:

* Intermittent prophylaxis includes oral clobazam for 3 days during the fever episode, if the febrile seizures recur at the rate of ≥3 seizures in 6 months, or ≥4 in 1 year.

* Continuous prophylaxis with sodium valproate and phenobarbitone can be used for failed intermittent prophylaxis and in recurrent atypical febrile seizures.

Note:

* Intermittent oral nitrazepam, clobazam, and clonazepam have also been used. Such therapies help reduce, but do not eliminate, the risks of recurrence of febrile seizures.

* Future epilepsy does not change with or without antiepileptic therapy.

* Iron deficiency is associated with an increased risk of febrile seizures, and thus screening and treating it would be appropriate.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect about colostrum?
options: It is the breastmilk that is seen in the initial 3-4 days.
Contains high amount of lactose and low amounts of protein.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Contains high amount of lactose and low amounts of protein.

Option D is incorrect as colostrum is the milk secreted in the initial days which has high amounts of protein and less amount of lactose.

Various transitional forms of breastmilk:

Colostrum

* In the initial 3 to 4 days

* Small quantity, thick, and yellow in colour

* A large number of antibodies, immune component cells like secretory IgA, lactoferrin, leukocytes, and vitamins like B12, A, D, E, and K.

* High in protein and low in lactose

Transitional milk

* Secreted after 3 to 4 days until 2 weeks

* Immunoglobulin and protein content decreases, while the fat and sugar content increases.

Mature milk

* Follows transitional milk.

* Thinner and more watery.

* Contains all the nutrients essential for the optimal growth of the baby.

Foremilk

* Secreted at the start of the feed

* Watery and rich in proteins, sugar, vitamins, minerals, and water that quenches the baby’s thirst.

Hindmilk

* Comes towards the end of the feed

* Provides more energy and a sense of satiety and it is richer in fat.

Preterm milk

* Milk of mother who delivers before 37 weeks.

* Contains more proteins, sodium, iron, immunoglobins, and calories as per the requirement of the preterm infant.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presented with a history of edema of the face which later progressed to generalised edema. Urine showed massive proteinuria and light microscopy was normal. Electron microscopy showed effacement of podocyte foot processes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Minimal change disease

This case of nephrotic syndrome shows effacement of the podocyte foot processes which is characteristic of minimal change disease (MCD).

Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome. It is seen in ages 2-6 years with a clinical picture of nephrotic syndrome, that is, heavy proteinuria, oedema, hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. They may be asymptomatic or can present with peripheral oedema.

A renal biopsy is not required for confirmation and treatment can be initiated if the child fits the standard clinical picture of nephrotic syndrome. Light microscopy shows normal glomeruli and electron microscopy shows effacement of podocyte foot processes.

They show excellent response to steroid therapy with prednisone or prednisolone. A daily dose of 60 mg/m2/day for 6 weeks, followed by a single dose of 40 mg/m2 on alternate days for the next 6 weeks is the standard treatment.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the clinic with a fever, cough, red eyes, running nose, and rash. The appearance of the child is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Measles

This child with a given clinical vignette and the rash has measles.

Measles is a common cause of fever with rash that spread via droplets. It is characterised by a prodrome of cough, conjunctivitis and coryza along with fever. Koplik spots are white grain lesions with surrounding erythema on the buccal mucosa opposite to the lower second molar. A reddish macular rash begins behind the ears on the 4th day, rapidly becomes maculopapular and spreads to the face, neck, chest, arms, trunk, thighs and legs.

Other options:

Option A: Mumps is caused by a paramyxovirus and spread by droplets and contact. It causes fever, malaise unilateral or bilateral parotitis. It also causes epididymo-orchitis in males.

Option C: Chickenpox is caused by varicella zoster and spreads by contact and airborne. It has a prodrome of fever, malaise, anorexia and headache which is followed by a rash in 1-2 days. It has pruritic erythematous macules that first appear on the trunk and spreads to face and extremities that evolve into papules, vesicles and pustules that become crusted. The presence of several crops of lesions that are in different stages of evolution is a characteristic of varicella.

Option D: Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) is caused by parvovirus B19 transmitted by airborne route. The prodromal consists of low-grade fever, headache and mild upper respiratory tract infection. An erythematous slapped cheeked rash that first appears on the face is characteristic. A macular rash then spreads to the trunk and extremities that undergoes central clearing giving a lacy or reticulated pattern.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-year-old child is brought for complaints of short stature. His height is comparable with his parent's height and his bone age corresponds to his chronological age. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Familial short stature

A child with short stature with his height comparable to his parent's height and bone age that equals chronological age, the likely diagnosis is familial short stature.

This child's height is normal according to his genetic potential determined by the parent's height. The body proportion is appropriate and bone age equals the chronological age with normal growth velocity. They achieve puberty at an appropriate age and their final height is within their target range.

The relationship between bone age and chronological age is summarised below

* Bone age = chronological age in familial short stature

* Bone age > chronological age in precocious puberty

* Bone age < chronological age in other causes like constitutional delay, undernutrition, genetic diseases, and endocrine causes.

Other options:

Option B: Children with constitutional delay are normal during the first year and fall behind till 3 years, after which the velocity becomes normal. Bone age is lower than chronological age(corresponds to the height age). The onset of puberty is also delayed and they achieve a normal final height. History of delayed puberty and delayed height spurt is usually present in one or both parents.

Option C: Children with undernutrition show other features of malnutrition such as low mid-upper arm circumference and low weight, with a bone age lower than chronological age.

Option D: Children with growth hormone deficiency have bone age lower than chronological age and other signs like crowding of mid-facial structures, and depressed nasal bridge.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with the findings shown in the image below. What is the true statement regarding this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kwashiorkor due to protein malnutrition

This malnourished child with a distended abdomen has kwashiorkor due to protein malnutrition.

Kwashiorkor is a form of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) characterized by edema and apathy. It usually affects infants and children, most often around the age of weaning till the age of 5.

It is due to an overall deficiency in protein and calories, with a much more severe protein deficit. It is due to a deficiency of proteins, such as albumin that exerts oncotic pressure in the blood that there is such extensive pitting edema which starts in the legs, and feet and then spreads to hands, face and later becomes generalized.

Skin changes occur over the swollen limbs and include dark, crackled peeling patches with pale skin underneath forming patches of hyper and hypopigmentation called flaky paint dermatosis or crazy paving. The skin gets easily infected.

The hair is dull, brittle, sparse, and can easily be pulled out. It may lose its curl. In dark-haired children, the hair may turn pale or reddish. Alternating bands of light and normal color hair may be seen, known as the flag sign. Children are miserable, apathetic, and often refuse to eat. There is marked muscle atrophy and growth retardation.

Marasmus is another form of SAM that occurs as a result of a calorie deficiency primarily. It is characterized by severe wasting that occurs due to the consumption of fat and muscle to release energy. The child has monkey facies and baggy pants appearance due to the loss of fat pad in the face and buttocks without edema.

Clinical features seen in marasmus are:

* Simian facies

* Lethargic and irritable,apathetic

* Bradycardia

* Thin, dry skin

* Thin and brittle hair, easily pluckable

* hypotension, and hypothermia

* The reduction of buccal fat pad gives rise to a wrinkled or aged look, while the term “baggy pants appearance” describes sagging skin of the buttocks that hangs downward.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child who has overdosed on iron tablets comes with nausea and abdominal pain. What is the antidote for this toxicity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Deferoxamine

The antidote used for iron overdose is deferoxamine.

Deferoxamine, a potent iron-chelating compound, can be given intravenously to bind iron that has already been absorbed and to promote its excretion in urine and faeces. Hypotension is a common side effect of deferoxamine infusion. The deferoxamine-iron complex can colour the urine reddish.

Iron toxicity presents as profuse vomiting and diarrhoea (often bloody), abdominal pain, and significant volume losses. Later patients develop multisystem organ failure, shock, and metabolic acidosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A neonate was brought with a history of frothiness from the mouth and respiratory distress. An X-ray of the neonate is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Esophageal atresia with tracheo-esophageal fistula

The given symptoms of frothiness and respiratory distress and an X-ray showing a nasogastric (NG) tube in proximal esophagus and stomach distended with gas are suggestive of esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF).

Longitudinal furrow separates the trachea from the esophagus during development. Deviation or altered growth in this septum results in the formation of an abnormal fistula communication between the esophagus and trachea called a tracheoesophageal fistula. It is associated with VACTERL (vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheal, esophageal, renal, and limb) anomalies.

The newborn has excessive drooling and frothing soon after birth. On feeding, the baby develops choking and cyanosis. Regurgitation of secretion and feed through the fistulous tract into the lungs results in aspiration pneumonia.

Type C consists of proximal esophageal atresia and distal TEF is the commonest. Here the air enters into stomach causing gastric distention which is seen as an air bubble. There is an inability to pass an NG tube for more than 7-10 cm, and a coiling in the proximal esophagus helps in the diagnosis.

Other options

Option A - Transient tachypnea of newborn is due to delayed clearance of lung fluid. They have tachypnea with minimal or no respiratory distress. Chest X-ray may show hyper-expanded lung fields, prominent vascular marking and prominent interlobar fissure.

Option B: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia occurs because of the failure to close the pleuroperitoneal membrane. Intestinal loops enter the thorax and compress the developing lung causing pulmonary hypoplasia. They present with respiratory distress and a scaphoid abdomen. Chest X-ray would show multiple air-filled spaces in the thorax, a shift of mediastinum, and the absence of an outline of the left diaphragm.

Option D: Respiratory distress syndrome/Hyaline membrane disease occurs primarily in premature infants due to a deficiency of surfactant in the alveoli. Clinical features include tachypnea, retractions, grunting, cyanosis, and decreased air entry. X-ray shows reticulogranular pattern, ground glass opacity, low lung volume, air bronchogram, and white-out lungs in severe disease.
