questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl is being evaluated for pubertal development. She has onset of breast development, pubic hair has appeared, and she is at Tanner stage 2. Which of the following is the next likely event to occur according to Tanner staging?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Peak growth spurt

Sequence of pubertal development shows that after thelarche (onset of breast development, tanner stage 2) and pubarche (appearance of pubic hair, Tanner stage 2), the next most likely event is the peak height velocity (growth spurt). The growth spurt occurs early in female puberty, generally after Tanner stage 2 breast and pubic hair development.

In females at 10 to 11 years, the breast bud (thelarche) appears, which is the first sign of puberty, followed by the appearance of pubic hair (pubarche), growth spurt, and menarche. Thelarche > pubarche > growth spurt > menarche .

Tanner staging
Breast changes
Pubic hair changes

Stage 1

B1 - Denotes the prepubertal breast. At this infantile stage, only the papilla is elevated.

P1 - No pubic hair

Stage 2

B2 - Denotes thelarche. The breast buds are palpable, areola enlarges and the breast is elevated like a small mound.

P2 - The appearance of pigmented hair sparsely over the labia, either long or slightly curved.

Stage 3

B3 - There is further enlargement of the breast and its areola without separation of its contours.

P3 - Darker, coarser and curly hair

Stage 4

B4 - Preferential growth of the areola and nipple leads to formation of a secondary mound over the mound of the breast.

P4 - Preadult stage cover short inverted triangular distribution.

Stage 5

B5 - Formation of the mature adult breast.

P5 - Adult inverted triangular distributuion.

Other options:

Option B: Appearance of axillary hair – Axillary hair development occurs later, with stages A1 (no axillary hair), A2 (sparse axillary hair), and A3 (adult distribution). This follows pubic hair development and usually appears after the growth spurt.

Option C: Menarche is a late pubertal event, generally following thelarche by about 2 years.

Option D: Thelarche refers to the onset of breast development.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with a respiratory rate of 66 breaths per minute, chest indrawing, nasal flaring, and poor feeding. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Severe pneumonia

The clinical presentation of a 4-month-old child with fast breathing (>50 beats/min for 2-12 months), chest indrawaing along with the presence of a danger sign(poor feeding) strongly points towards the diagnosis of severe pneumonia. The treatment for severe pneumonia is to administer IV antibiotics and refer to a higher centre.

The revised classification of acute respiratory infections is simplified to include only two categories of pneumonia:

* Pneumonia: with fast breathing and/or chest indrawing, which requires home therapy with oral amoxicillin.

Age of child

Fast breathing RR

<2 months

>60 breaths/min

2-12 months

>50 breaths/min

1-5 years

>40 breaths/min

* Severe pneumonia: Pneumonia with any general danger sign, which requires a referral and injectable therapy.

Danger signs of pneumonia in children include:

* Not able to drink

* Persistent vomiting

* Convulsions, lethargic or unconscious

* Stridor in a calm child

* Severe malnutrition

If a child has only a fever, cough or cold, it is categorised as no pneumonia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 9-month-old infant is brought to the pediatric clinic with a history of sudden jerky movements of the head, trunk, and limbs occurring in clusters. EEG shows a chaotic high-amplitude background with multifocal spikes, consistent with hypsarrhythmia. What is the treatment of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ACTH

The clinical scenario of infantile spasms along with hypsarrythmia in EEG is highly suggestive of West syndrome. Therefore, the drug of choice would be adreno-corticotropic hormone (ACTH).

West syndrome is severe generalized epilepsy that begins between the ages of 2 and 12 months. It is characterized by a triad of:

* Infantile epileptic spasms

* Developmental regression

* Hypsarrhythmia on electroencephalogram (EEG)

Hypsarrhythmia refers to a high voltage, slow, chaotic background with multifocal spikes as shown below.

West syndrome has been known by many names like infantile spasms, salaam attacks, salaam convulsions infantile spastic epilepsy, and jackknife convulsion syndrome. During an attack babies typically attain complete heaving of the head forward towards their knees, and then immediately relax into the upright position.

The image given below illustrates infantile spasms in a child.

Diagnosis is confirmed by EEG which typically shows hypsarrythmia.

The treatment of choice in West syndrome is either adreno-corticotropic hormone (ACTH) or corticosteroids. An antiseizure medication, mainly vigabatrin can be used when associated with tuberous sclerosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child can sit without support, turn diagonally, and babble bisyllables. Which of the following abilities is expected during this time?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Crawling

The described child is around 9 months of age, since sitting without support, turning diagonally(pivoting), and babbling bisyllables are key milestones of this age. At this stage, children typically start crawling, which is the expected gross motor milestone.

* Ability to sit unsupported(gross motor development): at 6-7 months

* To pivot while sitting(gross motor development): at 9-10 months

* Bisyllables(mama, baba, dada)(language milestone): at 8-10 months

Other options:

Option A: Mature pincer grasp appears later at about 12 months.

Option B: Walking without support develops much later, around 12–15 months.

Option C: Building a tower of two blocks usually occurs at around 15-18 months.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child diagnosed with Kawasaki disease developed multiple large coronary artery aneurysms. The child has now recovered from the acute phase. What is the most appropriate next step in long-term management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aspirin lifelong

Children with Kawasaki disease who develop large or giant coronary artery aneurysms (CAAs) are at high risk of thrombosis and long-term complications. Therefore, the child should continue lifelong aspirin for secondary prevention.

Kawasaki's disease is also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome. It is a vasculitis condition of unknown etiology.  Clinical features include a high spiking fever that is unresponsive to antipyretics. The fever can last between 5 days to 3-4 weeks.

Diagnosis of typical Kawasaki disease is made by fever for 5 or more days along with four of the symptoms listed below:

* Bilateral conjunctival congestion (not purulent conjunctivitis)

* Oral changes: erythematous, cracked lips, and strawberry tongue

* Non-suppurative cervical lymphadenopathy, usually unilateral

* Polymorphous rash

* Changes in extremities: erythema and edema, desquamation of palms and soles

Laboratory findings:

Important laboratory findings of Kawasaki disease are anaemia, elevated ESR and CRP.Thrombocytosis is a characteristic finding in Kawasaki disease and commonly occurs in the second week.

Treatment:

Acute KD:
• IVIG 2 g/kg over 10-12 hr
• High dose aspirin (80-100 mg/kg/day, q6h) until patient is afebrile for at least 48 hr
Convalescent phase:
• Aspirin 3-5 mg/kg once daily for 6-8 wk after illness onset, if  coronary findings are normal throughout the course.

Long term therapy for patients with coronary abnormalities

* Small aneurysms: Aspirin 3-5 mg/kg/d

* Medium aneurysms:

* Aspirin 3-5 mg/kg once daily plus

* Clopidogrel 1 mg/kg/day (maximum: 75 mg/day)

* Giant aneurysms: Aspirin + anticoagulation with warfarin, low molecular weight heparin, or direct oral anticoagulants

Acute coronary thrombosis
•Fibrinolytic therapy to be started with tissue plasminogen activator
or other thrombolytic agents.

Major complications of Kawasaki disease are arteritis and aneurysms of coronary vessels, myocarditis, myocardial infarction and pericarditis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with recurrent sinusitis and repeated lung infections. Genetic testing shows a mutation in the CFTR gene. Which test is considered the gold standard to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sweat chloride test

The clinical scenario of a child with recurrent sinusitis and lung infections along with a mutation in the CFTR gene is highly suggestive of cystic fibrosis. Sweat chloride test is the gold standard investigation for the confirmation of the cystic fibrosis.

Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the lungs, digestive system, and other organs. It is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, which leads to the production of thick and sticky mucus. The CFTR gene is on chromosome 7q. The most common CFTR mutation is F508 deletion. Features of CF include:

* Respiratory: Chronic cough, recurrent lung infections, bronchiectasis, and nasal polyps (Option A).

* Gastrointestinal: Pancreatic insufficiency, malabsorption, meconium ileus (Option C), and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies which cause bleeding diathesis (Option D).

* Sweat gland: Elevated sweat chloride levels.

* Reproductive: Infertility in males (due to absent vas deferens) and reduced fertility in females.

* Others: CF-related diabetes (CFRD), osteoporosis, and liver disease.

Diagnostic tests:
1. Immunoreactive trypsinogen for newborn screening of cystic fibrosis.
2. Sweat chloride test: Increased chloride concentration >60 mEq/L is diagnostic.
3. Genetic testing for CFTR gene mutations is the gold standard and should be done for all cases.
4. Nasal transepithelial potential difference can be estimated in equivocal cases.

The diagnosis is confirmed if both of the following criteria are met:

1. Presence of

* Clinical symptoms affecting at least one organ system (respiratory, gastrointestinal, or genitourinary) or

* Positive newborn screening or

* A sibling with cystic fibrosis.

2. Evidence of dysfunction of the CFTR gene by

* Two positive sweat chloride test results were obtained on separate days or

* Identification of two CFTR mutations by genetic testing or

* An abnormal measurement of nasal potential difference.

Cystic fibrosis requires a multidisciplinary approach to management. The correction of the defect can be done via lumacaftor, which corrects the misfolding and reverts the mutation defect, or ivacaftor, which potentiates CFTR channel opening and stimulates ion transport. End-stage pulmonary failure requires lung transplantation.

Note: Cholestasis is seen in CF. However, this is not due to biliary atresia, which is a congenital obstruction of the biliary tree.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with recurrent lung infections and sinusitis is diagnosed with Cystic Fibrosis. Which channel defect is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chloride channel

Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is caused by mutations in the CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene, which encodes a ATP-gated chloride ion channel present in the apical membranes of the epithelial cells. It regulates the flow of ions across epithelial membranes of sweat glands, respiratory airways, pancreatic ducts, etc. The defect leads to high salt concentrations in sweat and viscous luminal secretions in the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts.

The CFTR gene is on chromosome 7q. The most common CFTR mutation is F508 deletion. Features of CF include:

* Respiratory: Chronic cough, recurrent lung infections, bronchiectasis, and nasal polyps (Option A).

* Gastrointestinal: Pancreatic insufficiency, malabsorption, meconium ileus (Option C), and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies which cause bleeding diathesis (Option D).

* Sweat gland: Elevated sweat chloride levels.

* Reproductive: Infertility in males (due to absent vas deferens) and reduced fertility in females.

* Others: CF-related diabetes (CFRD), osteoporosis, and liver disease.

Diagnostic tests:
1. Immunoreactive trypsinogen for newborn screening of cystic fibrosis.
2. Sweat chloride test: Increased chloride concentration >60 mEq/L is diagnostic.
3. Genetic testing for CFTR gene mutations is the gold standard and should be done for all cases.
4. Nasal transepithelial potential difference can be estimated in equivocal cases.

The diagnosis is confirmed if both of the following criteria are met:

1. Presence of

* Clinical symptoms affecting at least one system (respiratory, genitourinary or gastrointestinal) or

* Positive screen during neonatal screening or

* A sibling with cystic fibrosis.

2. Evidence of dysfunction of the CFTR gene by

* Two positive sweat chloride test results obtained on different days or

* Identification of two CFTR mutations by genetic testing or

* Increased nasal potential difference.

Cystic fibrosis requires a multidisciplinary approach to management. The correction of the defect can be done via lumacaftor, which corrects the misfolding and reverts the mutation defect, or ivacaftor, which potentiates CFTR channel opening and stimulates ion transport. End-stage pulmonary failure requires lung transplantation.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn presents with a single palmar transverse crease and low-set ears. Which of the following is the most frequently associated with this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Down syndrome

A newborn with a single palmar transverse crease and low-set ears is most likely to have Down syndrome.

Down syndrome is a type of aneuploidy. It occurs due to the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21), leading to a total of 47 chromosomes instead of the normal 46.

There is a wide range of presentations. A few key features include characteristic facies such as a flat face, epicanthal folds, a small head, a flat nasal bridge, upward-slanting palpebral fissures, brushfield spots, a small nose, a protruding tongue, and small and low-set ears. Congenital heart defects can also be present.

Mechanism:

* Majority of cases – meiotic nondisjunction (95%) of chromosome 21 in the ovum

* Rarely – (4%) Robertsonian translocation of the long arm of chromosome 21 to another acrocentric chromosome (e.g., 22 or 14)

* Mosaic pattern: 1%

Clinical features of Down syndrome include (mnemonic: I C A PROBLEMS): Incurved or short fifth finger with clinodactyly, congenital heart disease, acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia/ alzheimer's disease/ atlantoaxial instability/ atresia of the duodenum, protruding tongue, round face, occiput flat/open wide fontanelle/open mouth, brachycephalic/Brushfield's spots, low (depressed) nasal bridge, epicanthal fold, low-set and dysplastic ears, mongoloid slant (oblique palpebral fissure), simian palmar crease and wider gap between first and second toes.

A score based on eight signs in the diagnosis of Down's syndrome in the newborn (Hall's criteria)

* Abundant neck skin

* Mouth corners turned downwards

* General hypotonia

* Flat face

* Dysplastic ear

* Epicanthic fold

* The gap between first and second toes

* Protruding tongue

The presence of the last 3 points is considered clinically proven Down syndrome.

Combined first-trimester screening consists of serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A (PAPP-A), and the measurement of the nuchal translucency (NT) on ultrasound. It is performed between 11 and 14 weeks of gestation.

The most common cause of intestinal obstruction in Down syndrome is duodenal atresia (double-bubble sign). Children with Down's syndrome have an increased risk of developing leukaemias, including acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). AML is more common during the first 3 years of life.

Other options:

Option A: Trisomy 18 results in Edward’s syndrome as a result of meiotic nondisjunction. The clinical features include micrognathia, low-set ears, prominent occiput, and rocker-bottom feet. Patients have significant hypertonia, including clenched hands with overlapping fingers. Cardiac anomalies (ventricular septal defects and patent ductus arteriosus) and gastrointestinal anomalies (Meckel’s diverticulum and malrotations) are common.

Option C: Turner syndrome (45, XO) results from the loss or structural abnormality of one X chromosome in females, leading to gonadal dysgenesis (non-functional ovaries). It is characterised by a short fourth metacarpal, a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, and short stature.

Option D: Trisomy 13 causes Patau syndrome. It is characterised by forebrain and midline facial abnormalities, including cleft lip, cleft palate, nasal defects, and a single central eye (“cyclops”). Other defects include polydactyly, renal defects, and congenital heart disease.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn, born to a diabetic mother, presents after 24 hours of life with a blood glucose level of 35 mg/dL. The baby is asymptomatic. What is the next best step in management?
options: Administer IV bolus of Hartmann solution
Initiate breastfeed and recheck blood glucose
Administer IV glucose and recheck blood glucose after 20 minutes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Initiate breastfeed and recheck blood glucose

In an asymptomatic newborn with hypoglycemia (<45 mg/dL), the first-line management is to initiate breastfeeding or provide expressed breast milk, followed by reassessment of glucose levels.

Infants of diabetic mothers are at a high risk of developing neonatal hypoglycemia. This is particularly applicable after the initial 2–3 hours of life. Blood sample is collected by heel prick. Babies showing plasma glucose <40 mg/dL on a reagent strip should be treated for hypoglycemia. Since reagent strips have high false-positive rates, a confirmation of hypoglycemia by a lab test is recommended.

Stepwise Management of Neonatal Hypoglycemia

* Initial Screening & Feeding

*

* All infants of diabetic mothers (IDMs) and other at-risk babies should be screened within 30 minutes of the first feed.

* Feeding should begin within 1 hour after birth.

* The target blood glucose is ≥40 mg/dL before feeds during the first 48 hours of life.

* Treatment is indicated if glucose <47 mg/dL in asymptomatic infants.

* First-Line Therapy for Asymptomatic Hypoglycemia

* Feeding is the initial treatment for asymptomatic hypoglycemia.

* Options include breastfeeding, formula, or oral gavage feeds.

* Dextrose gel can be used as a prophylactic alternative, but early oral feeds are equally effective.

* Recurrent or Persistent Hypoglycemia

* If hypoglycemia persists despite feeding, repeat feeds or IV glucose may be required.

* Infants with glucose <25 mg/dL in the first 4 hours after birth or <35 mg/dL between 4–24 hours should be started on IV glucose therapy, especially if symptomatic.

* IV Glucose Therapy

* Give a 200 mg/kg dextrose bolus (approximately 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose).

* To avoid a recurrence, administer glucose continuously via intravenous infusion (IV) at a rate of 4–8 mg/kg/min.

* Hypertonic (25%) glucose bolus injections should be avoided as they can result in rebound hypoglycemia from hyperinsulinemia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A teenage boy, who was previously raised as a girl, presents with primary amenorrhea and absence of secondary sexual characteristics. On examination, he is tall, has small testes, and shows gynecomastia. Serum testosterone levels are within normal range. Which of the following is the most likely genotype?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 47, XXY

The clinical scenario of a teenage boy who was previously raised as a girl, presenting with primary amenorrhea, tall stature, small testes, and gynecomastia is highly suggestive of Klinefelter syndrome; hence the most likely karyotype will be 47,XXY.

Klinefelter syndrome:

* Most common sex aneuploidy in males and  is the most common cause of infertility and hypogonadism in males

* Classically karyotype is 47, XXY. Other variants can have 48 XXXY; rarely, 49 XXXXY; or mosaics with some cells containing normal 46, XY and others 47, XXY

* Results from meiotic nondisjunction of sex chromosomes (mostly during 1st meiotic division)

Clinical features seen in Klinefelter’s syndrome are:

* Disproportionately long arms and legs,

* Gynecomastia

* Eunuchoid body habitus

* Mitral valve prolapse

* Mental retardation; IQ: 60-80,

* Minor developmental and learning disabilities,

* Lack of secondary sexual characteristics (due to a decrease in androgen production)

* Higher risk of breast carcinoma

* Testicular dysgenesis with small penis

* Infertility/azoospermia

* Type 2 diabetes mellitus

* Metabolic syndrome

* Higher risk of extragonadal germ cell tumors

Other options:

Option A: Turner syndrome (45, XO) results from the loss or structural abnormality of one X chromosome in females, leading to gonadal dysgenesis (non-functional ovaries). It is characterised by a short fourth metacarpal, a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, and short stature.

Option B: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) is a type of aneuploidy. It occurs due to the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21), leading to a total of 47 chromosomes instead of the normal 46. It is characterized by intellectual disability and distinctive physical features including a round face with flat occiput, protruding tongue, and flat nasal bridge. Characteristic facial features include oblique palpebral fissures (mongoloid slant), epicanthal folds, Brushfield's spots, and low-set dysplastic ears.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An 8-year-old child presents with enuresis. The parents mention that he had a fall from the bed once during early childhood, but there is no other significant medical history. There are no signs of urinary tract infection or neurological deficits. What is the best next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Behavioral modification

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of nocturnal enuresis. The next most appropriate management option is behavioral modification.

Nocturnal enuresis refers to the occurrence of involuntary voiding at night after 5 years of age. It may be a normal phenomenon in children up to 5 years of age.

If there are no daytime symptoms and physical and urine examinations are normal, then further evaluation for urinary tract pathology is not warranted. USG is done in an older child (usually >7 years) with enuresis or in those who do not respond to therapy.

Causes of Nocturnal Enuresis:

* Delayed maturation of cortical mechanisms that control voluntary micturition reflex.

* Defective sleep arousal, making it difficult for the child to awaken when the bladder is full.

* Reduced antidiuretic hormone production at night, leading to increased nocturnal urine output (nocturnal polyuria).

* Genetic predisposition, with associations noted on chromosomes 12 and 13, and a strong family history link.

* Bladder factors such as reduced capacity, overactivity, or lack of inhibition.

* Constipation, which can aggravate bladder dysfunction.

* Organic causes like urinary tract infection, obstructive uropathy, or sickle cell anemia nephropathy.

* Sleep disorders, including sleep-disordered breathing due to enlarged adenoids.

Treatment:

* Behavioral therapy with positive reinforcement and bladder alarms. It helps the child to deal with enuresis psychologically and motivates the child to void at night if he wakes up with a full bladder. Bedwetting alarms make a loud tone when they sense moisture. This helps to condition the child to wake at the sensation of a full bladder.

* Pharmacological therapy, including imipramine and desmopressin is reserved for cases resistant to behavioral therapy. It is intended to treat the symptoms of enuresis and thus is regarded as second-line and is not curative. In children above 5 years, Imipramine 25 mg at bedtime is effective for nocturnal enuresis. Intranasal desmopressin is also effective in the treatment of nocturnal enuresis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which action of a midwife is considered harmful to a newborn baby in the immediate postnatal period?
options: Cleaning the eyes with a wet sterile swab
Giving a bath immediately after birth
Helping to initiate breastfeeding within 1 hour
Placing the baby on the mother’s chest
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Giving a bath immediately after birth

The harmful practice in the immediate postnatal period is giving a bath immediately after birth. Newborn infants are highly prone to heat loss because their body surface area is relatively large, subcutaneous fat is thin, and heat production mechanisms are limited.

Bathing immediately after birth increases evaporative and conductive heat loss, which can cause hypothermia, metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia, and respiratory stress in the newborn. Thus, delaying the first bath is essential to avoid cold stress and to allow skin-to-skin contact and early breastfeeding, which help in maintaining warmth.

Heat loss occurs by four mechanisms:

* convection of heat energy to the cooler surrounding air

* conduction of heat to the colder materials touching the infant,

* heat radiation from the infant to other nearby cooler objects

* evaporation from skin and lungs.

Other options:

Option A: Cleaning the eyes with a wet sterile swab is a routine hygienic practice in newborn care.

Option C: Initiating breastfeeding within 1 hour is strongly recommended, since it provides colostrum, enhances immunity, and strengthens mother-infant bonding.

Option D: Skin-to-skin contact on the mother’s chest is a recommended practice for thermal regulation, bonding, and successful initiation of breastfeeding.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is associated with normal bone age compared to chronologic age?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Familial short stature

Here, the child with short stature has a normal US:LS ratio (1.1:1 at 12 years is within normal limits) and no other abnormalities, which makes familial short stature highly likely. Children with familial short stature have normal bone age compared to chronological age.

Familial short stature refers to short stature that is inherited within families. The parents are also shorter in stature, and there is usually no underlying pathology affecting growth and development. Therefore, bone age assessments are typically consistent with chronologic age in children with familial short stature.

Short stature can be defined as growth below the expected genetic potential or below -2 SD for age and sex. If a child's stature is less than -3 SD below the average for their age and gender, it is more likely to indicate pathological short stature. A child's height between -2 and -3 SD is more likely due to physiological, i.e. familial or constitutional short stature.

The 2 types of normal variants of short stature are as follows:

* Constitutional delay: Bone age < Chronological age

* Familial short stature: Bone age = Chronological age

Bone age is more than chronological age in precocious puberty. Bone age is less than chronological age in constitutional delay, undernutrition, endocrinologic short stature, and systemic illness.

Other options:

Option A: In constitutional delay, bone age is delayed compared to chronological age. These children have a delayed growth pattern and delayed puberty, but will eventually reach their genetic potential height.

Option C: Endocrinologic short stature entails conditions like growth hormone deficiency or hypothyroidism typically cause delayed bone age compared to chronologic age.

Option D: Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the gene encoding for fibroblast growth factor receptor type 3. It typically manifests at birth with short limbs, a long, narrow trunk, and a large head with midfacial hypoplasia and a prominent forehead (disproportionate short stature).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents for an antenatal check-up and is currently on lithium for her bipolar disorder. This drug must be stopped, due to the risk of development of which of the following conditions in the fetus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ebstein anomaly

Lithium should be stopped as it can cause an Ebstein anomaly in the newborn.

Ebstein anomaly is characterized by the downward displacement of the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which results in a thin-walled, low-pressure, “atrialized” segment of the right ventricle due to the anomalous attachment of the tricuspid leaflets.

Lithium can also cause macrocephaly as a teratogenic effect.

Lithium use in early pregnancy causes Ebstein anomaly in the fetus. Fetal lithium exposure is associated with neonatal goiter, CNS depression, hypotonia (floppy baby syndrome), and cardiac murmur.

questions.text: A 5-year-old child is brought to you with complaints of 18 episodes of loose stools in the last 24 hours and vomiting twice in the last 4 hours. The child is irritable but drinking fluids. The optimal therapy for this child is______
options: Intravenous fluid initially for 4 hours followed by oral fluids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Oral rehydration therapy with ORS

Oral rehydration therapy is the first line of treatment used in treating acute diarrheas due to all aetiologies, in all age groups, and in all countries and the recommended fluid is ORS.

Recommended formulation: Reduced osmolarity ORS solution, which has a reduced concentration of sodium (75 mmol/liter) and glucose (75 mmol/liter) helps in reducing the adverse effect of hypertonicity on net fluid absorption.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents to your outpatient department with the findings shown in the image below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kwashiorkor

The image showing flaky paint dermatosis is seen characteristically in Kwashiorkor.

Kwashiorkor is a form of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) characterized by edema and apathy. It usually affects infants and children, most often around the age of weaning till the age of 5.

Children with kwashiorkor have moon-shaped faces. Edema is most likely to appear first in the feet and then in the lower legs soon developing into generalized edema. Abdominal distension occurs with or without dilated bowel loops and hepatomegaly and fatty infiltrate.

Skin changes occur over the swollen limbs and include dark, crackled peeling patches with pale skin underneath forming patches of hyper and hypopigmentation called flaky paint dermatosis or crazy paving. The skin gets easily infected.

The hair is dull, brittle, sparse, and can easily be pulled out. It may lose its curl. In dark-haired children, the hair may turn pale or reddish. Alternating bands of light and normal color hair may be seen, known as the flag sign. Children are miserable, apathetic, and often refuse to eat. There is marked muscle atrophy and growth retardation.

Clinical features seen in marasmus are:

* Simian facies

* Lethargic and irritable,apathetic

* Bradycardia

* Thin, dry skin

* Thin and brittle hair,easily pluckable.

* hypotension, and hypothermia

* The reduction of buccal fat pad gives rise to a wrinkled or aged look, while the term “baggy pants appearance” describes sagging skin of the buttocks that hangs downward.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Identify the condition as shown below in the X-ray radiograph of a neonate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia

This rare anterior defect of the diaphragm is commonly referred to as Morgagni, retrosternal, or parasternal hernia. The above X-ray radiograph shows congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Note the presence of bowel loops in the chest and absence of bowel loops in the abdomen.

* Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a birth defect of the diaphragm.

* The most common type of CDH is a Bochdalek hernia; other types include Morgagni hernia, diaphragm eventration and central tendon defects of the diaphragm.

* Malformation of the diaphragm allows the abdominal organs to push into the chest cavity, hindering proper lung formation.

* CDH is a life-threatening pathology in infants and a major cause of death due to two complications: pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension.

Bochdalek hernia:

* The Bochdalek hernia, also known as a postero-lateral diaphragmatic hernia, is the most common manifestation of CDH, accounting for more than 95% of cases.

* In this instance the diaphragm abnormality is characterized by a hole in the postero-lateral corner of the diaphragm which allows passage of the abdominal viscera into the chest cavity.

Morgagni hernia:

* This rare anterior defect of the diaphragm is commonly referred to as Morgagni, retrosternal, or parasternal hernia.

* It accounts for approximately 2% of all CDH cases, and is characterized by herniation through the foramina of Morgagni which are located immediately adjacent and posterior to the xiphoid process of the sternum.

Diaphragm eventration:

* Diaphragmatic eventration refers to an abnormal contour of the diaphragmatic dome.

* Elevation of the affected portion of the diaphragm is usually seen as a smooth hump, while the remainder of the hemidiaphragm contour is normal.

* This rare type of CDH occurs because in the region of eventration the diaphragm is thinner, allowing the abdominal viscera to protrude upwards.

Treatment:

* The first step in management is orogastric tube placement and securing the airway (intubation).

* The baby will usually be immediately placed on a ventilator.

* Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) has been used as part of the treatment strategy in some cases.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Revised A 9 year old girl was brought to emergency room, with fever since 2 days, dyspnoea, drooling and inspiratory stridor. Lateral x ray neck findings were as seen below. Which is the most common organism( in India) which causes this condition in children?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Haemophilus influenza B

This is a case of acute epiglottitis since the child is having fever, dyspnoea, drooling and inspiratory stridor and the lateral x-ray neck shows thumb sign. The most common organism, overall in India in the case of acute epiglottitis, is Haemophilus influenza B.

Note:

The most common cause of epiglottitis:
In India - Hemophilus influenza.
Rest of the World - Strep. pneumonia.

Hemophilus influenza B is no longer the most common cause, overall in the world, after the widespread use of Hemophilus influenza vaccination. Streptococci including Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci and Streptococcus pneumoniae has become more prevalent in pediatric age group.

Though Nelson mentions that H.influenza is not the most common cause of this condition, the latest edition of O.P Ghai still mentions H.influenza as the most common cause of acute epiglottitis.

What it means is that, in India, even though cases of H. influenza are coming down due to increased vaccine coverage, still H. influenza remains the leading cause of acute epiglottitis in India.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome is defined as failure to achieve remission after _____ weeks when on a daily corticosteroid therapy regimen.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 4-6

Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome(SRNS) is defined as failure to achieve remission after 4-6 weeks of daily dose corticosteroid therapy.

Note:

The IAP guidelines mention SRNS as, remission not achieved even after 4-6 weeks of daily dose therapy with steroids.

Uptodate guidelines mention SRNS as remission not achieved even after 4 weeks of therapy at a dose of 60 mg/m2 per day.

According to Nelson and Ghai, it is defined as the absence of remission despite therapy with daily prednisolone at a dose of 2 mg/kg per day for 4 weeks and on alternate days for the next 4 weeks (meaning a total of 8 weeks).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The first primary tooth to erupt is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. lower central incisor

The lower (mandibular) central incisor is the first primary tooth to erupt at 5-7 months. However, the first secondary tooth to erupt is the first molar (maxillary or mandibular), at 6-7 years, followed by the lower central incisor.

* All primary teeth erupt by 1.5 – 2.5 years of age.

* All secondary teeth erupt by 17 -22 years of age.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The following image is of the most common cause of stridor in children. Identify it.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Laryngomalacia

The most common cause of stridor in children is laryngomalacia. It is also the most common congenital laryngeal anomaly.

Laryngomalacia:

It is the most common congenital abnormality of the larynx. It is characterized by excessive flaccidity of supraglottic larynx which is sucked in during inspiration producing stridor and sometimes cyanosis. The presentation is just after birth and subsides by 2 years. Stridor improves(decreases) in the prone position, worsens during feeding. The cry is normal.Laryngomalacia leads to the collapse of supraglottic structures during inspiration which results in airway obstruction.

Treatment of Laryngomalacia:

* Mostly, it self corrects by 2 years of age.

* Tracheostomy may be required for some cases of severe respiratory obstruction.

* Supraglottoplasty is required in cases of severe laryngomalacia.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. B

Lab investigations in vitamin D-dependent rickets will reveal normal/decreased serum calcium, decreased phosphorous, elevated PTH, and increased ALP levels.

Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1 is due to 1 α hydroxylase deficiency resulting in decreased hydroxylation of 25 hydroxy vitamin D leading to increased levels of 25 OH vitamin D and decreased levels of 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D.

Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 2 is due to the resistance of the vitamin D receptors to vitamin D in both bone and intestine. Here, the levels of 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D are raised, but despite this, the serum calcium and phosphate levels are low due to the lack of action of vitamin D.

Decreased vitamin D leads to decreased calcium and phosphate due to reduced absorption. The decreased calcium stimulates increased PTH production. PTH tries to normalise the calcium and further decreases the phosphate because of renal elimination. ALP level is increased as it is involved in bone mineralization.

X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (XLH) occurs because of a defect in the PHEX gene. Since the PHEX gene is responsible for inactivating FGF-23, there is an increased FGF-23 in XLH. Increased FGF-23 inhibits phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule of the kidney and causes phosphaturia. It also inhibits 1-α-hydroxylase, leading to decreased production of activated vitamin D.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following milestones in an infant is achieved at the earliest?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ulnar palmar grasp

The milestone which is achieved earliest in the above options is ulnar palmar grasp which is seen by 6 months of age.

Developmental progression of the grasp:

* At 6 months, the infant reaches and holds a larger object in a crude manner using the ulnar aspect of his hand-ulnar palmar grasp.

* At 8-9 months, the object is grasped by the radial side of the palm-radial palmar grasp.

* At 9 months, the immature pincer grasp develops. The object is secured between the adducted thumb and the extended index finger.

* At 12 months, the mature pincer grasp develops. The object is secured between the opposed thumb and the tip of the index finger.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old female child is brought to the OPD with cramping abdominal pain. On examination, she is found to have rashes on the back of her legs, buttocks and the extensor surface of her forearms. Laboratory analysis reveals proteinuria and microscopic hematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Henoch-Schönlein purpura

The diagnosis in this child with rash, abdominal pain and nephritis is Henoch-Schönlein purpura.

Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP), also known as IgA vasculitis, is a common small vessel vasculitis in childhood. It is a type III hypersensitivity reaction characterized by the deposition of IgA in the small vessels of the skin, joints, gastrointestinal tract, and kidney, resulting in vasculitis

Children usually present with the following features:

* Palpable purpura is symmetric and occurs in the lower extremities, extensor aspect of the upper limbs, and buttocks.

* Arthralgia and arthritis- commonly affecting hip, knee, or ankle joints.

* Gastrointestinal manifestations like abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, and intussusception.

* About 30% of the patients with HSP develop renal manifestations, presenting as microscopic hematuria, hypertension, and progressive glomerulonephritis.

Laboratory studies generally show mild leukocytosis, a normal platelet count, and occasionally eosinophilia. Serum complement components are normal.

Most clinical features of IgA vasculitis are self-limiting and resolve in a few days. Supportive management with the maintenance of hydration and pain relief is done. Patients developing nephritis due to IgA vasculitis may need aggressive management with immunosuppressants.

The image given below shows palpable purpura in the lower limbs seen in HSP.

Correct answer: A. Kwashiorkar

A poor diet history (rice water) and a swollen belly are suggestive of Kwashiorkor.

questions.text: A mother complains that her child is reluctant when it comes to taking feeds appropriately. Her 15-month-old boy has a length-for-age ≤ –2 SD below the median. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Correct answer: D. Moderate stunting

This child with a length-for-age ≤ –2 SD below the median is having moderate stunting.

The anthropometric measures used are weight for age, height for age, weight for height, BMI, and mid-upper arm circumference.

* Low weight for height, or wasting, indicates acute malnutrition. It is also called as wasting as a result of a recent food deficit or an acute illness such as diarrhea.

* High weight-for-height indicates overweight.

* Low height-for-age, or stunting, indicates chronic malnutrition. This is the best indicator of long-term nutritional status in the pediatric population.

* Low weight for age, or underweight indicates acute or chronic malnutrition. It does not differentiate between wasting and stunting. Hence, it has limited clinical significance.

SD - Standard deviation (from the median)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A young boy with fatigue is found to have a haemoglobin of 9 g/dl. Peripheral smear showed sickle-shaped RBCs. What is the next best step in managing this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Blood transfusion

The given clinical scenario and image are diagnostic of sickle cell anemia. The next best step is blood transfusion.

Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to the T-to-A point mutation in the sixth codon of the β-globin gene. This results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. This causes the production of sickle-shaped red blood cells due to the polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbS).

The clinical features of sickle cell disease are due to the tendency of HbS molecules to stack into polymers when deoxygenated. The features are:

* Moderately severe hemolytic anemia with jaundice.

* Painful bone crisis- hand-foot syndrome or dactylitis of the bones of hands and feet.

* Acute chest syndrome typically presents with fever, cough, chest pain, and pulmonary infiltrates.

* Hyposthenuria- inability to concentrate urine.

* Aplastic crisis stems from the infection of red cell progenitors by parvovirus B19, which causes a transient cessation of erythropoiesis and a sudden worsening of the anemia.

* Spleen

* In children- splenic sequestration crises occur which results in splenomegaly due to red pulp congestion.

* Adolescence or early adulthood- autosplenectomy occurs due to splenic infarction, fibrosis, and progressive shrinkage.

* Increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms like pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenza septicemia, but can be reduced by vaccination and prophylactic antibiotics.

* Other clinical features- priapism, leg ulcers, stroke, retinopathy, pigment gallstones, and growth retardation.

The diagnosis is suggested by the clinical findings, the presence of irreversibly sickled RBCs on peripheral smear, and hemoglobin electrophoresis showing increased HbA2, HbF, and S spike.

Disease-modifying drugs such as hydroxyurea can be given to patients with sickle cell anemia since it reduces the incidence of adverse vaso-occlusive vents. Blood transfusions are used to treat and prevent complications of sickle cell disease, including preparation for surgery, symptomatic anemia, acute stroke, multi-organ failure and acute chest syndrome

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Revised A 1.5-year-old child is brought to the hospital with a history of breathlessness, body temperature of less than 37 degrees, cough, and cold. On examination, the respiratory rate was 46/min, and there were no chest retractions. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Administer IV antibiotics and refer to higher centre
Administer oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Administer oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home

This child with a respiratory rate of 46 breaths/min has tachypnea/fast breathing without any danger signs has pneumonia according to IMNCI guidelines. The next best step of management is to administer oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home.

The treatment for pneumonia for a child between 2 months and 5 years of age is oral amoxicillin and home care advice.

The revised classification of acute respiratory infections is simplified to include only two categories of pneumonia:

* Cough and cold, no pneumonia - requires home remedy

* Pneumonia - with fast breathing and/or chest indrawing, which requires home therapy with oral amoxicillin.

* Severe pneumonia - pneumonia with any general danger sign, which requires a referral and injectable therapy.

Danger signs:

* Not able to drink

* Persistent vomiting

* Convulsions, lethargic or unconscious

* Stridor in a calm child

* Severe malnutrition

Tachypnea or Fast breathing is defined based on the age and respiratory rate:

Age of child
Rate

<2 months
60 breaths/min

2-12 months
50 breaths/min

1-5 years
40 breaths/min

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the most common cause of seizures in a 2-year-old child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Febrile seizures

The most common cause of seizures in the said age group is febrile seizures.

Febrile seizures are defined as seizures that:

Occur between the age of 6 to 60 months
Associated with a temperature of ≥38°C (100.4°F)
Do not occur as a result of central nervous system infections or any metabolic imbalance.
Occur without a history of afebrile seizures in the past.

Depending on the duration and recurrence of the febrile seizure, they are classified as follows:

Simple febrile seizure
Complex febrile seizures
Febrile status epilepticus

Generalised, tonic-clonic seizure
Focal seizure
Febrile seizure

Last for ≤15 minutes, without another episode in 24 hours
Lasts >15 minutes and/or recurs in 24 hours
Duration of >30 minutes

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the pattern of inheritance in neural tube defects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Multifactorial inheritance

The pattern of inheritance in neural tube defects(NTDs) is multifactorial inheritance.

Multifactorial inheritance refers to traits that are caused by a combination of inherited, environmental, and stochastic factors. NTDs and a number of other congenital malformations, such as cleft lip and palate, can recur in families, but inheritance for the majority of affected individuals does not occur in a straightforward, mendelian inheritance pattern. In this situation, multiple genes and environmental factors together likely contribute to the pathogenesis.

These include the following:

Children (congenital malformation)

Adults

Pyloric stenosis

Neural tube defects

Congenital heart defects

Congenital dislocation of hip

Cleft lip and cleft palate

Diabetes Mellitus

Hypertension

Coronary heart disease

Gout

Schizophrenia

Pearl PF1857: Inheritance pattern of important diseases

Autosomal dominant

Autosomal recessive

HEAVy DOMINANT
