• Esophageal foreign body: Sudden onset, drooling, dysphagia, respiratory distress, no fever or cough.
• Acute epiglottitis: High fever, toxic appearance, drooling, tripod position, muffled (“hot potato”) voice.
• Croup: Barking cough, hoarseness, inspiratory stridor, usually preceded by a viral prodrome.
• Bronchiolitis: Fever, cough, wheezing, tachypnea in infants, typically following an upper respiratory tract infection.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-month-old infant presents with acute watery diarrhea and mild dehydration. Along with oral rehydration therapy, oral zinc supplementation is initiated. Which of the following is the standard recommended daily dose of elemental zinc for this infant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 10 mg

Zinc supplementation is recommended by the WHO and UNICEF for all children with acute diarrhea, as it reduces the duration and severity of diarrhea and decreases the risk of subsequent diarrheal episodes.

Recommended elemental zinc dose:

• Infants <6 months: 10 mg once daily for 14 days
• Children ≥6 months: 20 mg once daily for 14 days

Zinc should be given in addition to oral rehydration solution (ORS) and continued for the full 14-day course, even if diarrhea resolves earlier.

Why not the other options?

• A. 6 mg: Not a recommended therapeutic dose.
• B. 7 mg: Not recommended in standard guidelines.
• D. 20 mg: Appropriate for children ≥6 months, not for a 4-month-old infant.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and acute diarrhea is started on ReSoMal for oral rehydration. Compared with standard WHO low-osmolarity ORS, ReSoMal contains:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lower sodium and higher potassium

• ReSoMal (Rehydration Solution for Malnutrition) is specially formulated for children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM).
• Children with SAM have excess total body sodium but marked intracellular potassium deficiency.
• Therefore, ReSoMal contains:

• Lower sodium (45 mmol/L vs 75 mmol/L in low-osmolar ORS)
• Higher potassium (40 mmol/L vs 20 mmol/L)

• It also contains more glucose and added magnesium, zinc, copper, and other micronutrients.
• ReSoMal helps prevent sodium overload while correcting potassium depletion.
• Exception: In SAM with profuse watery diarrhea or suspected cholera, standard low-osmolarity ORS is preferred because ReSoMal may not adequately replace sodium losses.
• Rehydration should be slow and carefully monitored to avoid heart failure.

High-yield values

| Component | ReSoMal | Low-osmolar ORS

| --------- | ------- | ---------------

| Sodium | 45 mmol/L | 75 mmol/L

| Potassium | 40 mmol/L | 20 mmol/L

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn delivered at 37 weeks gestation and birth weight 2.7 kg presents at 12 h of life with bilious vomiting. On examination, RR is 36/m, HR is 110/m, CRT is <3s, and there is abdominal distention. Abdominal radiograph reveals multiple air-fluid levels with absent distal gas pattern. The most likely etiology is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Jejunal-ileal atresia

• The neonate presents with early-onset bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and multiple air-fluid levels with absent distal bowel gas, which strongly suggests intestinal obstruction due to jejunoileal atresia.
• Jejunoileal atresia is a congenital intestinal obstruction that typically presents in the neonatal period with bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and failure to pass meconium. Abdominal radiography shows multiple dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels and little or no distal bowel gas.

Why not the other options?

• A. Malrotation with volvulus: Causes bilious vomiting, often acutely, but the radiograph may show nonspecific obstruction; multiple air-fluid levels with complete absence of distal gas is more suggestive of intestinal atresia.
• B. Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: Produces non-bilious projectile vomiting, typically beginning at 2–8 weeks, not at 12 hours of life.
• D. Necrotizing enterocolitis: Usually occurs in preterm or sick neonates, typically after feeds have been established; abdominal X-ray classically shows pneumatosis intestinalis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A term newborn has not passed meconium within 48 hours of birth. Abdomen is distended, and digital rectal examination produces an explosive passage of stool and flatus. What is the gold standard investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Rectal biopsy showing presence of ganglion cells
Barium enema showing narrow distal segment
Rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells
Anorectal manometry showing absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells

Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon) should be suspected in a newborn with:

• Failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life
• Abdominal distension
• Bilious vomiting (may occur)
• Explosive passage of stool and flatus after digital rectal examination (squirt sign)

The gold standard for diagnosis is a rectal suction biopsy demonstrating:

• Absence of ganglion cells in the submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses
• Hypertrophied nerve trunks
• Increased acetylcholinesterase-positive nerve fibers

Role of other investigations

• Contrast (barium) enema: Shows a narrow aganglionic distal segment with a dilated proximal colon (transition zone); useful as a screening investigation but not confirmatory.
• Anorectal manometry: Demonstrates absence of the rectoanal inhibitory reflex (RAIR); useful in older infants and children but not the gold standard.
• Rectal biopsy showing presence of ganglion cells: Rules out Hirschsprung disease.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All of the following statements regarding Hirschsprung disease are true except:
options: Failure of migration of ganglion cells.
Colonic segment proximal to the affected area is constricted.
Failure of passage of meconium in the postnatal period.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Colonic segment proximal to the affected area is constricted.

Hirschsprung disease is caused by failure of neural crest cell migration, leading to absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel (aganglionosis). This results in loss of coordinated peristalsis and functional obstruction.

Key concepts:

• The affected distal segment is spastic and constricted due to aganglionosis
• The proximal segment becomes dilated due to accumulation of intestinal contents (megacolon)
• Newborns typically present with failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours
• There is absence of the rectoanal inhibitory reflex

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding the management of trachea-esophageal fistula in neonates: 1. The baby should be nursed in prone position. 2. The neonate should be kept nil per orally and started on intravenous fluids. 3. The neonate needs continuous oral suction using a slow suction device. 4. Surgery should be planned once the neonate attains 2.5 kg weight. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2 and 3 only

• Statement 1. The baby should be nursed in prone position: incorrect. The neonate should be nursed propped-up (head elevated 30–40°), not prone. This position reduces reflux of gastric contents through the distal fistula into the tracheobronchial tree and minimizes pooling/aspiration of secretions from the proximal esophageal pouch.
• Statement 2. The neonate should be kept nil per orally and started on intravenous fluids: Correct. Oral feeding is withheld to prevent aspiration through the fistula/proximal pouch, and hydration is maintained intravenously pending surgery.
• Statement 3. The neonate needs continuous oral suction using a slow suction device: Correct. A Replogle tube (double-lumen) is placed in the proximal pouch on continuous gentle/low suction to clear pooled saliva and secretions, preventing overflow aspiration into the airway.
• Statement 4. Surgery should be planned once the neonate attains 2.5 kg weight: Incorrect. This reflects outdated teaching. Modern management does not mandate delaying surgery until a specific weight threshold; timing is guided by the infant's overall clinical stability, associated anomalies, and type of TEF rather than a fixed weight cutoff. Even low-birth-weight neonates are managed early (with staged approaches if unstable), not simply held until 2.5 kg.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: In a mildly dehydrated child, which of the following is the recommended management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. ORS and continue breastfeeding

The cornerstone of treatment for mild to moderate dehydration due to acute diarrhea is oral rehydration solution (ORS) along with continued breastfeeding or age-appropriate feeding.

WHO Plan B (Some dehydration):

• Give ORS 75 mL/kg over 4 hours
• Reassess hydration status after 4 hours
• Replace ongoing stool losses with additional ORS
• Continue breastfeeding throughout treatment
• Add zinc supplementation for 14 days

Intravenous fluids (Ringer lactate or normal saline) are reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or when the child cannot tolerate oral fluids (persistent vomiting, ileus, altered consciousness).

Why not the other options?

• A. Normal saline: Used for severe dehydration/shock, not first-line for mild or moderate dehydration.
• B. Ringer lactate: Preferred IV fluid for severe dehydration (WHO Plan C), but unnecessary if ORS can be given.
• C. Normal saline in 5% dextrose: Not recommended for initial rehydration in acute diarrheal dehydration.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the fluid of choice in pediatric patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. DNS

In pediatric patients, maintenance fluid therapy should provide both water and glucose to prevent hypoglycemia and ketosis; hence dextrose-containing fluids are commonly used.

• DNS (dextrose normal saline) provides glucose along with sodium, making it suitable for many pediatric maintenance needs
• Children have limited glycogen stores and are prone to hypoglycemia during illness or fasting
• Pure crystalloids like normal saline or Ringer lactate do not provide glucose
• 5% dextrose alone lacks electrolytes and is not appropriate for routine use
• In emergency resuscitation (e.g., shock), isotonic fluids like normal saline are preferred initially

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following are approximate daily requirements of the common electrolytes in an adult? 1. Sodium 50–90 mM/day 2. Calcium 1 mM/day 3. Potassium 50 mM/day 4. Magnesium 1 mM/day Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Adequate daily electrolyte requirements are essential for maintaining fluid balance, neuromuscular function, acid-base homeostasis, and cellular metabolism. In hospitalized adults, these requirements are considered while prescribing maintenance intravenous fluids.

• 1. Sodium 50–90 mM/day ✓

• The approximate daily sodium requirement in adults is 50–100 mmol/day.

• 2. Calcium 1 mM/day ✗

• Adults require approximately 5–10 mmol/day of calcium (about 100–200 mg elemental calcium intravenously if required), not 1 mmol/day.

• 3. Potassium 50 mM/day ✓

• The normal daily potassium requirement is approximately 40–80 mmol/day, with 50 mmol/day being an accepted average.

• 4. Magnesium 1 mM/day ✓

• The approximate daily magnesium requirement is 0.5–1 mmol/day, making 1 mmol/day an acceptable value.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is the best indicator of some dehydration?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Irritable status

Some dehydration” is diagnosed when ≥2 of the following are present:

• Restless / irritable  (early & sensitive sign)
• Sunken eyes
• Thirsty, drinks eagerly
• Skin pinch goes back slowly

Why Irritability is BEST indicator

• Reflects early CNS response to dehydration
• Appears before severe signs
• More reliable clinically than isolated physical signs

| Parameters | No Dehydration | Some Dehydration

| ---------- | -------------- | ----------------

| Appearance | Well, alert | Restless, irritable

| Eyes | Normal | Sunken

| Thirst | Drinks normally,
not thirsty | Thirsty, drinks eagerly

| Skin pinch | Goes back quickly
(˂1 second ) | Goes back slowly
(1 second)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which one of the following statements regarding the composition of common crystalloid solutions is correct?
options: Normal saline contains 100 mEq/L of Na
Hartmann’s solution contains 111 mEq/L of Cl
Normal saline contains 130 mEq/L of Cl
Hartmann’s solution contains 111 mEq/L of Na
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hartmann’s solution contains 111 mEq/L of Cl

Hartmann’s solution (Lactated Ringer’s) is a balanced crystalloid whose electrolyte composition closely resembles plasma.

Why not the other options?

• A. Normal saline contains 100 mEq/L of Na+: Normal saline contains 154 mEq/L of Na⁺.
• C. Normal saline contains 130 mEq/L of Cl⁻: Normal saline contains 154 mEq/L of Cl⁻.
• D. Hartmann’s solution contains 111 mEq/L of Na⁺: Hartmann’s contains 131 mEq/L of Na⁺.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which statement is incorrect regarding a child presenting with abdominal pain and bloating after consuming a milk-containing product?
options: He is likely to have a deficiency of the enzyme lactase
Steatorrhea is likely to be associated.
Skim milk will make his symptoms worse than whole milk.
Hydrogen Breath test is a sensitive test to diagnose the condition.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Steatorrhea is likely to be associated.

This child most likely has lactose intolerance, a condition caused by lactase deficiency in the brush border of the small intestine. Undigested lactose reaches the colon, where it is fermented by bacteria, producing gas and osmotic diarrhea.

Steatorrhea (fatty, greasy stools) is not a feature of isolated lactose intolerance because fat digestion and absorption remain normal. Steatorrhea suggests a disorder causing fat malabsorption, such as celiac disease, pancreatic insufficiency, or giardiasis.

Explanation of Other Options:

A. He is likely to have a deficiency of the enzyme lactase

• Lactase deficiency is the underlying cause of lactose intolerance.

C. Skim milk will make his symptoms worse than whole milk

• Skim milk contains the same amount of lactose as whole milk but lacks fat, which normally delays gastric emptying.
• Therefore, lactose reaches the intestine more rapidly, potentially worsening symptoms.

D. Hydrogen Breath Test is a sensitive test to diagnose the condition

• It is the preferred non-invasive test.
• Undigested lactose is fermented by colonic bacteria, producing hydrogen that is detected in expired air.
